1108-the-two-gentlemen-of-verona:
Valentine and Proteus, two young gentlemen of Verona, fall out over love when Proteus, sent to Milan, betrays his friend and woos Valentine's lady, Silvia. William Shakespeare's early comedy adds a forest of outlaws, a cross-dressed heroine, and Launce with his scene-stealing dog Crab.

Julia, Proteus's first love, follows him in disguise and watches his faithlessness firsthand. The play ends in a tangle of pardons that modern readers find hasty, but its wit and its songs still charm. It shows Shakespeare testing the comic forms he would soon master.
11367-a-history-of-china:
Wolfram Eberhard's History of China surveys Chinese history from prehistory through the present day in twelve chapters. Early sections treat Peking Man, Yang-shao and Lung-shan cultures, the Shang dynasty, Chou feudalism, contending states, Ch'in unification, and. Han rule, followed by divisions, Sui and T'ang empires, absolutism, the Republic of 1912 to 1948, and present-day China. A transcriber's note explains diacritical marks and spelling adjustments.

Eberhard, a sociologist as well as historian, stresses social structure, material culture, and long patterns over dynastic anecdote. The book was a standard mid-century introduction in English. Students still use it as a broad framework, even where archaeology and scholarship have since revised its details.
12577-strange-true-stories-of-louisiana:
George W. Cable's 1890 Strange True Stories of Louisiana, illustrated and dedicated to James Birney Guthrie, explains how he got his tales. It then tells of a young aunt with white hair and the adventures of Françoise and Suzanne. Two sisters, an expedition, embarkation, Alix Carpentier, a fight with wild nature down Bayou Plaquemine, a twice-married countess and a bolero dance follow.

A bad storm in a bad place, Maggie and other stories complete the Louisiana picture. Cable, author of The Grandissimes, writes from Creole New Orleans and bayou country, mixing history, legend and local colour. The book offers true stories that read like romance, told by a writer who knew Louisiana's peoples and past.
13071-helena:
Mrs. Humphry Ward's 1919 novel Helena opens with Lord Buntingford scorning a Middle Class Defence League circular. The league warns that the middle classes, fewer but better educated, hold England's greatness, and must not be snuffed out without a struggle. Buntingford, pacing his shabby library, doubts the claim and wonders aloud.

The story then follows Helena, Geoffrey, Philip Buntingford, and Cynthia Welwyn, an unmarried woman who feels she has fallen between two stools. Sir Richard Watson has proposed to Cynthia twice, but she loves her cousin Philip more. Ward sets young love against post-war class anxiety, and her novel reads as a study of rank, marriage, and change in England after the war.
13567-clementina:
A. E. W. Mason's 1901 romance Clementina opens with a lady asking in Italian for a postillion, and follows Wogan through chance meetings, bad news, proposals, and hiding places better than a window curtain. A dishonest landlord should avoid white paint, Wogan is mistaken for a more notable man, and a month of waiting follows at Schlestadt.

Night streets ring with footsteps, windows show shadows growing to monstrous giants and shrinking to pygmies. A walled town modelled on Aigues Mortes hides its chimneys behind a perfect circle of wall. Caravans and traders crowd its gates into ringing streets, while merchants creep across the flat, silent plain outside. Mason writes Jacobite adventure with colour and pace.
13940-the-problem-of-china:
Bertrand Russell published The Problem of China in 1922 after visiting the country. He opens with a Taoist parable of Shû, Hû, and Chaos, who gain seven orifices and die for the gift. Russell then studies China's politics, industry, education, and foreign relations. He weighs Japan, Britain, America, and Russia as powers pressing on China.

Russell argues China may recover and retain liberty, despite a possible consortium of Japan and Western powers. He doubts Japan and the West can cooperate for long. His tone is clear, sceptical, and humane. The book blends travel observation with political analysis. It remains a landmark of early twentieth-century writing on China.
14345-the-fight-for-the-republic-in-chin:
B. L. Putnam Weale wrote this 1918 study of China's fight for a republic, with 28 pictures. It runs from the Manchu abdication through Yuan Shih-kai's rule, the Twenty-One Demands, and the monarchist plot. Weale, a Peking watcher, writes from close knowledge of courts and treaties. The book treats Japan's pressure as a central factor. It aims to explain a republic born in storm.

A memorandum by Dr. Goodnow argues that a country's government fits its history, habits, and wealth, not the people's choice alone. An unsuited form may stand a while, but a better suited system will take its place. Later chapters weigh war with Germany as a path to cancel old treaties and consular rights. China, Weale notes, had already earned German ill will by breaking ties. The book gives a sharp, firsthand view of a republic at risk.
1437-juana:
Balzac's tale, also called The Maranas, opens during the French siege of Tarragona in Spain. Amid the disorder of a captured town, a young woman named Juana, of mixed Spanish and Moorish blood, becomes the centre of a struggle between love, honour. The harsh code of war.

Soldiers, monks, and kin press rival claims on her future, and Juana's own choice carries a heavy price. The story blends battle scenes with a close study of pride and passion. It is a short, intense romance of Spain under occupation, where private feeling meets public violence.
14370-zanetto-and-cavalleria-rusticana:
This souvenir libretto pairs two one-act operas by Pietro Mascagni, with Italian text and English translation side by side. Zanetto, a short pastoral piece, and Cavalleria rusticana, the Sicilian tragedy that made Mascagni famous, were sold together for opera audiences.

In Zanetto, the innkeeper Silvia, courted by many suitors, meets a wandering minstrel who stirs her heart. In Cavalleria, jealousy over Santuzza and Turiddu ends in a duel on Easter morning. The booklet gives plots, characters, and full sung text, a handy guide for listeners in the theater. Both operas remain staples of the verismo repertory today.
14427-true-love-s-reward-a-sequel-to-mon:
This 1891 sequel continues Mrs. Georgie Sheldon's Mona, picking up where the earlier novel left its heroine's mystery unsolved. Mrs. Montague, suspicious and sharp-tongued, again confronts Mona in her room.

New discoveries deepen the puzzle: a robe in a wardrobe, a torn skirt, and a scrap of cloth that fits the rent exactly, proving a link Mona had only guessed. Suitors press their claims while Mona guards her secret. Sheldon keeps the revelations coming chapter by chapter, and the sequel rewards readers who followed Mona's first adventures to their romantic close.
14492-notable-women-of-modern-china:
Margaret E. Burton profiled leading Chinese women of the early twentieth century in this volume from Fleming H. Revell, following her earlier book on women's education in China. Burton wrote as a missionary educator with close knowledge of her subjects.

The biographies include Dr. Hü King Eng, a physician trained abroad, and other teachers, doctors, and reformers who built schools and hospitals amid political upheaval. Burton stresses their courage, faith, and service to a changing nation. The book offers a window on Chinese women entering public life, told with admiration and period missionary framing.
1450-pollyanna:
Eleanor H. Porter's beloved novel brings Pollyanna Whittier, an orphan of eleven, to live with her stern Aunt Polly in a Vermont town. Sent to a little attic room, Pollyanna answers every hardship with the glad game she learned from her father: find something to be glad about in any trouble.

Her cheer spreads through the town, softening a sick neighbour, a lonely minister, and at last Aunt Polly herself. When an accident tests her own gladness, the town returns the gift. The book is simple, warm, and hopeful, and its heroine's name has entered the language for stubborn optimism.
1509-the-two-gentlemen-of-verona:
Shakespeare's early comedy follows two friends from Verona: Valentine, who leaves for Milan and loves Silvia, and Proteus, who follows, forgets his Julia, and pursues Silvia himself. Julia, in disguise as a page, watches her lover's betrayal, and the plot tangles through forests, outlaws, and a faithful dog.

Forgiveness at the close, swift and startling, restores friendship and love, though modern readers may question its ease. The play's charm lies in its youth and its lyric grace. It is Shakespeare's first comedy of love and friendship, and a rehearsal for greater works to come.
15125-the-awakening-of-china:
W. A. P. Martin, former president of the Chinese Imperial University, surveys China in this large early twentieth-century study. Part one tours the provinces, from Kwangtung to Manchuria, Mongolia, and Tibet. Part two traces history from mythic times through Chou, Han, Tang, Sung, and Ming to the Manchu dynasty.

Part three, China in transformation, treats the opening of China as a drama, starting with the Opium War and the Taiping rising. Martin writes as a longtime resident and educator, with sympathy and a missionary's outlook. The book remains a useful, if dated, guide to how Western observers saw a changing China.
15246-the-tragedy-of-st-helena:
Walter Runciman's 1911 book argues that Napoleon, Boney to British sailors, was ill-treated on St. Helena. He opens with a sailors' song on the theme. He then recalls buying Scott's Life of Napoleon on a bookstall and finding, against his own views, that Scott's evidence pointed the same way. The tragedy is exile and a broken heart.

Runciman, a seaman author, writes as a convert to sympathy, not as a scholar, and his case is partisan. The book shows how popular feeling about Napoleon shifted in Britain. Readers of Napoleonic history will find it a lively, opinionated voice from the sea.
15250-myths-and-legends-of-china:
E. T. C. Werner, a retired British consul at Foochow and member of China's historiographical bureau, wrote this 1922 survey of Chinese myth. Chapters move from the sociology of the Chinese and the nature of myth to P'an Ku and creation, the gods, stars, thunder, waters, fire, and epidemics. The Goddess of Mercy and the Eight Immortals follow.

Later chapters tell how the Monkey became a god, fox legends, and a battle of the gods, with notes on pronouncing Chinese words. Werner writes for Western readers new to the subject, with care and respect. The book remains a classic, readable guide to China's rich mythic world.
15274-the-girl-from-montana:
Grace Livingston Hill's 1922 novel, The Girl from Montana, follows a young woman from the West into a world of city manners, love, and faith. Hill's long list of books fronts the volume, from April Gold and The Honor Girl to Marigold and The Red Signal. Montana roots set her heroine apart.

Through trials, romance, and moral choices, the girl holds to pluck and Christian principle, in Hill's warm, popular style. The novel offers clean, earnest entertainment for readers who liked early twentieth-century inspirational fiction. Its Western freshness still gives the story charm.
15455-life-s-progress-through-the-passio:
An anonymous London author, known only as the writer of The Fortunate Foundlings, published this novel in 1748, printed by T. Gardner in the Strand. Its heroine is Natura, and its plan is laid out chapter by chapter: how the passions show themselves from birth, grow with reason, and take hold of the mind. The book treats a life as a moral experiment.

Early chapters trace Natura's fond, innocent affection for Delia, and later ones follow love, pride, and other passions through youth and grown life. The author uses story to argue a point: our senses and our constitution shape us, but reason must learn to govern feeling. As an eighteenth-century novel of feeling, it joins adventure to conduct, and it rewards readers curious about how the early novel taught its readers to live.
17022-the-first-discovery-of-australia-a:
George Collingridge de Tourcey wrote this history of the first discovery of Australia and New Guinea. It is the narrative of Portuguese and Spanish discoveries in Australasian regions between 1492 and 1606, with descriptions of old charts, first published in 1906. Contents run from a quest for the Spice Islands into voyages to Papua and Ribero's map. Villalobos, the first map of New Guinea, and Jave-la-Grande as first map of Australia follow. Desceliers' and Desliens' maps appear. Mendana and Sarmiento finding the Solomons close the set.

Collingridge weighs old maps and voyages with care, arguing for early Iberian claims in Australia's discovery. His book mixes narrative with map study, quoting Camoens at its head. Readers of discovery history will find a detailed, partisan but learned account, useful for its charts and its challenge to English-first tales.
18842-elizabethan-sonnet-cycles-delia-di:
Martha Foote Crow edited this 1896 volume of Elizabethan sonnet cycles for Kegan Paul, Trench, Trübner of London. It pairs Samuel Daniel's Delia with Henry Constable's Diana, two sequences from the great age of the English sonnet.

Crow's introduction calls Daniel's series a prototype of Shakespeare's, sharing themes of beauty's fleetness, truth, the lover's woes, and the hope of immortality in verse. Both poets drew on Petrarch and a common store of conceits, and Daniel's cruel fair echoes the Italian master in sighs, golden hair, and darting eyes. The volume lets readers compare two sonneteers side by side, with Shakespeare's echoes sounding behind them.
19172-an-australian-in-china:
George Ernest Morrison, an Australian doctor, wrote this narrative of a quiet journey across China to Burma, here in its third edition of 1902. He dedicates the book to John Chiene, the Edinburgh surgeon who gave him back the power to walk. The journey is overland, slow, and close to daily life.

At Hankow he counts a swarm of missions, from London and American societies to French, Italian, and Spanish orders, divided by sect yet alike in comfort. Costs, converts, and rival claims fill his notes. Readers get a sharp, observant travel account of late Qing China through Australian eyes.
2076-the-civilization-of-china:
Herbert A. Giles, professor of Chinese at Cambridge, offers a general outline of Chinese civilisation from early times to the rapid changes of 1911. He writes for readers who know little of China and want a clear first survey. Giles served as consul at Ningpo, so his outline rests on years spent in China itself.

Chapters move from the feudal age through empire, thought, art, and daily life, asking what the word China itself covers, from Mongolia to the eighteen provinces. Giles keeps the tone plain and inviting, aiming to lead readers toward deeper study. He wrote in 1911, as the old empire was falling, which gives his survey a sense of a world ending.
21861-the-doll-and-her-friends-or-memoir:
A doll tells her own story in The Doll and Her Friends, or Memoirs of the Lady Seraphina, printed at Boston in 1852. The author, who also wrote Letters from Madras, says her aim was to amuse children and plant small morals. Chief among them: the happiness that kind tempers and thought for others bring to a home. She also speaks up for the good old-fashioned doll, then being scorned by sensible people without children.

Seraphina opens by confessing her race has no great minds, but lives to give pleasure. Hablot K. Browne, Dickens's famous illustrator, drew the four pictures. The little book is a Victorian nursery classic: gentle, funny, and firmly on the side of kindness in small things.
22144-good-old-anna:
Mrs. Belloc Lowndes, author of The Lodger, wrote Good Old Anna during the First World War. Anna is a German servant in an English household. Her mistress's friend cries that Anna has all the virtues of the German woman: faithful, kindly, industrious, and thrifty. Yet war has made every German in England a suspect in neighbours' eyes.

Lowndes builds the novel on that tension between loyalty and suspicion. Anna's long service argues one way; wartime fear argues the other. The book asks what a household owes a servant when nations go mad. It is a quiet, humane war novel, written while the guns still fired across the Channel.
2236-the-two-gentlemen-of-verona:
William Shakespeare's early comedy pairs two friends, Valentine and Proteus, whose bond frays when both fall for the same woman. The Two Gentlemen of Verona moves from Verona to Milan and into a forest of outlaws, mixing love letters, disguise, and the famous dog Crab. It is Shakespeare learning his craft in public.

The play's charm lies in its wit, its songs, and its youthful energy, even where the plot strains belief. Julia's disguise as a page and Launce's comic scenes with his dog steal the show. Readers new to Shakespeare will find this an easy, funny place to start.
2275-the-pioneers-or-the-sources-of-the-:
James Fenimore Cooper's Leatherstocking world comes to Templeton, a frontier settlement on Lake Otsego, where Judge Temple tries to impose law on a wilderness. The Pioneers follows Natty Bumppo, now old, clashing with game laws, settlers, and the clearing of the forest he loves. Chingachgook, the last of the Mohicans, walks beside him toward the novel's elegiac end.

Cooper writes the vanishing frontier with both pride and regret, staging a famous turkey shoot and a forest fire among the set pieces. The book is the first written, though fourth in story order, of the Leatherstocking Tales. It offers a founding portrait of American settlement and its costs.
2330-religions-of-ancient-china:
Herbert A. Giles, the great British sinologist, surveys the faiths of old China in this compact study. Religions of Ancient China covers ancestor worship, Confucianism, Taoism, and Buddhism, explaining their doctrines, rites, and history for Western readers. Giles writes clearly, with translations and examples drawn from Chinese texts.

The book reflects the scholarship of its age, respectful but shaped by missionary-era views. It still serves as a readable introduction to a vast subject. Students of Chinese religion will find a useful starting point here. Giles also compiled a famous Chinese-English dictionary used for decades.
2382-memoir-of-the-proposed-territory-of:
Sylvester Mowry, a soldier and delegate-elect, argues the case for a new Territory of Arizona in this 1857 memoir. The pamphlet describes the Gadsden Purchase lands between the Gila River and Mexico, praising their mines, climate, and routes, and urging Congress to organize them. Mowry writes as both booster and surveyor, with maps of interest in mind.

The memoir captures a moment when Arizona was still a proposal, not a place on the map. Its arguments reveal the politics of expansion, mining, and the coming Civil War. Historians of the Southwest will find a revealing primary source.
24078-bonaventure-a-prose-pastoral-of-ac:
George W. Cable set this pastoral novel among the Acadian people of Louisiana, along Bayou Teche and the short-turfed prairies west of it. First published in 1887, it gathers three linked tales titled Carancro, Grande Pointe, and Au Large. Its people include Sosthène, Bonaventure and Zoséphine, Claude, and the fiddler called 'Thanase.

Cable follows courtship, family duty, faith, and quarrels across bayou towns and open prairie, with floods, a tornado, and a chase among the later scenes. The book's care for Acadian speech, music, and custom gives it lasting value as a portrait of a place. Readers meet a Louisiana that is at once hard-working, devout, and full of local color.
24611-the-adventures-of-samuel-and-selin: Jean C. Archer wrote this tiny picture book, number 13 in the Dumpy Books for Children, published at London in 1902 with colour pictures. In short rhymed captions it follows Samuel and Selina through the seasons. In spring Sam tells Selina of his love. In summer she plights him her troth. In autumn a gayer swain wins her away. In winter she longs to have Sam back.
24673-a-phenomenal-fauna:
Carolyn Wells wrote this book of nonsense verse, published at New York in 1901 and 1902 with pictures by Oliver Herford. Its beasts are imaginary and punning. The Reg'lar Lark is a very gay old bird, heard at sunrise trilling a merry roundelay. The Humbug is doubted by learned entomologists, though each of us has surely seen one.

Wells gives each creature a short rhymed portrait, matched by Herford's droll drawings. The book is a joke bestiary, witty and light, for children and for grown-ups who love wordplay. Readers who enjoy Edward Lear's nonsense will find Wells's fauna a bright American cousin.
26133-trial-of-duncan-terig-alias-clerk-:
Printed at Edinburgh in 1831, this volume records a June 1754 trial. Walter Scott presented it to the Bannatyne Club. It covers Duncan Terig, alias Clerk, and Alexander Bane MacDonald, tried for the murder of Arthur Davis, a sergeant in General Guise's regiment of foot. Scott calls attention to a curious point of evidence in the case, which is why the club chose to print it.

Witness statements trace Davis going missing after he set out to meet a patrol from Glenshee, and the search parties sent out over the following days. The trial text gives a close view of Scottish criminal procedure in the 1700s. It moves from sworn depositions to a murder charge where the body and the facts came to light only slowly.
27061-the-rider-of-waroona:
Firth Scott's 1912 Australian novel The Rider of Waroona opens with Crotchety Dudgeon and a riddle, then a disappearance that sets Durham riding. Durham stumbles on a clue on the track, but sets his face against following it that day, with a long ride to Dudgeon's homestead at Taloona before sunset.

Later chapters bring Mrs. Burke's presentiment, a face at the window, a snaring, and a note that failed. Scott, praised for knowing the colonial native-born to the bones, writes a straightforward, vigorous tale of the Australian bush, its stations, and its secrets.
27339-the-pagan-madonna:
Harold MacGrath's The Pagan Madonna, with frontispiece by W. H. D. Koerner, opens with Cunningham thanking a visitor for coming up, since it makes him feel trusted. MacGrath, author of The Adventures of Kathlyn, Arms and the Woman, and The Drums of Jeopardy, sets a tale of cabins, prisoners, and strange wills.

The prisoner in Cabin Two suggests a planchette once owned by the actress Rachel, since everybody is doing it, while Cleigh eyes Cabin Four and doubts. A strong will in a woman is a novelty to him, and the lure that brought him sixteen thousand miles is losing its bite, in MacGrath's exotic romance.
27475-that-girl-montana:
Marah Ellis Ryan, author of Told in the Hills and The Bondwoman, published this western novel with Grosset and Dunlap in New York, from a 1901 Rand, McNally copyright. Its prologue opens with two men in hunting costume, strangers in the Northwest, talking over a local mystery as they take in the country.

That girl, one says, the murderer of Lee Holly, that pretty little girl? The other corrects him: she was suspected, not said to have killed him, and though cleared, the renegade's death adds one more mystery to the new West. The scene is set where the Kootenai River meets the Great Northern road. Ryan's heroine carries suspicion lightly, and the novel follows her through it.
27481-a-wayfarer-in-china-impressions-of:
Elizabeth Kendall published these impressions of a trip across West China and Mongolia with Houghton Mifflin in Boston and New York in February 1913. The book has illustrations, and Kendall dedicated it to her mother. Her route runs by caravan and sedan chair, with a little fu t'ou, or caravan headman, as frontispiece.

Kendall crosses Tonking into Yunnan, spends days in Yunnan-fu, and crosses Yunnan and the Chien-ch'ang. She follows the Mandarin Road to Tachienlu, crosses the Chengtu plain, visits sacred Omei Shan, and goes down the Yangtze. Then she travels to the Great Wall, the Mongolian grassland, the desert of Gobi, sacred Urga, and north to the Siberian railway. It is a remarkable journey, plainly told.
27932-history-of-the-division-of-medical:
Number forty-three in Smithsonian Institution United States National Museum Bulletin 240 gives the history of the Division of Medical Sciences, published by the Smithsonian Press in 1966. The bulletin also gathers papers thirty-four to forty-four on science and technology from the Museum of History and Technology.

Front material also explains the museum's two publication series, the Proceedings begun in 1878 and the Bulletin begun in 1875, covering anthropology, biology, history, geology, and medical technology. The paper traces how the medical sciences division grew steadily within the national museum, for specialists and libraries.
2801-the-commonwealth-of-oceana:
James Harrington published Oceana in the 1650s as a plan for a stable English republic after years of civil war. Born in 1611, Harrington argued that political power follows the ownership of land, so a lasting commonwealth must spread land and rotate its offices. He imagined a state where magistrates and honors pass from hand to hand each year instead of settling in one family or faction.

The book works out its scheme in detail, drawing on Athens, Sparta, Rome, and Venice as models and warnings. Harrington's orators and laws fill long passages, and his confidence in rules over rulers gives the work its force. It still matters as an early English argument that institutions, not good intentions, keep a republic free.
2802-ramona:
Helen Hunt Jackson wrote this novel of Southern California, opening at sheep shearing time on Senora Moreno's ranch. Shearing is late, for Felipe Moreno, the Senora's eldest son and head of the house since his father's death, has been ill, and without him nothing can be done.

Ramona, a part Indian orphan, loves Alessandro, an Indian shepherd, and their flight exposes the theft of Indian lands by Americans. Jackson wrote the book as a protest, and it became a bestseller. The novel remains a landmark of reform fiction, and a tragic romance of California.
28543-rex-ex-machina:
Frederic Max's Rex ex Machina opens as a dying father's final letter to his son, completing the young man's education. The father, content after a lifetime from the early Atomic era to a peaceful age, recalls a government citation for services too secret to name. Forty years earlier he was an obscure Army captain teaching at the Monterey Armed Forces Language School.

After a Korean tour, orders sent him to Washington, where news broke of a Hungarian physicist's mass-hypnosis device under Russian supervision. Four agents trained three months in physics and psychology to destroy scientist and machine. He slipped into Russia in December 1955, and never saw the other three again.
28780-peter-the-brazen-a-mystery-story-o:
George F. Worts wrote this 1919 mystery novel set in modern China, in three parts: The City of Stolen Lives, The Bitter Fountain, and The Green Death. Its hero, Peter Moore, is a wireless operator who spent five adventurous years pounding brass on ships across the Pacific before landing in China. There he is drawn into a tangle of pursuit, stolen lives, and danger in city streets, with rickshaws, chases, and narrow escapes.

Worts writes in the popular adventure style of the Munsey magazines, mixing romance, action, and an exotic setting for American readers. Peter's skill with the wireless and his bold temper carry the plot from one peril to the next. The book offers a fast-moving period thriller, and a picture of how China appeared in American pulp fiction just after the First World War.
2941-the-chinese-classics-prolegomena:
James Legge wrote the Prolegomena to his translation of the Chinese Classics as an introduction to the Confucian texts. The volume discusses the Great Learning, the Doctrine of the Mean, and the catalogues that record them, noting where a classic survives incomplete or divided. Legge weighs Chinese commentary against the texts themselves, including disputes over chapters counted as one or two.

The prolegomena explain how the classics reached the West and what a reader needs before tackling the translations. Legge's notes on the Great Learning stress its fragmentary front, evidence the student must face rather than smooth away. The volume still serves as a scholarly gateway to Confucius, Mencius, and their commentators.
29479-the-night-riders-a-romance-of-earl:
Ridgwell Cullum's 1913 romance of early Montana, printed in Philadelphia by George W. Jacobs, opens where Forks Settlement once nestled in the hills. Chapters move from the hands of the Philistines and Mosquito Bend, through the blind man, to the night-riders themselves. Tresler begins his education, Manson Orr is killed, and drink does its damage.

Cullum, author of The Watchers of the Plains and The Sheriff of Dyke Hole, writes a western of masked riders, rough justice, and frontier love. The night-riders ride as both terror and law in a land still settling its codes. Readers of classic westerns will find a sturdy, atmospheric tale of Montana before the railroad tamed it.
29824-diana:
Susan Warner, author of The Wide, Wide World and Queechy, published Diana in London in MDCCCLXXVII. The tale opens in a little brown house somewhere in the wilds of New England. A sewing society, a new minister, and Mother Bartlett set the village scene. Haymaking, sugar work, a September storm, and a snowstorm mark the seasons of the story.

Thirty-seven chapters follow parish life in close detail: catechizing, dairy work, a party, a post office meeting, and the minister's wife at her tasks. Evan's sister, Miss Collins, and Mrs. Starling add their voices. Warner writes with warm, earnest piety, and the book reads as a domestic chronicle of faith, work, and family in a New England town.
30402-the-making-of-mona:
Mabel Quiller-Couch tells a children's story about Mona, a girl lost in a book while a kettle sits idle on the hob. Mona plans to wait until the kettle begins to sing, then sinks back into her story and hears nothing.

The kettle hums softly, then loudly, then sings, and its cover rattles as it boils. Still Mona does not notice, and the fire at last leaves it no power to try. An illustration shows Granny staring at broken treasures, hinting at the household mishaps to come. Quiller-Couch writes a gentle tale of daydreaming, duty, and small disasters at home.
31091-cedar-creek-from-the-shanty-to-the:
The author of Golden Hills, a Tale of the Irish Famine, and The Foster-Brothers of Doon wrote this tale of Canadian life. It was published by the Religious Tract Society in London and printed by Morrison and Gibb in Edinburgh. Its subtitle promises the journey from the shanty to the settlement. Its frontispiece shows Andy helping an Indian squaw to construct a wigwam.

Thirty-two chapters run from Why Robert Wynn Emigrated and Crossing the Ferry through Up the St. Lawrence, Wooden-Ness, and Debarkation, to Concerning an Incubus, The River Highway, and Jean Baptiste at Home. Later chapters bring From Mud to Marble, Corduroy, The Battle with the Wilderness Begins, Camping in the Bush, The Yankee Storekeeper, and The Corner. It is a warm settler tale of clearing land and building a home in Canada.
31274-lady-anna:
Anthony Trollope's Lady Anna, published by Chapman and Hall in London in 1874 in two volumes, of which this is the first, turns on a marriage, a will, and a daughter's legitimacy. Its opening chapters tell the early history of Lady Lovel, born Josephine Murray and married to Earl Lovel in the mountain parish of Applethwaite in June 181-. She was brought as a bride to the sombre, ill-built Lovel Grange near Keswick.

Later chapters follow the Earl's will, the solicitor-general's propositions and perseverance, the tailor of Keswick, and Yoxham Rectory. They also follow Lady Anna's return to London, as lawyers and family dispute what is law and what is right. Trollope's tale of inheritance and honor remains one of his most absorbing domestic novels.
31417-psychic-phenomena:
Edward T. Bennett's Psychic Phenomena is a brief account of the physical manifestations observed in psychical research. It was published by Brentano's of New York in 1909, the year given as MCMIX, with a foreword by Sir Oliver Lodge. Bennett, assistant secretary to the Society for Psychical Research from 1882 to 1902, writes from inside the society's work. The book includes facsimile illustrations of thought-transference drawings and automatic writing.

Bennett describes sittings, tests, and claimed phenomena with the care of a researcher reporting experiments. He does not ask readers to believe without evidence, but to weigh what was observed. For readers of the history of psychical research, the book is a firsthand, moderate account from a period when science and the supernatural were still in open conversation.
32374-dick-hamilton-s-fortune-or-the-sti:
Howard R. Garis's boys' novel, copyrighted in 1909, follows Dick Hamilton, the son of a millionaire, after a strange will changes his prospects. His uncle Ezra threatens trouble, and Dick must prove himself through a string of scrapes and ventures. Chapters take him to New York, to a circus in town, and into business schemes, including gold mine stock and a party for fresh-air youngsters.

Later the action moves west to the mines, where a vanished man, a conspiracy, and a night trip underground test Dick's nerve. He also turns detective, faces a panic, and tries a flying machine. The story mixes money, adventure, and schoolboy loyalty, with Dick learning to use wealth well rather than simply spend it.
32417-the-girl-from-arizona:
Nina Rhoades's girls' novel follows Marjorie, a fourteen-year-old girl living on an Arizona ranch. The story opens with Miss Graham, who uses a wheeled chair, calling for Marjorie across a hot, still afternoon. Miss Graham pauses, as she often does, to gaze over the vast prairie toward the California mountains, almost a hundred miles off, a view she has known for twelve years.

Marjorie, a pretty girl with soft light hair and bright blue eyes, appears from a tiny log cabin with a book in hand. From ranch house, stables, and out-buildings, the novel builds a story of western home life, friendship, and growing up under a blazing Arizona sun. Rhoades, author of the Brick House Books, writes warmly for young readers about ranch country and family bonds.
3313-a-bit-of-old-china:
Charles Warren Stoddard sketches San Francisco's Chinatown in this piece. China is not more Chinese than this section of a Christian city, he writes, nor the heart of Tartary less American. Little China flaunts scarlet streamers overhead and flanks its doors with legends in saffron and gold. Even the window panes look foreign, and within lies a glimmer of tinsel, subdued light, and china lamps.

The lamps flicker before graven images of barbaric hideousness, in Stoddard's phrase, and the sketch mixes wonder with the prejudice of its age. Its value now is double: a vivid street scene from old San Francisco, and a record of how a sympathetic visitor could still exoticize his neighbors. Readers should take both, the color and the blind spot, together.
33236-the-history-of-the-european-fauna:
R. F. Scharff's study traces how the animals of Europe came to live where they do, from Britain and the Arctic to the lands reached by Siberian and Oriental migrations. Published in 1899, it opens with broad principles, then works region by region, asking which beasts are native, which came late, and what ice, sea, and land bridges did to their spread. Scharff draws on fossils, maps, and the range of living species to build his case.

The book belongs to a science series edited by Havelock Ellis, and it speaks to readers who want reasons, not just lists. Its chapters link past climates to present ranges, showing why some animals stop at a sea or a mountain line. Clear and careful, it remains a useful guide to the deep history behind Europe's wild life.
33244-maximina:
Armando Palacio Valdés's novel Maximina, translated from the Spanish by Nathan Haskell Dole, opens with Miguel reaching Pasajes late on a Friday afternoon. There he finds Ursula's boat moored to the shore, and the boat-woman greets him with warm courtesy. Copyrighted in 1888, the tale follows Miguel and Maximina through a Spanish world of coasts, towns, and family ties, where love and duty pull in different ways.

Palacio Valdés, author of The Marquis of Peñalta, writes with a keen eye for Spanish life and character. His novel moves at a gentle pace, rich in scene and talk. For readers who enjoy translated classics of Spain, Maximina offers a tender, well-observed story of a young man's heart and the woman who shapes his fate.
33566-ecological-observations-on-the-woo:
Henry S. Fitch and Dennis G. Rainey report eight years of ecological observation of the eastern woodrat on the University of Kansas Natural History Reservation, from February 1948 to February 1956. The woodrat shapes its community by eating vegetation, by sheltering many other small animals in its stick houses, and by feeding certain flesh-eaters. As its population rose and fell in density and range, those effects changed greatly.

Two sets of field data, overlapping little in time or space, support the report, with Fitch's work covering roughly the western half of the reservation. Three figures illustrate the account. The study is a detailed, patient record of one rodent's place in a Kansas landscape, useful to ecologists and to anyone curious about how a common animal quietly engineers its surroundings.
33799-the-blood-of-the-arena:
Vicente Blasco Ibanez wrote this Spanish novel of the bull ring, translated by Frances Douglas and published in Chicago in 1911. Its hero is Gallardo, a matador whose wedding becomes a national event and whose fame brings wealth, lovers, and danger. Chapters follow him from the ring to the salon, the bandit's table, and the face of death.

Blasco Ibanez paints Spain through the matador's rise and fall: guitars at night, diamonds in the ring, and crowds that lift a man up and watch him bleed. The novel asks what glory costs when the crowd owns the hero. It remains a vivid, unsparing look at fame in old Spain.
390-a-lute-of-jade-selections-from-the-c:
L. Cranmer-Byng translates selections from the classical poets of China into English verse, under the title A Lute of Jade. The poems span court lyrics, nature pieces, and songs of parting and return. Cranmer-Byng, a translator of Chinese verse, worked when few English readers knew the originals.

Cranmer-Byng keeps the images plain and musical, letting moonlight, rivers, and autumn speak for the originals. The book serves as a gentle first door into Chinese poetry for readers who know no Chinese. His lute image, a Chinese instrument, signals music as the heart of the poems he chose.
4492-farina:
George Meredith sets this romance in the old Rhine country, in and around Cologne, when emperors, merchants, and legends still shared the same streets. At its centre stands Gottlieb Groschen, a rich and shrewd trader whose wealth reaches from vineyards and corn land to quarries and mineral springs. His daughter Margarita, called the White Rose of Germany, draws a band of young admirers who compete for her favour.

Through chivalry, jokes, and sudden turns of fortune, the tale follows honour, love, and pride among merchants, princes, and would-be knights. Meredith tells it in a high, playful style, full of local colour and old German lore. Readers get a light but sharp romance about what wealth can buy, what honour demands, and how a famous beauty unsettles a whole town.
4522-the-fight-for-the-republic-in-china:
B. L. Putnam Weale wrote this account of China during the First World War, when the young republic faced pressure from abroad and trouble at home. The first part sets the European war beside the Chinese question, showing how a war fought far away still changed what foreign powers wanted in China. The second part turns to the Chinese question and a defensive alliance, and to the bargains struck between governments.

Weale writes as a close observer of Peking politics, naming ministers, treaties, and rival claims rather than telling a simple story of heroes and villains. Readers who want to understand why China's republic struggled in those years will find a detailed, partisan contemporary record. It suits readers of diplomatic history, and anyone tracing how the war reshaped Asia before its end.
4680-manuel-pereira-or-the-sovereign-rul:
F. C. Adams wrote Manuel Pereira, or The Sovereign Rule of South Carolina, at Charleston, South Carolina, published at Washington in 1853, with views of Southern laws, life, and hospitality. Its contents open with an unlucky ship, a steward's bravery, and a second storm. Charleston police, Mr. Grimshaw, the man of the county, and the Janson in the offing follow, with arrival of the Janson and a new dish of secession.

Later chapters take up points of law, a darkening prospect, the sheriff's office, and the old jail. How it is, Manuel Pereira committed, the law's intricacy, and a plea of just consideration follow. Little George, the captain, and Mr. Grimshaw, little Tommy and the police, and the mayor's verdict lead to an emeute among stewards. Readers get a mid-century Southern legal tale, about free Black sailors, state law, and hospitality tested by statute.
5196-their-mariposa-legend-a-romance-of-:
Charlotte Herr's romance Their Mariposa Legend is set on Santa Catalina, fairest of the Channel Islands, where spring arrives in a rush of rain over lilac thickets and lark song. Part One, Sir Francis Starts It, begins centuries ago, while Part Two, Miss Hastings Brings It to an End, carries the legend into modern days.

Herr weaves island history, flowers, and romance into a gentle legend for readers who love California's coast. The book offers a lyrical, old-fashioned tale in which a place's past and present meet through a story passed from one generation to the next.
5350-farmers-of-forty-centuries-or-perma:
F. H. King's Farmers of Forty Centuries, published in 1911 with a preface by L. H. Bailey, studies permanent agriculture in China, Korea, and Japan. Bailey's preface argues that tilling the earth is the bottom condition of civilisation, yet mankind's experience in tilling has scarcely been gathered, and few books describe real rural conditions.

King, an agricultural traveller, records how East Asian farmers sustained their soils for forty centuries, without the waste that exhausted Western farms. The book offers readers a classic of sustainable agriculture, written before the term existed, and it remains influential among farmers and historians of farming.
589-catriona:
Robert Louis Stevenson continues David Balfour's story in this sequel to Kidnapped, also known as David Balfour. David, fresh from his Highland trials, seeks justice in Edinburgh, tangles with the Lord Advocate, and falls for Catriona Drummond, daughter of the outlaw James More. Flights, trials, and a voyage to Holland follow.

Stevenson writes with brisk, Scots-flavored prose, mixing law, love, and adventure. Alan Breck returns, but Catriona's father and daughter steal the heart. The novel endures as a fine romance of honor and affection, where a young man learns that loyalty and love pull in different directions.
6708-china:
Demetrius Charles Boulger writes a short history of China, with a supplementary chapter on recent events by Mayo Hazeltine. He dedicates the book to Sir Halliday Macartney, praising his defense of China's right to be treated with dignity by European powers. A frontispiece shows the emperor receiving the diplomatic corps.

Chapters run from the early ages and the first national dynasty through later dynasties, wars, and treaties. Boulger writes for English readers who want a clear, compact survey. China is a useful, period history, best read as a window on how the West viewed China a century ago.
7736-tomlinsoniana:
Augustus Tomlinson, professor of moral philosophy in a German university, speaks from beyond the grave in Edward Bulwer Lytton's Tomlinsoniana. The narrator, who knew him in his last days, recalls a bald man in a green silk gown and black velvet cap, dying in 1822 while still debating ethics.

His posthumous papers offer maxims on the popular art of creating, shown through ten characters, as a guide by which any man may become his own rogue. Short essays, critical and moral, follow. It is a sly companion to Paul Clifford, turning its hero's tutor into a mock philosopher.
7889-erotica-romana:
Johann Wolfgang von Goethe's Erotica Romana, or Roman Elegies in this rendering, plants a garden of love in Rome itself. The speaker sorts love's blossoms in plots, sets Priapus to guard golden fruit, and warns hypocrites who bridle at nature to expect punishment for shame.

Stones, palaces, and streets are asked to speak, for within Rome's walls each object holds a soul, yet all stay mute to the lover seeking one window where his beloved may appear. Through churches and palaces, the poems blend classical Rome, sensual joy, and a poet's longing in frank, musical verse.
8390-buddhism-and-buddhists-in-china:
Lewis Hodous, a missionary scholar, wrote this study of Buddhism as it lived in China, not only as it was taught in books. Chapters trace its entrance and rise to the dominant religion. They then turn to the peasant, the monastery, and daily practice, asking how Buddhism met ancestor worship, degenerate Taoism, and Confucian order, and why it proved so inclusive.

Hodous wrote from years in China, and his book balances history with observation of temples, monks, and village rites. Readers get both a history of a faith's spread and a portrait of Chinese religious life in the early twentieth century. For students of Buddhism outside India, it remains a grounded, readable introduction.
8651-with-moore-at-corunna:
G. A. Henty sets this adventure in the Peninsular War, following a young British officer through Portugal and Spain toward the retreat to Corunna. Early chapters cover the Mayo Fusiliers, landings, camps, and the battles of Rolica and Vimiera, before the army turns north in a hard winter retreat. The hero faces false alarms, escapes, dangerous missions, and skirmishes in the mountain passes.

Sir John Moore, the general whose retreat and death at Corunna anchor the story, gives the book its historical spine. Henty fills the campaign with marching detail, soldier talk, and steady heroics, in the style that made him a favourite with schoolboys. Readers get both a brisk adventure and a readable outline of one of Britain's most famous retreats, though the politics stay firmly those of Henty's own day.
9104-the-naval-war-of-1812-or-the-histor:
Theodore Roosevelt wrote this history of the United States Navy in the War of 1812 while still a young man, before his political career. It covers the war with Great Britain at sea. Single-ship duels open the tale, such as Constitution against Guerrière. The Battle of Lake Erie follows, with an account of New Orleans added.

Roosevelt works from logs, reports, and ship lists, judging captains and tactics with a young scholar's rigor. The book won praise for its care and helped launch its author. It remains a clear, spirited naval history, and a first sign of the energy Roosevelt later brought to public life.
9659-the-gentleman-from-indiana:
Booth Tarkington wrote The Gentleman from Indiana, a novel of small-town Indiana life and politics. The hero, a young man who came to stay, settles in a flat farm country of mud, snow, and summer dust. Chapters follow a strange lady, lonesomeness, and a court-house bell, with John Brown's Body and a rescue beside. Tarkington, later famed for Penrod, writes with humor and warmth.

The young man wins friends, faces treachery from H. Fisbee, and at last comes home to honor. A pretty marquise, Helen's toast, and a teller named Jerry fill the social round. A reader gets a fond, early Tarkington tale of Hoosier pluck, love, and local politics, told with wit and heart.
a-bit-of-old-china:
Charles Warren Stoddard walks the reader into old San Francisco's Chinatown, in a sketch taken from his book In the Footprints of the Padres, as the opening note explains. China is not more Chinese, he writes, than this section of a Christian city, with its scarlet streamers, saffron and gold signs, and lamps flickering before images. A talk about Confucius and confusion starts the stroll.

With an artist friend he pushes through theaters, temples, restaurants, and opium dens, watching faces and customs with a poet's sympathy. Stoddard knew California from its early days and wrote against the cheap contempt of his time for the Chinese. His sketch preserves a quarter that fire and rebuilding later erased.
a-history-of-china: Wolfram Eberhard writes a history of China from the earliest times onward. The opening chapters treat prehistory, Peking Man, the Palaeolithic and Neolithic ages, and eight principal prehistoric cultures. Yang shao and Lung shan cultures lead toward historic China. Eberhard's history serves students of Chinese civilization. Later chapters carry the tale on through dynasties and change.
a-lute-of-jade-selections-from-the-class:
L. Cranmer-Byng renders classical Chinese poems into English verse, with an introduction covering the ancient ballads, verse forms, and the influence of religion. His contents move from the Odes of Confucius and the exiled poet Ch'u Yuan to the great masters of the T'ang dynasty. Short lyrics fill most pages.

Tu Fu appears with The Little Rain and Chants of Autumn; Li Po with drinking songs, moonlight thoughts, and memories at dusk. Other poets sing of war, travel, lost friends, and court love. Cranmer-Byng's versions are free rather than literal, shaped to sing in English, and they introduced many Western readers to Chinese poetry.
an-australian-in-china: George Ernest Morrison, an Australian in China, narrates a quiet journey across China to Burma, in a third edition published in London. The doctor and traveller records towns, people, and roads with a keen eye, travelling without fanfare. His account remains a valued record of inland China at the turn of the century.
antonina:
Antonina, published in 1850 under this shorter title, is the first published novel of Wilkie Collins. Before The Woman in White and The Moonstone made him a master of mystery and suspense, Collins tried his hand at the fall of Rome. His subject is the western empire under the Emperor Honorius, rendered as a tale of ancient Rome in its last weakness.

Collins said the spirit of that age is carried by his fictitious characters rather than by the historical names. The heroine Antonina stands at the center of that design, amid the pressures closing on the city. This edition, under the plain title Antonina, preserves the same debut novel in the shorter-titled form in which it also circulated.
britannica-1911-abendana: Abendana is the headword of a short entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica, naming two Jewish theologians, brothers. Jacob Abendana, born 1630, served as rabbi, or Hakham, of the Spanish Jews in London from 1680. Christian friends filled his circle, and his standing raised regard for Jewish learning among Christian theologians of the day. Isaac Abendana, born about 1650, taught Hebrew at Cambridge and then at Oxford. He built a Jewish calendar and wrote Discourses on the Ecclesiastical and Civil Polity of the Jews in 1706.
britannica-1911-acta-diurna:
Acta Diurna were a sort of daily gazette in ancient Rome. The name means daily public acts or records. Officially authorized narratives of events filled their pages. Court news stood beside decrees of emperor and senate. Private notices of births, marriages, and deaths appeared too. To that extent they filled a modern newspaper's place. Julius Caesar began the practice in 59 B.C. He ordered public officers to keep and publish the acts.

Daily mechanics are described with care. Clerks drew the Acta up day by day. They exposed them publicly on a whitened board. After a reasonable time the boards came down. Archives preserved them for later research. No genuine fragments survive today, the entry says. Publication lasted until the empire's seat moved east.
britannica-1911-adana:
Adana is a vilayet in south-eastern Asia Minor. It includes the ancient land of Cilicia. Mountain districts hold unexploited mineral wealth. A fertile coast-plain lies below the Taurus range. Cotton, rice, cereals, and sugar grow there. Much fruit and abundant pasturage feature too. Rivers descending from Taurus water the plain well. Mersina handles the province's imports and exports.

Its chief town commands the mountain passage northward. Adana town stands thirty miles from the sea. The Seihan river flows past it, navigable by small craft. A stone bridge there dates partly from Justinian's age. Restorations came under caliphs in 743 and 840. The town rose on Rome's military road east. Egyptians held it from 1832 until 1840. Population approaches fifty thousand at its maximum.
britannica-1911-agostino-and-agnolo-da-s:
Agostino and Agnolo da Siena were Italian architects and sculptors. They worked in the first half of the fourteenth century. Some writers deny that they were brothers. Both studied under Giovanni Pisano in any case. In 1317 Siena appointed them its joint architects. They designed the Porto Romana for their native town. The church and convent of St Francis were theirs too. Other buildings in Siena carry their names.

One commission crowned their fame. Giotto recommended them for a great tomb. He called them the best sculptors of the time. In 1330 they made Bishop Guido Tarlati's tomb. Arezzo cathedral housed that Giotto-designed monument. Contemporaries esteemed it among the century's finest works. French troops under Anjou destroyed it later.
britannica-1911-ahtena: Ahtena, glossed in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica as ice people, names an Athapascan tribe of North American Indians. The tribe lived in the basin of Copper River in Alaska, the river country where its people made their home. The entry is only a definition and a reference, giving the name, its meaning, the tribe's language stock, and its location. For fuller information it points readers to the Handbook of American Indians, edited by F. W. Hodge and published at Washington in 1907, where the tribe is treated in more detail.
britannica-1911-alcoforado-marianna:
Marianna Alcoforado (1640–1723), a Portuguese nun, won fame for five short letters to the lover who left her. She was a landed owner's daughter from Alemtejo, born at Beja, the chief garrison town of that region. Her father, a widower with army duties, put her as a small child into the rich convent of the Conception.

She took Franciscan vows at sixteen or sooner, with no true calling. At twenty-five she met Noel Bouton, later marquis de Chamilly, a French officer then serving in Portugal in its long war with Spain. Her letters trace the love that grew and, by the fifth, her first steps in beating it down. A life of strict penance followed, and she died at eighty-three. The letters passed to the comte de Guilleragues, who put them into French, and they were printed at Paris in 1669.
britannica-1911-angra-pequena:
Angra Pequena is a bay in German South-West Africa. Bartholomew Diaz discovered it in 1487. A Bremen merchant, F. A. E. Lüderitz, opened a trading station there in 1883. His agent made treaties with neighbouring chiefs. Those chiefs ceded large tracts of country. Lüderitz transferred his rights to the German government in April 1884. A German protectorate followed that August.

The Germans renamed the bay Lüderitz Bay. The surrounding country is sometimes called Lüderitzland. The harbour itself is poor. A small town stands at the head of the bay. A railway eastward began there in 1906. Desert surrounds the settlement for many miles. Rare thunderstorms briefly fill the dry Little Fish river. Offshore islands, including Seal and Penguin, passed to Cape Colony earlier, in 1874.
britannica-1911-anna:
Anna is an Indian coin denomination. The Hindustani word is ana. Sixteen annas make one rupee. The term belongs to the Muslim monetary system. No actual one-anna coin exists. Half-annas circulate in copper instead. Two-anna pieces circulate in silver. The entry points to the rupee article for context.

Usage extends well beyond money. Anna frequently expresses a fraction generally. Anglo-Indians speak of two annas of dark blood. That phrase denotes an octoroon's ancestry. A four-anna crop means a quarter crop. An eight-anna gallop means a half gallop. Such phrases show colonial slang at work. Fractions of sixteen structured everyday speech. The short entry captures money and metaphor together.
britannica-1911-anna-comnena:
Anna Comnena was a Byzantine princess and historian. She was born on 1 December 1083. Her father was Emperor Alexius I Comnenus. She was his favourite daughter. Teachers trained her in poetry and science. Greek philosophy also filled her studies. Learning did not soften her ambition, though. She intrigued persistently for power. Her husband was Nicephorus Bryennius, an accomplished nobleman.

Anna tried to redirect the succession. She wanted her husband crowned over her brother. The dying Alexius refused the scheme. She then conspired against her brother's rule. Her husband refused to join that plot. Discovery cost her property and fortune. Her brother spared her life in clemency. She retired into a convent afterwards. There she wrote the Alexiad. That Greek history covers her father's reign. It supplements her husband's historical work. Critics call it family panegyric more than science.
britannica-1911-anna-leopoldovna:
Anna Leopoldovna (1718–1746) was regent of Russia briefly. Her infant son Ivan was emperor. Her mother Catherine was Empress Anne's sister. Her father was Charles Leopold of Mecklenburg-Schwerin. In 1739 she married Anton Ulrich of Brunswick. Their son Ivan was born soon after. Empress Anne adopted Ivan in 1740. She proclaimed him heir to the throne.

The empress died days after that proclamation. Her favourite, Ernest Biren, became regent first. Russians detested Biren intensely, though. Anna overthrew him with little difficulty. She assumed the regency as grand-duchess. Ignorance of Russian government hampered her badly. She quarrelled with her principal supporters quickly. Elizabeth, Peter the Great's daughter, struck in 1741. The guards revolted at her prompting. Elizabeth took the throne that December. Ivan went to prison as an infant.
britannica-1911-avadana:
Avadāna is a type of Buddhist romance literature. Large Sanskrit collections represent the type. Those collections come from Nepal especially. The Avadānasataka is a chief collection. Its name means Century of Legends. The Divyāvadāna is the other chief collection. Its name means the Heavenly Legend. These works are later than most canonical Buddhist books.

Orthodox Buddhists hold them in veneration nonetheless. Their position in Buddhism is comparable to the Purānas. The Purānas hold that place toward Brahminism. The entry is short and classificatory. It defines a genre rather than a single work. Legend collections served devotion and teaching both. Sanskrit literary history gives them their context.
britannica-1911-avicenna:
Avicenna (980-1037), born at Afshena near Bokhara, was an Arabian philosopher whose father, a Persian from Balkh, served as tax-collector under the Samanid amir. Moved to Bokhara as a child, he amazed neighbors by knowing the Koran and much Arabic poetry by heart at ten.

Greengrocers, wandering scholars, and his own reading taught him arithmetic, logic, geometry, and the Almagest. Before sixteen he knew medical theory and, by treating the sick for free, found new methods of his own. He read Aristotle's Metaphysics forty times before a small commentary by Farabi, bought for three dirhems, unlocked its meaning. By seventeen his apprenticeship of study was complete, a start the entry tells with pride.
britannica-1911-avigliana:
Avigliana is a town of Piedmont, Italy, in the province of Turin, fourteen miles west of the city of Turin by rail. Its population in 1901 was 4,629. Medieval buildings of some interest survive in the town, the entry notes, giving it an older face than its best-known workplace would suggest.

That workplace is a large dynamite factory employing over 500 workmen, the fact for which Avigliana is mainly remarkable in this account. Two sides of one small Piedmont town meet here. A medieval past is still visible in its buildings. Modern industry runs on a scale large next to its population of under five thousand.
britannica-1911-avogadro-amedeo-conte-di:
Avogadro, Amedeo, Conte di Quaregna (1776-1856), was an Italian physicist born and long resident at Turin, where he died in 1856. For many years he held the chair of higher physics at Turin University. His memoirs ranged over electricity, the swelling of liquids by heat, specific heats, and capillary attraction.

His fame rests on an 1811 essay. It sets out the rule named for him. Under the same heat and pressure, equal volumes of all gases hold the same number of smallest particles, or molecules. Those particles may be single atoms or groups of atoms, alike or different. He also published a four-volume treatise on the physics of ponderable bodies between 1837 and 1841, but the gas rule is what kept his name alive.
britannica-1911-badalona:
Badalona, the ancient Baetulo, is a town of north-eastern Spain in the province of Barcelona, six miles north-east of that city on the river Besós and the Mediterranean coast. Its 1900 population was 19,240, and it stands on the coast railway running from Barcelona toward Perpignan in France.

A small harbour serves fishing and boat-building, while gas, chemical, and mineral-oil works stand in the town. Makers there produce woollen and cotton goods, glass, biscuits, sugar, and brandy. The fertile plains around yield grain, wine, and fruit in plenty. Badalona thus feeds Barcelona's export trade so fully that the entry calls it, in effect, that city's industrial suburb.
britannica-1911-baillie-joanna:
Baillie, Joanna (1762-1851), was a British poet and dramatist born at the manse of Bothwell on the Clyde, of an old Scottish family claiming descent kin to William Wallace. She moved to London with her sister Agnes, settled at Hampstead on a small inherited income, and lived there the rest of her life.

Her design, from 1798, was a Series of Plays on the passions. Each great passion would get a tragedy and a comedy. Hate, jealousy, fear, and love were among them. Each play would show one person wholly under that passion's sway. The volumes won success, first credited to Walter Scott before her name came out. The entry judges the plays weak for the stage. A hero who is one passion only lacks incident and range. Yet it grants them remarkable power as reading. It also notes De Monfort's London run, carried by Kemble's and Siddons's acting.
britannica-1911-ballymena:
Ballymena is a town of County Antrim, Ireland, standing on the Braid river near its meeting with the Maine. It lies 33 miles north-west of Belfast on the Northern Counties railway, with branch lines to Larne and Parkmore. Its urban district held 10,886 people in 1901.

Linen made the town. The trade, brought in during 1733, employed the greater part of the people, and brown linen was its specialty. Iron ore was raised nearby. The 1911 Britannica entry notes few old remains: the castles at Ballymena and Galgorm were modern builds. One older site stands out, Gracehill, a Moravian settlement founded in 1746.
britannica-1911-banana:
Banana is a giant herbaceous plant of the genus Musa. It is perennial, sending up from an underground rootstock a seeming stem 15 or 20 feet high. That stem is no stem at all, but leaf sheaths wrapped tight together, topped by blades that can run ten feet long and form a spreading crown.

A true stem rises only at flowering, growing up through the hollow sheath tube to bear many small tube-shaped flowers guarded by large, often bright bracts. The fruits hang in dense clusters. The 1911 Britannica entry counts about forty Musa species across the Old World tropics, and stresses their weight in hot lands: there they feed people much as grain feeds cooler regions. Most thrive only in a hot, damp climate.
britannica-1911-bandana:
Bandana, or bandanna, is a word probably drawn through Portuguese from the Hindustani bāndhnū. That term named an early way of dyeing: cloth was tied up in places so the tied parts would not take the dye. The name passed to the richly coloured silk handkerchiefs made by that process, known for their bright colours.

By 1911 most bandanas were cotton, made in Lancashire and sent abroad for sale. The 1911 Britannica entry adds a second method: in calico printing, the same look can be got by discharging, or removing, colour from cloth in a set pattern. The entry is short, keeping to the word's origin and the two ways of making the cloth.
britannica-1911-bassi-laura-maria-cateri:
Laura Maria Caterina Bassi (1711–1778), an Italian scholar born at Bologna, is the subject of a short 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry. Her extraordinary attainments in learning won her a doctor's degree, a rare honour for a woman of her century. She was appointed professor in the philosophical college at Bologna. There she lectured publicly on experimental philosophy, the study of nature through experiment, until her death in 1778.

Recognition spread well beyond Bologna. Bassi was elected a member of many literary societies in Italy and abroad. She carried on an extensive correspondence with the most eminent European men of letters of her day. The entry also notes her wide reading: she was well acquainted with classical literature and with the literature of France and Italy as well. In 1738 she married Giuseppe Verrati, a physician, and she left several children at her death.
britannica-1911-belladonna:
Belladonna is the roots and leaves of Atropa belladonna, the deadly nightshade, much used in medicine. Its Italian name means “beautiful lady,” since the berries once served as a cosmetic. The plant’s power comes from alkaloids it holds, chiefly atropine, with hyoscyamine, hyoscine and belladonine beside it.

Long sections work through atropine’s chemistry, its dose, and its actions on skin, nerves, heart, brain and eye. Medical uses follow, from easing pain to treating the bed-wetting of children, and the entry ends with the signs of poisoning and its treatment. Few drugs of the time get so full a hearing, which shows belladonna’s weight in the medicine of the day.
britannica-1911-bellona:
Bellona, first called Duellona, was the Roman goddess of war, matching the Greek Enyo. Later writers made her by turns the sister, daughter or wife of Mars, or his charioteer or nurse. Her worship at Rome was pushed chiefly by the Claudii family, and she may be one with the Sabine war goddess Nerio.

Her temple, vowed in 296 B.C., stood outside the city gates in the Campus Martius. There the senate heard generals claiming a triumph and received foreign envoys, and before it war was declared by throwing a spear. A second, Asiatic Bellona came from Cappadocia under Sulla, her priests cutting themselves and sprinkling their blood on the crowd.
britannica-1911-berezina:
Berezina is a river of Russia in the government of Minsk, a tributary of the Dnieper. It rises in the marshes of Borizov and flows south, bending east, for 350 miles, of which 250 can be sailed. Low, well-wooded country lines most of its course.

As part of the canal system joining the Black Sea with the Baltic, the Berezina matters for trade, though hard floods trouble it. Its fame is grimmer. Just above Borizov, Napoleon’s army forced the river crossing on 26–28 November 1812 during the retreat from Moscow, with enormous losses. That disaster fixed the river’s name in European memory, and the short entry centres on it.
britannica-1911-berners-juliana:
Juliana Berners (born about 1388?) is named as an English writer on hawking and hunting. Tradition makes her prioress of Sopwell nunnery near St Albans. She is said to be the daughter of Sir James Berners, beheaded in 1388. The 1911 Britannica entry is careful about the evidence. Only the closing line of her hunting treatise names her directly. No such person appears in the Berners family pedigree.

She is the supposed author of the Boke of St Albans, first printed in 1486. The book covers hawking, hunting, and coats of arms. It also treats horses and, in later form, fishing. The work stayed popular through the 16th century. Gervase Markham reissued it in 1595 as The Gentleman's Academie.
britannica-1911-bimana:
Bimana, Latin for two-handed, is a zoology term coined by the naturalist Blumenbach. He used it to set man apart from the Quadrumana, the four-handed mammals. Cuvier popularized the term, and most writers followed him. The 1911 Britannica entry then shows the label coming apart. In 1863 Huxley argued that the higher apes fit fairly inside Bimana.

The entry piles up proof that feet can learn hand-like work. Artists have painted while holding the brush with their toes. Violinists have played the same way, and sailors show strong foot-grasp. A baby, Haeckel noted, can grip a spoon with its big toe. Man, the article concludes, is potentially four-handed after all.
britannica-1911-blamire-susanna:
Susanna Blamire (1747–1794) was an English poet from Cumberland whose songs became favourites in the north country. Born at Cardew Hall near Dalston, the daughter of a yeoman farmer, she lost her mother young and was raised by an aunt. She went to the village school at Raughton Head and lived quietly among farming neighbours.

Her humour and good temper made her loved in local society, and she wrote poems with her friend Catharine Gilpin during winters in Carlisle. Some songs are in Scots, shaped by visits to her sister in Perthshire. Her poems were gathered only in 1842, long after her death. Songs such as And ye shall walk in silk attire still stood among the best north-country lyrics, the entry says.
britannica-1911-blavatsky-helena-petrovn:
Helena Petrovna Blavatsky (1831–1891) was a Russian traveller and founder figure of theosophy. Born at Ekaterinoslav, a colonel's daughter, she married a much older Russian official at seventeen and left him within months. Twenty years of travel followed, across Canada, Texas, Mexico, and India, with two attempts to enter Tibet.

Stories of a hidden Himalayan retreat belong to what she called the veiled period of 1848–1858. Back in Russia she drew crowds as a spiritualist medium, and about 1870 she rose among American spiritualists and took citizenship there. The later pages follow her occult studies and the building of the theosophical movement. She died in London in 1891 at the head of a body said to number near 100,000.
britannica-1911-bologna:
Bologna is a city of Emilia in Italy, capital of its province and seat of an archbishop, set at the foot of the Apennines 82 miles north of Florence by rail. Its people numbered 102,122 in the town and 153,501 in the commune in 1901. The Roman street grid can still be traced inside the later walled city.

Churches fill the opening survey. Santo Stefano is a group of seven buildings of many dates, and the great church of San Petronio, begun in 1390, is the largest in town. The long entry then works through the city's towers, palaces, university, art, and trade, and its history from Roman times through wars and papal rule to modern Italy.
britannica-1911-bona:
Bona, or Bône, is a seaport of Algeria on a bay of the Mediterranean, 220 miles by rail west of Tunis and 136 miles north-east of Constantine. It is the chief town of its arrondissement and sits at the foot of the wooded Edugh heights. A modern rampart rings it outside the old Arab wall.

Much of the old town had been pulled down, and the entry presents a flourishing French city of wide, steep streets. A broad tree-lined promenade runs through the centre, holding the theatre, banks, and hotels. The cathedral of St Augustine keeps a relic said to be the saint's right arm, brought from Pavia in 1842. The Grand Mosque was built from the ruins of ancient Hippo, and barracks for 3000 men are noted.
britannica-1911-bosnia-and-herzegovina:
Bosnia and Herzegovina are two Balkan provinces that passed from Turkish rule to form, with Dalmatia, the southernmost lands of Austria-Hungary. Together, shaped roughly like a triangle with its base on top, they cover 19,696 square miles in the north-west of the Balkan Peninsula. Croatia-Slavonia bounds them north, Dalmatia west, and Servia north-east.

Bosnia is wholly inland, and Herzegovina touches the Adriatic only in two short strips with no good harbour. The Dinaric Alps run along the Dalmatian border and through central Bosnia, reaching 6000 to 7500 feet near Travnik, Serajevo, and Mostar, with high shut-in valleys such as the plain of Livno. The vast entry goes on through rivers, climate, peoples, towns, farming, and the provinces' history under Rome, Turkey, and Austria.
britannica-1911-buccina:
The buccina was a brass wind instrument of ancient Rome. Roman armies used it for signals in camp. This 1911 Britannica article describes the instrument closely. Its tube measured some 11 to 12 feet. The bore was narrow and cylindrical. The player blew through a cup-shaped mouthpiece.

The tube bends back on itself in a broad C shape. A crossbar steadies it in the player's hand. The bell curves over his head or shoulder. It worked much like a modern helicon. Three Roman buccinas survive from Pompeii. They are kept in the museum at Naples. A copy made in Brussels is pitched in G. Its notes match the French horn and trumpet closely. With the cornu and the tuba, the buccina sounded the four night watches.
britannica-1911-cardona:
Cardona is a town of north-eastern Spain. It stands in the province of Barcelona. It lies about 55 miles north-west of Barcelona itself. Its population in 1900 was 3855. This 1911 Britannica entry describes the town and its salt hill. Cardona sits on a hill near the river Cardoner. That river, a branch of the Llobregat, almost surrounds it. Moorish walls and a citadel crown the town.

The town's fame rests on its great rock-salt deposit. The salt forms a mountain about 300 feet high. The mass measures some 3 miles in circumference. A thick bed of reddish clay covers it. The salt is generally translucent in its masses. Large pieces of it are quite transparent to light. The hill is worked like a mine by the townsfolk. Artists in Cardona carve the salt into ornaments. Images and crucifixes are made from the mined blocks.
britannica-1911-carmona:
Carmona is a town of south-western Spain. It stands in the province of Seville. It lies 27 miles north-east of Seville by rail. Its population in 1900 was 17,215. This 1911 Britannica entry describes the town and its remains. Carmona is built on a ridge over the Andalusian plain. The Sierra Morena bounds that view to the north. The peak of San Cristobal closes it to the south.

The town trades in wine, olive oil, grain and cattle. Its annual fair is held each April. The citadel of Carmona now stands in ruins. It was once the chief fortress of Peter the Cruel. A spacious palace stood within its defences then. An old Moorish gateway forms the town's main entrance. The Cordova gate is partly Roman in its building. In 1881 a large Roman necropolis was found nearby. Its rock-hewn chambers held niches for cinerary urns.
britannica-1911-civita-castellana:
Civita Castellana, ancient Falerii, is a town and episcopal see in the province of Rome, 45 miles by rail from Rome, holding 5,265 people in 1901. Its station lies five miles north-east of the town itself. The cathedral of Santa Maria has a fine portico built in 1210 by Laurentius Romanus, his son Jacobus and his grandson Cosmas. Ancient columns and mosaic work in the cosmatesque style enrich that portico, while the interior was modernised in the 18th century.

Pope Alexander VI erected the citadel from designs by Antonio da Sangallo the elder, and Julius II and Leo X enlarged it later. A lofty bridge of the 18th century gives approach to the town across its gorge. Mount Soracte lies about six miles to the south-east, a landmark named at the close. Cathedral, citadel and bridge form the town's chief fabric in this short account.
britannica-1911-cochin-china:
Cochin-China is a French colony in the extreme south of French Indo-China, comprising the six southern provinces of the Annamese empire annexed by France in 1862 and 1867. The term formerly included the whole Annamese empire, Tongking, Annam and Lower Cochin-China together. It is bounded by the Gulf of Siam, Cambodia, Annam and the China Sea. Its area is about 22,000 square miles in the entry's measure.

Population in 1901 numbered 2,968,529, of whom 2,558,301 were Annamese, with 231,902 Cambodians, 92,075 Chinese and 4,932 French besides troops. Geography here is chiefly an immense flat, monotonous plain traversed by the Mekong, running from Ha-Tien in the west to Baria in the east. Last spurs of the Annam mountains reach the north-east and east but nowhere exceed 2,900 feet. Low hills in the north-west complete the relief of the colony as described.
britannica-1911-crotona:
Crotona, also called Croto or Croton, was a Greek town on the east coast of Calabria in Italy. Achaeans under Myscellus founded it in 710 before Christ. Legend tied its name to a local prince who hosted Heracles and was killed by him by accident. Like Sybaris, the city soon grew to power and wealth. Its athletes won fame at the Olympic games from 588 before Christ, Milo above all.

Pythagoras settled at Crotona between 540 and 530 before Christ and formed a society of 300 disciples. That body gained great sway with the council of 1,000 that ruled the city. In 510 before Christ Crotona grew strong enough to defeat the Sybarites. The hosted text breaks off at that point, mid-sentence, with the war between the two cities just begun. Nothing later in the city's story survives in the hosted copy.
britannica-1911-cumana:
Cumaná is a city and port of Venezuela, capital of the state of Bermudez, on the Manzanares river a mile above its mouth. It stands 52 feet above the sea and 180 miles east of Caracas. Founded by Diego Castellon in 1523 as Nueva Toledo, it is the oldest lasting European settlement on the South American mainland. Earthquakes destroyed it almost wholly in 1766 and again in 1797. Small shocks still come often, and some damage its buildings.

The mean yearly temperature is 83 degrees, and the entry calls the climate enervating. In colonial times the city was rich, with a fine trade to the mother country and some 30,000 people. Much of that wealth has gone, and the people now number about 10,000. Fine fruits grow round the city. Its exports include cacao, coffee, sugar, hides, and tobacco, and a tramway links it to its port at the river mouth.
britannica-1911-elmina:
Elmina is a town on the Gold Coast of British West Africa, about eight miles west of Cape Coast, with a population of about 4000. The hosted file holds several articles together; this entry is the Elmina article within it.
