Facing the Atlantic on a rocky peninsula stands Fort St George, counted the finest fort on the Guinea coast.

Elmina is the earliest European settlement on the Gold Coast, visited by the Portuguese in 1481, and the Portuguese at once began Fort St George. The Dutch captured the town in 1637 and held it by treaty from 1640, making it the chief port for Ashanti produce. It passed to Great Britain in April 1872 with the other Dutch posts on that coast. The Ashanti king's objection to the transfer led to the Ashanti war of 1873 to 1874. Most of the gold trade moved to Sekondi after 1900.
britannica-1911-etna:
Etna is a volcano on Sicily's east coast, its summit 18 miles north by west of Catania. Its height measured 10,758 feet in 1900, down from 10,870 feet in 1861. It covers about 460 square miles, and the railway round its base runs 86 miles. The cone is cut on the west by the Valle del Bove, a sterile abyss 3 miles wide. Some 200 smaller cones, a few over 3,000 feet high, stud its flanks.

Three zones of growth climb the slopes. Below about 3,000 feet lies the cultivated zone of vegetables, vines and olives, densely peopled. The wooded zone above holds evergreen pines, then birch woods up to about 6,800 feet. The highest zone is stunted and snow-covered most of the year. Only five flowering species grow in its last 2,000 feet, and three are peculiar to the mountain. Ancient writers placed Typhoeus or Enceladus beneath it, or the forge of Hephaestus and the Cyclopes.
britannica-1911-fauna:
Fauna takes its name from a Roman country goddess of fields and cattle. She was known sometimes as sister and sometimes as wife of the god Faunus. From her name the word came to serve a wider use in natural history. It stands for all the animals of a given place, taken together. It can also mean a listing or enumeration of those animals.

The term pairs with flora, which does the same work for plant life. A writer may speak of the fauna of a district or an age. That phrase means its whole animal population, not any single species. The hosted file also carries the closing pages of the Fault article before this short entry. The Fauna text itself is only a few lines long, giving the goddess and the derived meaning.
britannica-1911-fayetteville-north-carol:
Fayetteville is a city and the county-seat of Cumberland county, North Carolina. It stands on the west bank of the Cape Fear river at the head of steamboat navigation. It lies about 80 miles north-west of Wilmington. Its population rose from 4,222 in 1890 to 7,045 in 1910. Railways and steamboat lines to Wilmington serve it. A federal project of 1902 planned an eight-foot channel up the river.

Pine forests surround Fayetteville, and old oaks and elms shade its streets. It has two hospitals, a state coloured normal school and a military school. Creeks and the upper Cape Fear give water-power for local mills. Those mills make cotton goods, silk, lumber, turpentine, carriages and flour. Once a great inland market, it remained a shipping centre for fruit and vegetables. Truck-gardening is important around it, and a large vineyard stands nearby.
britannica-1911-francavilla-fontana:
Francavilla Fontana is a town and episcopal see of Apulia, Italy, in the province of Lecce. It stands 22 miles by rail east by north of Taranto and 460 feet above sea-level. Its population in 1901 was 17,759 in the town and 20,510 in the commune. It sits in a fine situation and has a massive square castle of the Imperiali family. To them, with Oria, the town was sold in the sixteenth century, and the price carries the story that fills this very short entry.

The seller was St Carlo Borromeo, and the price was 40,000 ounces of gold. He distributed the whole sum in one day to the poor, the entry says. That single act of charity is all the history the notice gives. The rest is place and number: an Apulian town, its bishops, its castle, and the saint who sold it and gave away the gold before the day was out.
britannica-1911-francis-iv-of-modena:
Francis IV (1779-1846), duke of Modena, was the son of the archduke Ferdinand, Austrian governor of Lombardy. His father had gained the duchy of Modena through his wife Marie Beatrice, heiress of the house of Este and of many fiefs besides. At the French invasion of 1796 Francis was sent to Vienna to be educated. In 1809 he was appointed governor of Galicia. Later he went to Sardinia, where the exiled King Victor Emmanuel I lived in retirement with his wife Maria Theresa.

Maria Theresa arranged a marriage between her daughter Marie Beatrice and Francis. A secret family compact was made with it. If the king and his two brothers died without male issue, the Salic law would be changed so that Francis, not Charles Albert of Carignano, should succeed to Sardinia's throne. On Napoleon's fall the entry follows him into Modena as its restored duke.
britannica-1911-fuente-ovejuna: Fuente Ovejuna is a town of Spain in the province of Cordova, near the sources of the river Guadiato. It held 11,777 people in 1900 and stands on a hill in a well-watered district. The farms yield wheat, wine, fruit, and honey, and the ground holds silver-bearing lead mines and stone quarries. Cattle breeding is a leading local trade, and leather, preserved meat, soap, and flour are made in the town. The parish church once belonged to the knights of Calatrava.
britannica-1911-galatina: Galatina is a town of Apulia in Italy, in the province of Lecce, fourteen miles south of that city, with 12,917 people in 1901. It is chiefly remarkable for the Gothic church of St Caterina, built in 1390 by Raimondello del Balzo Orsini, count of Soleto, with a fine portal and rose window. Inside are frescoes by Francesco d'Arezzo of 1435, and the apse holds the mausoleum of the founder's son, who died in 1454.
britannica-1911-galena:
Galena is an ore of lead, consisting of lead sulphide, PbS, and mentioned by Pliny under this name. It crystallizes in the cubic system, commonly as cubes or cubo-octahedra, and is always known by its perfect cubical cleavage, on which the lustre is brilliant and metallic. The colour of mineral and streak is lead-grey, the hardness 2½ and the specific gravity 7.5. Its formula gives lead 86.6 and sulphur 13.4 per cent, and it nearly always carries a little silver, so that argentiferous galena is a source of that metal.

Galena occurs widely in veins and as pockets in limestones, often with blende and pyrites, and fine crystals come from Derbyshire, the Isle of Man, the Harz and Missouri. Coarsely grained galena, called potters' ore, serves for glazing pottery. The hosted file also holds neighbouring entries, including the tail of the Galen article and the cities Galena and Galesburg.
britannica-1911-gallia-cisalpina: Gallia Cisalpina was the part of northern Italy south of the Alps and north of Liguria and Umbria, held by Celtic and other peoples in hostility to Rome. Its bound was early the Aesis and in Caesar's time the Rubicon. After the Second Punic War, in 203 B.C., Rome punished its tribes for the help they had given Hannibal. Sulla split the district, setting the part between the Aesis and the Rubicon directly under Rome and the north under a separate command. The hosted file also holds neighbouring entries.
britannica-1911-gatchina:
Gatchina is a town of Russia in the government of St Petersburg, 29 miles by rail south of the capital. The 1911 Britannica entry gives its population as 14,735 in 1897, up from 9,184 in 1860. It sits in flat, well-wooded, partly marshy country, with two lakes on its south side.

Its chief building is the imperial palace, founded in 1770 by Prince Orlov and built to plans by the Italian architect Rinaldi. The entry also names a military orphanage founded in 1803, a school for horticulture, and a porcelain factory among its few works. One event is recorded: at Gatchina, Russia and Sweden concluded an alliance on 29 October 1799. The notice is a short gazetteer entry of place, growth and buildings.
britannica-1911-gilbert-marie-dolores-el:
Marie Dolores Eliza Rosanna Gilbert (1818-1861), known as Lola Montez, was a dancer and adventuress, daughter of a British army officer. The 1911 Britannica entry has her born at Limerick in 1818, educated in Europe, and making a runaway marriage in 1837 with a Captain James of the Indian army.

Divorce followed her return to England in 1842, and she took to the stage as a Spanish dancer, first in London in 1843 without success. Germany, Poland and Russia received her better. At Munich in 1847 she became mistress of Ludwig I of Bavaria, was made countess of Landsfeld, and, the entry says, became the real ruler of Bavaria on a liberal, anti-Jesuit line. Driven out in 1848, she married again in England in 1849 and fled a bigamy charge to Spain.
britannica-1911-guarino-da-verona:
Guarino da Verona (1370–1460) helped restore classical learning in Italy. He was born at Verona in 1370. He studied Greek at Constantinople for five years. His teacher there was Manuel Chrysoloras. He collected precious Greek manuscripts for his return home. One case of them was lost by shipwreck. The loss, legend says, turned his hair grey in a night.

He supported himself by teaching Greek. Verona, Venice and Florence all employed him. In 1436 Lionel, marquis of Este, made him professor at Ferrara. He acted as interpreter for the Greeks in 1438. That was at the councils of Ferrara and Florence. His works include translations of Strabo and Plutarch. He also wrote a compendium of Chrysoloras' Greek grammar. Commentaries on Persius, Juvenal and Martial came from his hand too.
britannica-1911-guibert-of-ravenna:
Guibert of Ravenna (c. 1030–1100) was an antipope. He took the title Clement III in 1080. He held it until his death in 1100. Born at Parma, he came from the imperialist Corregio family. The empress Agnes made him chancellor and imperial vicar in Italy. He presided at the synod of Basel in 1061. That synod set up the antipope Honorius II.

In 1073 he obtained the archbishopric of Ravenna. He swore fealty to Pope Alexander II. Soon he quarrelled with Gregory VII over Imola. He became the soul of the imperial faction. Gregory suspended and later banned him by name. In 1080 Henry IV had him elected pope at Brixen. He was installed in the Lateran in 1084. A week later he crowned Henry emperor. Crusaders drove him from Rome in 1097. He died at Civita Castellana in 1100.
britannica-1911-hanover-indiana:
Hanover is a town of Jefferson county, Indiana. It stands on the Ohio river, below Madison. Its population in 1910 was only 356. River boats and stages to Madison serve it. Hanover College gives the town its importance. The college stands on a bluff 500 feet above the river. Presbyterians control the institution. It offers classical, scientific and music courses. Tuition carries no charge at all.

The school opened in a log cabin in 1827. Incorporation as Hanover Academy came in 1828. The Presbyterian Synod adopted it in 1829. A theological department was the price of adoption. That department later became Chicago's McCormick Seminary. The college tried a manual labour system after 1833. Debt and failure followed that experiment. A stronger charter rescued the college. It became coeducational in 1880. In 1908–1909 it taught 211 students.
britannica-1911-henna:
Henna is the Persian name for a small shrub. It grows in India, Persia, the Levant and Mediterranean Africa. Botanists call it Lawsonia alba. Young trees are spineless, older ones spiny. Hence the names Lawsonia inermis and spinosa. The shrub reaches 8 to 10 feet high. Its leaves are opposite, lance-shaped and smooth. Small white four-petalled flowers scent its panicles. Egyptians call it Khenna, Indians Mendee. England calls it Egyptian privet.

Powdered leaves made into paste form the cosmetic henna. Egyptian and Indian women dye nails, hands and feet with it. The orange-red colour is held to add beauty. It lasts three to four weeks before renewal. Hair, beards and horses' manes take the same dye. Morocco leather takes a reddish-yellow from it too. Egyptian mummies show stained nails from remote ages. Preparation is reducing leaves and young twigs to powder. Flower water serves as a perfume.
britannica-1911-horton-christiana: Christiana Horton (c. 1696–c. 1756) was an English actress. She first appeared in London as Melinda in The Recruiting Officer in 1714, at Drury Lane. She stayed twenty years at that house, then spent fifteen more at Covent Garden. Across that long career she played all the leading parts in tragedy and comedy. Barton Booth, who discovered her, held her the best successor of Mrs Oldfield. She was the first Mariana in Fielding's Miser in 1733. The entry is a short life of a leading stage career.
britannica-1911-horton-samuel-dana:
Samuel Dana Horton (1844–1895) was an American writer on bimetallism, born in Pomeroy, Ohio, on the 16th of January 1844. He graduated at Harvard in 1864 and at its law school in 1868, studied Roman law in Berlin, and entered the Ohio bar in 1871. He practised in Cincinnati and then Pomeroy until 1885, when he gave up law to push the cause of bimetallism.

Money questions had caught Horton during Ohio's greenback campaign of 1875, where he spoke for the Republicans, with special effect in German. He was secretary of the American delegation to the Paris Monetary Conference of 1878 and edited its report. He was a delegate to the 1881 conference, and in 1889 President Harrison sent him to Europe as special commissioner for the restoration of silver. He died in Washington on the 23rd of February 1895. His chief works were The Silver Pound (1887) and Silver in Europe.
britannica-1911-hosanna:
Hosanna is the cry of praise shouted in recognition of Jesus as Messiah on his entry into Jerusalem, and used in the Christian church ever since. It is also a Jewish liturgical word. It named the branches carried in procession at the Feast of Booths or Tabernacles, whose seventh day was called the Hosanna-day. Palm Sunday carries the same echo in Syrian usage.

That feast was joined to a rite of drawing water, believed to secure fertilizing rains for the coming year, with drought the penalty for neglect. Plutarch already thought the festival looked like a rite for Dionysus. The account weighs the evidence from Leviticus, the Maccabees, Josephus and the Talmud. It points toward rites of nature-worship, in which the word may once have had some other use than praise.
britannica-1911-john-of-ravenna:
John of Ravenna is not one man but a name shared by distinct figures of the late 14th and early 15th centuries. They were long confused with each other and with a third, unnamed Ravennese in Petrarch's letters. The entry works to pull the lives apart and give each man his own record.

The first was a young Ravennese, born about 1347. He lived with Petrarch as his secretary from 1364 and left him for good in 1368 after restless travel. The second, a son of Conversanus, became professor of rhetoric at Florence in 1368. He served the Carrara house of Padua and was chancellor to Francis of Carrara from 1395 to 1404. His pupils included Vittorino da Feltre and Guarino of Verona. The third, Malpaghini, born about 1356, was Petrarch's pupil. He taught rhetoric at Florence from 1397 and died in May 1417. He left nothing behind him, but his pupils included Poggio Bracciolini.
britannica-1911-jumna:
The Jumna, or Jamuna, is a river of northern India. Its segment sits in a hosted file shared with the Jumala, Jumièges, and Jumilla entries. It rises in the Himalayas in Tehri state, near the Jamnotri hot springs, and runs south and southwest through the hills. At its 95th mile it forces a way through the Siwalik hills and comes out on the plains at Fyzabad.

From Fyzabad it gives off the eastern and western Jumna canals. It then flows south to Delhi, on past Muttra, and east past Agra, Ferozabad, and Etawah. The Chambal joins it from the west, and the Betwa and the Ken join in its last reach. Below Allahabad it falls into the Ganges. The entry is a course record, reach by reach, with the towns, feeders, and canals of each stretch named in turn.
britannica-1911-katsena:
Katsena was an ancient state of the western Sudan, now counted in the province of Kano in the British protectorate of Northern Nigeria. It ranked among the oldest of the Hausa states. Manuscripts carry its history back about 1000 years. Tradition traces the Hausa people to Bajibda of Bagdad and a primeval queen of Daura.

The Fula conquest of the Habe of Katsena, early in the 19th century, changed the country little. The more cultivated Habe were already Muslim, and the new rulers took up the customs and the system of rule they found. Those systems were in many ways highly grown, with set forms of taxation and justice. The capital is a town of the same name, 160 miles east by south of Sokoto and 84 miles northwest of Kano. Its walls run 13 to 14 miles round, though little of the ground inside is built on.
britannica-1911-krishna:
Krishna, "the Dark One," is an incarnation of Vishnu, and the form in which Vishnu is most loved across northern India. In origin he was a hero of the Kshatriya caste raised to godhood. In the older frame of the Mahabharata he stands as a great chief and ally of the Pandava brothers. In the Bhagavad-gita he is named as Vishnu himself, teaching bhakti, or devotion. The hosted text for this entry sits inside a shared file that holds parts of neighbouring entries; the passage described here is the Krishna article itself.

Later legend makes him a king's son saved from a slaughter of children and raised by a cowherd near Muttra on the Jumna. His cult runs through the sect founders Vallabha and Chaitanya. His lawful wife was Rukmini, yet Radha is the figure always joined with him in his temples.
britannica-1911-laguna:
Laguna, or La Laguna, is an episcopal city and was formerly the capital of the island of Teneriffe in the Canary Islands. Its population in 1900 was 13,074. It stands 4 m. N. by W. of Santa Cruz, in a plain 1800 ft. above sea-level and ringed by mountains. Snow is unknown there and the mean annual temperature passes 63° F., but the rainfall is very heavy and in winter the plain is sometimes flooded.

That damp air, with the warm climate and rich volcanic soil, makes the district exceptionally fertile: wheat, wine, tobacco, oranges and other fruits grow in abundance. Laguna is the favourite summer residence of the wealthier people of Santa Cruz. Besides its cathedral it has secularized convents, a fine modern town hall, hospitals, a large public library and old palaces of the Spanish nobility. Even modern buildings look ancient, from damp decay and climbing plants.
britannica-1911-leon-of-modena:
Leon of Modena (1571-1648) was a Jewish scholar born in Venice. His French family had moved to Italy after the Jews were cast out of France. A bright child, he lacked the steady bent to ripen his gifts. Graetz lists a crowd of trades he took up to live.

Preacher, teacher, reader of prayers, broker, rabbi, and maker of amulets all appear. Real weight came from his attacks. One work struck at the Kabbala. It showed the Zohar to be a modern piece. That book saw print only in 1840. Wider fame came from Riti Ebraici in 1637. The book set out synagogue customs for Christian readers. An English version by Edward Chilmead came in 1650. It fed strong interest in London at the time.
buddhism-and-buddhists-in-china:
Lewis Hodous wrote a study of Buddhist faith and folk in China. Seven chapters frame the work, each split in fine parts. Entry of the faith into China holds the second place. Its rise to first place in the land holds the third, worked through spirit world, forebear rule, Taoist decay, and Confucian order.

The farm folk's faith holds the fourth place, told through the Kushan monastery. Rain prayers, feng-shui rule, and monastery funds fill it. Home life comes next: Kuan Yin as giver of children and guard of women leads. Social life and the life to come close the frame. Purgatory, heaven, and the harm of the faith get plain heads there. Death rites, veg-only sects, and pilgrim roads fill out the lived side of the creed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abbey-of-vads:
The Catholic Encyclopedia entry on Vadstena describes the motherhouse of the Brigittine Order, on Lake Wetter in Sweden's Linköping diocese. St. Bridget founded it in 1346 with Magnus the Second and Blanche of Namur's help. Yet St. Catherine, arriving in 1374 with her mother Bridget's relics, found just a handful of novices under an Augustinian head.

The novices chose Catherine as abbess, and after her death in 1381 the Bishop of Linköping blessed the abbey in 1384. Bridget's canonisation in 1391 and translation in 1394 greatly increased Vadstena's fame and riches. In 1400 Eric of Pomerania was invested there by Queen Margaret with royal rights over Denmark, Norway and Sweden. Brigittine literature, mostly Swedish translations of Bible portions and saints' legends, survives through the Old Swedish Texts Society.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-adana:
Adana is an Armenian-rite diocese in Asia Minor, in Asiatic Turkey. An ancient Phoenician colony of willows, it sits some nineteen miles inland, in the heart of Cilicia Campestris, on the Sarus's right bank, or Seyhoun. Once part of the Seleucid kingdom, it took the name Antioch of Sarus after Antiochus Epiphanes in 171 BC. It then took Hadriana from Hadrian and Maximiana from Maximianus, and it holds weight as capital of its district.

Adana emerges in the fourth century as a see under Tarsus and Antioch's patriarch. In the Middle Ages the Greek hierarchy faded, leaving a single prelate styling himself Metropolitan of Tarsus and Adana. Most diocesans, foreigners from Cappadocia or the Archipelago, cling to Hellenism and quarrel with Antioch over an Arabic-speaking prelate elected in 1899. Medieval Adana had an Armenian bishop under Sis.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-agustin-quint:
Agustin Quintana was a missionary and Indian philologist born at Antequera, capital of Oaxaca, Mexico, about 1660. He died at Oaxaca in 1734, having entered the Order of Preachers in Antequera in 1688 and soon been sent as missionary priest to southern Oaxaca's Mixe Indians. Among them he laboured twenty-eight years, mastering their difficult language beyond any other white man.

Superior of Zacavila's convent followed, but broken health soon retired him to the main convent at Antequera. There he spent his remaining life writing in the Mixe language, the earliest publication in which prompted several journeys to Puebla despite age and infirmity to supervise the making of several types. A grammar and articles on the Faith's principal articles, Institucion cristiana, Puebla 1729, stands as his most important work.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alonzo-de-bar:
Alonzo de Barcena, also Barzana, was a native of Baeza in Andalusia, born in 1528, dead at Cuzco in Peru in January 1598. He became a Jesuit in 1565, went to Paris in 1569. Ordered in 1577 to Juli, on Lake Titicaca, he became one of the founders of that important mission. After eleven years in central Bolivia, Provincial Atienza sent him to Tucumán in Argentina. His work among the tribes of that region and Paraguay continued until he became Inquisition Commissary in those provinces.

Exhausted by long labours, Barcena died at Cuzco. He is credited with practical knowledge of eleven Indian languages and grammars, vocabularies, and catechisms in most of them, manuscripts possibly still in Lima's archives. Only one writing is known published: a letter of ethnographic and linguistic detail on the Tucumán Indians, the Calchaquis, and others. It is dated 8 September 1594 at Asunción, Paraguay, addressed to Provincial John Sebastian.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alphonso-de-s:
Alphonso de Spina, Spanish Franciscan, died about 1491. A convert from Judaism, he long headed Salamanca's Friars Minor house of studies, and in 1491 became Bishop of Thermopylae in Greece. A man of great learning and preaching renown, his chief title to fame is Fortalitium Fidei. Mariana calls it learned, splendidly titled, barbarously voiced, excellent in divinity. The anonymous work disputed authorship.

One edition under Totani, O.P., explains its inclusion in the Dominican Scriptores. Its author was certainly a Franciscan, as Echard notes, and scholars attribute it to Alfonso de Spina. Fortalitium Fidei arms preachers and others against Christianity's enemies. It has five books: deniers of Christ's divinity, heretics, Jews, and Mohammedans. A fifth treats the battle against the Gates of Hell, dwelling on demons hating men. Besides the Fortalitium, Spina published three other works, including twenty-two Sermons on the Name of Jesus, about 1454.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-altoona:
Altoona is a suffragan see of Philadelphia province, its city on the Allegheny Mountains' eastern slope, midway between Harrisburg and Pittsburgh, 1,175 feet above sea level. Its name comes from the Cherokee Allatoona, meaning high land of great worth. The town, little over fifty years old, is largely the Pennsylvania Railroad's creation, its workshops employing about fourteen thousand men.

The Diocese of Altoona was established in May 1901, comprising Cambria, Blair, Bedford, Huntingdon, and Somerset counties. Pioneer priests included Father James Bradley of Newry, and Carroltown, founded in 1839 and named for Archbishop Carroll, ranks next to Loretto in historical importance. The diocese counts seventy-four secular priests and sixteen regulars, with forty lay brothers.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ancona-and-um:
Ancona and Umana form an Italian diocese in the archdiocese of Ancona, covering ten towns in the province of Ancona. Ancona is an important Adriatic seaport for trade between East and Italy. A Christian community must have stood within its walls at a very early date. Excavations at Varano, near Ancona, turned up a burial stone with a Christian inscription from the end of the third century.

That find suggests Ancona's church had no catacombs, but an open burial ground. Harnack argued it proves a well-organized community before Constantine. Eusebius records that Bishop Cornelius of Rome held a synod of sixty Italian bishops against Novatian in 250. Since not every bishop attended synods, Rome's rule about 250 must have covered at least two hundred bishoprics. Christians thus lived in all chief cities, Ancona among them. The city stands under the protection of the very ancient saints Primianus and Cyriacus.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-andrea-adami-:
Andrea Adami da Bolsena, an Italian musician, was born at Bolsena in 1663 and died at Rome in 1742. Through Cardinal Pietro Ottoboni's influence he was appointed master of the papal choir, the body of singers serving the pope's chapel. The post placed him at the heart of Roman church music in his day.

He left a history of the choir, with portraits and memoirs of its singers. Its long title was Osservazioni per ben regolare il coro dei cantori della Cappella Pontificia. It was published at Rome in 1711. Romans held him in high esteem, for his personal gifts as well as his musical ones, and his book remains a first-hand record of the papal singers.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-andrea-manteg:
Andrea Mantegna, an Italian painter, was born in 1431, at Vicenza by some accounts and Padua by others, and died at Mantua in 1506. Of honourable parentage, he was adopted in childhood by Francesco Squarcione, who reared him as a son. He worked on masterpieces at an age when most artists still learn their craft. He owed little to Squarcione, founder of the Paduan school, whose ability was mediocre.

His earliest known work, a Madonna in Glory painted at seventeen for Saint Sofia at Padua, no longer survives. The Eremitani frescoes for the Ovetari, probably from 1448 to 1455, made his name. After two years of persuasion he accepted the Mantuan court in 1459 and stayed there, apart from decorating a Vatican chapel for Innocent VIII, for the rest of his life. His manner, called dry and hard, shows marvellous modelling, and he ranks among Italy's earliest copper engravers.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-andreas-agnel:
Andreas Agnellus of Ravenna, historian of his church, was born in 805, and his death date is unknown, though probably about 846. Called abbot of Saint Mary ad Blachernas and later of Saint Bartholomew, he seems to have stayed a secular priest, titular abbot only of each house. He is best known for his Liber Pontificalis Ecclesiae Ravennatis, an account of his native see's occupants, modelled on the Roman Liber Pontificalis.

It runs from Saint Apollinaris to Georgius, the forty-eighth archbishop, in 846. Though it holds much unreliable material, it stands as a unique and rich source on Ravenna's buildings, inscriptions, manners, and religious customs in the ninth century. The author shows strong bias, exalting Ravenna's traditional independence, or autocephalia, against the Holy See, a polemical Gallican stance for his time. Personal vanity marks the work, and his erudition often falls into grave errors, with barbarous diction and a corrupt text.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-anna:
Anna, Hebrew for graciousness, is the name of four women in Scripture. Anna, mother of Samuel, was a wife of Elcana of Ramah. She felt keenly the reproach of barrenness, as her rival Phenenna reminded her of her affliction. On a pilgrimage to Silo, Anna vowed to consecrate a son to God's service as a Nazarite. Her prayer was heard, and after weaning him she brought him to the temple.

Anna, wife of Tobias, of Nephtali, was taken with husband and son captive to Ninive by Shalmanaser. Her role is secondary, but her passionate nature brings out Tobias's religious character and her love for her son. Anna the prophetess, daughter of Phanuel, of Aser, widowed early, never married again, and devoted her life to Temple service, where she praised God. Anna is also the traditional name of the mother of the Blessed Virgin Mary.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-anna-comnena:
Anna Comnena, Byzantine historian, was the eldest daughter of Emperor Alexius Comnenus. Born in 1083, she received an excellent education in Greek classics, history, and philosophy. Married to Nicephorus Bryennius, she joined a 1118 conspiracy to place her husband on the throne. Failing, she retired with her mother Irene to a monastery and wrote her Alexiad in fifteen books.

Finished by 1148, it describes her father's career, 1069 to 1118, continuing her husband's Materials. The Princess is the historian of the Comneni fortunes, and her observations carry personal knowledge. As a true Byzantine she views the Crusades from Constantinople's standpoint, detests all Latins, and her chronology is defective. She loves scenes of splendour, state actions, and feasts, and is not adverse to satire and court gossip, while financial matters escape her. Krumbacher calls it a remarkable effort of medieval Greek historiography. She strains for Attic elegance, imitating Thucydides, yet her prose seems mummy-like.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-anthony-of-si:
Anthony of Sienna took his name from his veneration of Saint Catharine of Sienna. This Dominican theologian, born near Braga in Portugal, hence Lusitanus, died at Nantes in 1585. He studied at Lisbon, Coimbra, and Louvain, taught philosophy for several years at Louvain, became Doctor of Theology in 1571, and took charge of the Dominican college there in 1574. He backed the Portuguese pretender Antonio de Beja, was banished from Spanish dominions, and then travelled in Italy, England, and France for scientific purposes.

He helped make the Roman edition of Saint Thomas's works (1570-71), prepared by order of Saint Pius V. At Antwerp in 1569 he published an edition of the Summa Theologica. A Genesis commentary he edited at Antwerp as a work of Saint Thomas is not authentic. His edition of the saint's Machabees commentary, prepared at Paris in 1584, came out in 1612 through Cosme Morelles in the Antwerp edition of Saint Thomas's works.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-antonello-da-:
Antonello da Messina, a Sicilian painter born about 1430, brought Flemish oil painting to Italy. After study in Sicily and Naples, he saw a Van Eyck owned by the king of Aragon and set himself to master the northern method. Whether he sailed to Bruges remains disputed, but his command of oil colour, learned from Van Eyck's disciples, is certain.

Back in Messina he painted a triptych of the Virgin with Gregory and Benedict, later lost in an earthquake, and works praised for strong, clear landscapes. His Crucifixion sets a crowded Calvary scene inside a harmonious landscape. The entry traces a painter who helped bring oil painting into Italian practice.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-antonino-dian:
Antonino Diana, a Sicilian moral theologian born at Palermo in 1586, became famous for solving cases of conscience. A Theatine clerk from 1630, he received hard moral questions from all parts, and his Resolutions in Moral Theology won wide esteem. Popes Urban the Eighth, Innocent the Tenth, and Alexander the Seventh valued his learning and made him an examiner of bishops.

Diana usually followed the milder opinion, and admirers played on his name, calling his book a Diana to guide hunters for truth through the woods of moral theology. Later theologians, including Saint Alphonsus, judged that he often went too far toward laxity, excusing too much. Epitomes of his work spread even in his lifetime, despite his protests that admirers distorted his meaning.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-antonio-de-mo:
Spanish Carthusian Antonio de Molina was born about 1560 and dead at Miraflores in 1612 or 1619. He wrote ascetical books, works on the spiritual life, that became the most popular of their kind in Spain. He first joined the Augustinian Hermits, taught theology, and served as a house superior. Then he sought a stricter order and became a Carthusian at Miraflores, where he later died as prior, the head of the monastery. His books were written in Spanish and aimed above all at priests.

The most famous, Instruction of Priests, ran to twenty known editions and was translated into Latin and Italian. The Jansenist Antoine Arnauld attacked it sharply in 1643, and the theologian Petavius defended it in reply. The entry shows a writer whose plain guidance for clergy travelled widely, drew fire from critics, and kept its place through many reprintings.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-argentina:
Argentina, the Argentine Republic, is a South American confederation of fourteen provinces, called states, united by a federal constitution framed along the lines of the United States constitution. The provinces run from Buenos Aires, Santa Fé, and Entre Ríos through Córdoba, Mendoza, and Tucumán to Salta and Jujuy, each with its own constitution and self-government. The federal constitution was promulgated on 25 September 1860, and the union's official name is the Argentine Nation.

Besides the fourteen commonwealths, fourteen national territories depend on the federal executive, governed by presidential appointees with Senate consent. They are Misiones, Formosa, Chaco, Los Andes, La Pampa, Neuquén, Río Negro, Chubut, Santa Cruz, and Tierra del Fuego among them. The long article moves from that federal frame to church history, dioceses, and Catholic life across a vast republic still filling its territories.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-arizona:
Arizona, probably in its original form Arizonac, a Pima Indian word of unknown meaning, though a Spanish origin has also been suggested, bears the motto Ditat Deus, God enriches. It was then a continental territory of the United States, bounded by Utah to the north and Mexico to the south. New Mexico territory lay to the east, and California and Nevada to the west. It lay between latitudes 31 and 37 north and longitudes 109 and 115 west.

The region passed to the United States from Mexico in part in 1848 under the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo and the rest in 1854 by the Gadsden Treaty. Up to 1863 it formed part of New Mexico territory, and at acquisition Indians were almost its only inhabitants, in a country reputed rich in precious metals. Those who flocked to the new domain included miners, settlers, and missionaries, and its history follows territory, church, and frontier together.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-augustin-more:
Agustin Moreto y Cabana was a Spanish dramatist born at Madrid in 1618 who died at Toledo in 1669. He studied at Alcala, took his arts degree in 1639, and began writing for the stage while still very young. From about 1640, likely through friendship with Calderon, his plays reached production. Spanish drama had peaked in his boyhood and was now in decline, while clergy preached against the stage.

In 1644 the Royal Council reformed the theater, cutting companies, curbing costumes, and imposing strict censorship. Only historical plays and lives of saints might now be staged, and Moreto turned to those forms for a time. He lacked the creative genius of his peers but beat them all in stagecraft and in reaching the point fast. His best play, El Desden con el Desden, borrowed from Lope de Vega, is judged better than its source, while Moliere's attempt to match it fell far short.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ave-regina:
Ave Regina, named from its first line Ave Regina Caelorum, Hail, Queen of Heaven, is one of four antiphons of the Blessed Virgin sung through the year. It is assigned from Compline of 2 February to Holy Thursday. It holds two stanzas of four lines each, with its versicle, response, and prayer. Its date is uncertain, and Stella's guess that it predates the fourth century lacks warrant.

The antiphon appears in the St Alban's book of the twelfth century and a Munich manuscript of the thirteenth. It also appears in a Sarum Breviary of the fourteenth and York and Roman Breviaries of the fifteenth. Bernard holds that Clement VI brought it into the Divine Office in the fourteenth century. Sung through Septuagesima, Lent, and Passiontide, it recalls Mary's part in reopening Heaven as Queen of Angels. Caswall's version, Hail, O Queen of Heaven Enthroned, is used in the Manual of Prayers.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-avicenna:
Avicenna, in full Ibn Ali al-Hosain Ibn Abdallah Ibn Sina, was a physician and philosopher born at Bokhara in 980, who died at Hamadan in Persia in 1037. Though the Latins gave him an Arabic-sounding name, he was Persian, not Arabian. A precocious youth, he knew the Koran by heart at ten. He mastered physics, mathematics, logic, and metaphysics before sixteen, and began medicine at sixteen. Before twenty-one he wrote his Canon of medical science, the chief authority in medical schools for centuries.

He served Persian rulers in turn as physician and adviser, traveling with their courts, and wrote some hundred volumes. Besides the Canon he wrote commentaries on Aristotle and two encyclopedias, al-Shifa, meaning healing, and al-Najat, meaning deliverance. Latin versions appeared from the twelfth century and reached print at Venice in 1493 to 1495. The Schoolmen, sensing pantheistic drifts in his philosophy, grew wary of his Aristotle.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-balthasar-sen:
Balthasar Sena was a missionary and philologist born at Barcelona about 1590, who died at Guarambare, Paraguay, in 1614. He entered the Jesuit novitiate at Tarragona in 1608, then volunteered for Paraguay's Guarani missions before finishing his studies. Sailing from Lisbon in 1610 with veteran Juan Romero, he kept studying on the voyage.

The rest of his life passed at Guarambare and among the kindred Itatines, whose language he studied and set in dictionary form. Indians loved him for his virtues and his courage in defending natives against slave-dealers. He refused preferment at Santa Fe to stay with his mission work. After fearless ministry through a contagious epidemic, he caught a fever no medicine could reach and died in great suffering.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-barcelona:
Barcelona, ancient Barcino, is a suffragan diocese of Tarragona and the capital of Catalonia, on Spain's northeastern coast. Familiarly called the Queen of the Mediterranean, it ranks as Spain's most important city after the capital. Founded by Hamilcar, it passed from Carthage to Rome, which favored it highly. Julius Caesar named it Julia Augusta Faventia, made it a colony, and granted its people full Roman citizenship.

Ataulf made it his Visigothic residence in 415, and Arabs took it in 713, Franks in 801. Wilfrid the Hairy then declared independence, founding the County of Barcelona. Petronilla's 1137 marriage to Barcelona's count united Aragon and Catalonia, one kingdom from 1164. By 1906 the diocese held 231 parishes, 1,180 secular priests, and a population of 1,054,531, nearly all Catholic.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bartholomew-m:
Bartholomew Medina was a Dominican theologian born at Medina in 1527, who died at Salamanca in 1581. With Soto, Canus, and Bañez, he studied theology at Salamanca under Francis Vittoria. He spent his life teaching theology there, first in the chair of Durandus, then as principal professor. Winning a public contest against the Augustinian John of Guevara, he took the cathedra primaria.

Though versed in Greek and Hebrew, he loved theology more, writing chiefly commentaries on St Thomas's Summa. He is usually called the Father of Probabilism, for his dictum that a probable opinion may be followed even when its opposite is more probable. Writers divide over whether he introduced, merely formulated, or only opened the way to the system. His chief works include commentaries of 1577 and 1584 and a 1580 instruction on administering penance.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bartolomeo-mo:
Bartolomeo Montagna was an Italian painter, chief representative of the Vicenza School, born about 1450, who died at Vicenza in 1523. Little is known of his life. His work happily combines Padua and Venice: grand forms and draperies with Bellini-like symmetry and coloring. Early Madonnas at Vicenza and Bergamo show stiffness and dryness, in the old distemper manner.

His best period ran from 1490 to 1505, years of work and travel across the district. At Verona he painted house façades in fresco, along with the graceful, now damaged Chapel of St Blaise paintings of 1493. Their cupola's angel panels, saint figures, and Nereid frieze show the Renaissance's delightful inconsistency. His son Benedetto, chiefly an engraver, proved only a feeble imitator of his father as a painter.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bartolomeo-pl:
Bartolomeo Platina, originally Sacchi, was born near Mantua in 1421 and died at Rome in 1481. First a soldier, then tutor to the Gonzaga sons, he studied Greek at Florence under Argyropulos in 1457. In May 1464 he joined Pius II's reorganized College of Abbreviators. When Paul II abolished Pius's ordinances, Platina lost his office and answered with an insolent pamphlet demanding recall.

Imprisoned in Castel Sant'Angelo, he was freed after four months on condition he stay at Rome. In February 1468 he was jailed again with some twenty Humanists on suspicion of heresy and conspiracy, but acquitted on both. Paul II still refused his services, and at Sixtus IV's suggestion Platina wrote his Lives of the Popes in revenge. His tale of constancy under trial and torture is unfounded.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bartolommeo-s:
Bartolommeo Spina was a scholastic theologian born at Pisa about 1475, who died at Rome in 1546. Joining the Dominicans about 1494, he taught for many years in his order's schools. In 1536 Venice's Senate gave him Padua's theology chair, and in July 1542 Paul III made him Master of the Sacred Palace.

For four years he served the Holy See and Trent's Fathers on difficult, disputed questions. From 1518 he fought a heated controversy with Cardinal Cajetan, and he denounced Ambrose Catharinus for heresy in 1546. His chief works defend the soul's immortality against Pomponazzi, and his 1523 treatise treats witches and sorceresses. In a 1533 treatise he opposed the doctrine of the Immaculate Conception.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bernard-of-bo: Bernard of Bologna, a Capuchin theologian also called Bernardine, was born at Bologna in 1701 and died in 1768. He entered the Capuchins in 1717 and taught moral and dogmatic theology. His best-known work, a bibliography of Capuchin writers published at Venice in 1747, mirrors Wadding's famous list of Franciscan authors, with an appendix at Rome in 1852.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bernardo-de-b: Bernardo de Balbuena, a Spanish poet, was born at Val de Peñas in 1568 and died in Puerto Rico in 1627. Taken young to Mexico, he was educated there, spent twelve years in Jamaica, and ended as Bishop of Puerto Rico from 1620. His Mexican Grandeur of 1604 and his pastoral romance Golden Age in the Woods of Eriphile of 1608 show learned, beautiful verse, though the romance ignores New World scenery and history.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bibbiena:
Bibbiena, the Italian cardinal and comedy writer Bernardo Dovizi, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born at Bibbiena in 1470, he died at Rome in 1520. Obscure birth did not bar him from the best Florentine scholars, and a jovial temper with racy Tuscan wit made him tutor and boon companion to Giovanni de' Medici.

When the Medici fell in 1494, the gay man of the world showed steel, following his patron into exile and service. As cardinal under Leo X, the former Giovanni, he served as diplomat and patron of letters. His comedy La Calandria, a witty stage piece, keeps his name alive as a writer.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bl-ambrose-of:
Blessed Ambrose of Siena, a Dominican friar, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born at Siena in 1220 to the noble Sansedoni family, he died there in 1286. Cured of a birth deformity as an infant in the Dominican church, he grew noted for charity to pilgrims, hospital sick, and prisoners.

He entered the Dominicans at seventeen, studied at Paris under Albert the Great beside Thomas Aquinas, and taught with Thomas at Cologne from 1248. Later missions as peacemaker between Italian cities marked his age. The entry presents a gentle friar whose learning served reconciliation.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-blessed-marga:
Margaret Colonna, a Roman Poor Clare, gave up a rich marriage prospect to live in prayer and serve the poor near Palestrina. Orphaned young, she was raised with her brothers, one a cardinal. She refused the chief magistrate of Rome and withdrew to a lonely retreat of penance and charity.

Through her cardinal brother she gained canonical standing for a Palestrina community of Urbanist Poor Clares. She probably led it herself. A painful ulcer marked her last seven years. She bore it with resignation until her death in 1284. Her community later moved to San Silvestro in Rome, and her body to Santa Cecilia in Trastevere.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bosnia-and-he:
Bosnia and Herzegovina, the northwestern corner of the Balkan Peninsula, form a near-triangle of Karst mountains between Croatia, Serbia, Montenegro, and Dalmatia. The joint land covers about 19,702 square miles and belonged in name to the Turkish Empire. By Article 25 of the Berlin Treaty of 1878, Austria-Hungary won the right to occupy and rule it as crown provinces.

Limestone highlands shape the country, with fertile valleys in the forested north and one flat district, Posavina, on the Save. The Save drains Bosnia, the Narenta drains Herzegovina, and peaks near Sarajevo top 6,800 feet. Later sections give population, a history from Illyrian and Roman times through Slav settlement and native bans, the coming of Christianity, and church statistics.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cana:
Cana, a city of Galilee, is famed as the scene of Christ's first miracle, turning water into wine at the marriage feast. John's Gospel names it twice more, for the healing of the ruler's son at a distance and as the birthplace of Nathanael, or Saint Bartholomew. No Gospel clue fixes its site, except that it lay near Nazareth and Capernaum and higher than the latter.

Old tradition, reaching back at least to the eighth century, matches Cana with Kefr' Kenna. The village lies four or five miles northeast of Nazareth, where Franciscans now hold a large new church over remains of the old one. Greeks nearby keep a church with two great jars claimed as the original water pots, though their genuineness is doubtful. A church of Saint Bartholomew stands at the town's far end, said to mark his house.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-carlo-fontana:
Carlo Fontana was an architect and writer born near Como in 1634 who died at Rome in 1714. No proof ties him to the famous family of architects sharing his name. In Rome he studied under Bernini and built widely. His works include the Ginetti and Cibo chapels, the cupola and great altar of the Madonna de' Miracoli, and the façades of Beata Rita and San Marcolo in the Corso.

For Innocent XI he raised the vast San Michele at Ripa and finished Monte Citorio. For Clement XI he built granaries at Termini and the portico of Santa Maria in Trastevere. He restored the Minerva Library and the Montefiascone cupola, sent models to Fulda and Vienna, and wrote on the Flavian Amphitheatre, the aqueducts, and the Tiber floods. Aided by his nephews Girolamo and Francesco, he counted, the entry judges, a better architect than writer.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-carlo-maderna:
Carlo Maderna, who lived from 1556 to 1629, is known above all for extending St. Peter's at the pope's command from a Greek-cross plan to a Latin-cross plan. Regard for church tradition favored the long nave, even though it weakened the dome's effect. Beginning in 1605, forty years after Michelangelo's death, he drew the columns closer to soften the harm, at the cost of the once unbroken side-aisle views.

The widened façade, an ornamental screen apart from the building itself, measures 112 metres long and 44 high. Eight giant columns 27 metres tall stand below statues of Christ and the Apostles. Corner masses meant for bell towers still stand towerless, softening the effect. Maderna also built part of the Palazzo Mattei, shared the Palazzo Barberini with Bernini, worked in the Quirinal Gardens, and designed fortifications at Ferrara.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cesena:
Cesena, the ancient Cæsena, is an Emilian city in Forlì province, in the former States of the Church, set picturesquely on a hill above the Savio river. Probably of Gallic origin, it fell to Roman rule in the third century B.C., was destroyed in the civil wars of Marius and Sulla, and after the Ostrogoths' fall joined the exarchate. By the Donation of Pepin in 752 it became a fief of the Holy See, confirmed by Rudolph of Hapsburg in 1278.

In medieval times the Ordelaffi of Forlì and the Malatesta governed it, the latter remembered for just and good government. After Caesar Borgia's death it acknowledged the Holy See directly in 1503. Among its famous sons were Popes Pius VI and Pius VII. Its bishops include St. Maurus, who died in 946, and Vincenzo Maria Orsini, a Dominican who became Benedict XIII. The diocese, suffragan to Ravenna, counted 59 parishes and 66,700 inhabitants.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-china:
A vast general entry on the Chinese Empire, Eastern Asia's largest political division, stretching from Siberia to the Pacific and from Russian Turkistan to Burma. China proper, the Eighteen Provinces, covers about two million square miles, and its population was reckoned in 1906 at over 438 million, though estimates ranged lower. The entry lists the empire's many names, from Chung Kwo, the Middle Kingdom, to the literary T'ien Hsia, Under Heaven.

History fills much of the article, from early dynasties through foreign pressure in the nineteenth century to the Boxer rising of 1900. Missionaries were murdered, the German minister was killed, and the Peking legations were besieged until an international army relieved the city and the Catholic cathedral. Leases of ports to foreign powers, and the reform attempt of 1898 cut short by the Empress Dowager, frame the empire's troubled close to the century.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cinna:
Kinna, a titular see of Asia Minor, lay probably in the north-west of the rich corn country called Haimane, west of Angora. Its exact site cannot be fixed, though it must have stood near Balyk Koyounji or closer to the River Sangarius. The see was suffragan to Ancyra in Galatia Prima.

Lequien names ten bishops of Kinna. The first, Gorgonius, attended Nicaea in 325. The tenth, Angonius, backed Photius in 879. Another bishop, Sabas, probably supported Saint Ignatius. The see also appears in the later lists of bishoprics known as the Notitiae episcopatuum.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ciriaco-d-anc:
Ciriaco of Ancona, whose family name was Pizzicolli, was an Italian antiquary born about 1391 and dead about 1455 at Cremona. On trading voyages through the East he gathered a great store of inscriptions, manuscripts, and antiquities. By 1426 he had visited Rhodes, Beirut, Damascus, Cyprus, Mitylene, and Thessalonica. In 1443 he worked in the Morea, copying inscriptions known from the letters of Filelfo and others.

Eugenius the Fourth, Cosimo de Medici, and the Visconti of Milan patronised him. He counts as the best equipped and most accurate worker in Renaissance epigraphy, the study of inscriptions. De Rossi called his copying accuracy Ciriaco's chief credit and undying glory. Most of his manuscripts are lost, though his Itinerarium and a rare volume of epigrams found in Illyricum reached print after his death.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-colonna:
James Loughlin's entry follows the Colonna, a celebrated family of medieval and Renaissance Italy. Branches still flourish in Rome and Naples. The house is commonly traced to the Counts of Tusculum, taking its name from the castle of Colonna on the Alban hills. Its name enters history with Petrus de Columna, owner of Colonna, Monte Porzio, and Zagarolo. Paschal II seized his castles in 1101 for lawless raids. When Romans destroyed Tusculum in 1191, the old counts vanished and the Colonna stepped forward.

From the first their policy was anti-papal and Ghibelline, more from rivalry with Rome than from love of emperors. A long line of Colonnese cardinals opened in 1192 with Giovanni the Elder. Punished for their Ghibellinism, no Colonna entered the Sacred College again until 1278, under the Orsini pope Nicholas III. Later figures, like Prospero's nephew Giovanni, served the family across five pontificates, from Sixtus IV to Julius II.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-comana:
Comana, a titular see of Asia Minor in Cappadocia's district of Cataonia, is traced here by Sophrone Pétridès. Eustathius surnamed it Chryse, or Golden, and inscriptions add Hieropolis, from its temple of the goddess Enyo, or Ma. Strabo and Caesar visited it. Strabo details its site on the Sarus, its temple, and its temple servants. Saint Basiliscus died there and was buried there. Palladius calls him its bishop, though Pétridès marks that claim doubtful.

Known bishops run from Elpidius at Nicaea in 325 to Theodorus at the Fifth Ecumenical Council in 553. Leontius, a Semi-Arian, held the see under Emperor Jovian. Heraclius appeared at Chalcedon in 451, when Comana stood as suffragan of Melitene. Its ruins lie ten miles northwest of Guksun, in the vilayet of Adana. A second Comana in Pontus, with its own temple of Ma, and a third in Pamphylia, rightly Conana, get notes.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-copacavana:
Adolph Francis Bandelier's entry describes Copacavana, also Copacabana, a village of about four hundred people, Indians chiefly, on Lake Titicaca in Omasuyos province, northern Bolivia. It holds a famous sanctuary of Our Lady of Carmel and a convent of Franciscan Recollects. Independence wars stripped it of most rich ornaments and gifts, while plundering by faithless custodians during political disturbances further impoverished it. Pilgrims from Bolivia and southern Peru frequent the shrine, thousands attending the patron feast on 6 August.

Before 1534 Copacavana served as an Inca outpost, perhaps the only prominent one on Bolivian soil. The Incas held it as key to a very ancient shrine and oracle nearby. In 1582 an Indian from Copacavana, struck by statues of the Blessed Virgin seen in La Paz churches, tried to fashion one himself, succeeding after many trials. Old pagan practice mixed with Christian observance mortifies Bolivian clergy unable to modify it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cortona:
Umberto Benigni's entry covers the Diocese of Cortona, Cortonensis, immediately subject to the Holy See. Cortona is a small city in Arezzo province, Tuscany, Central Italy, on a commanding hill overlooking Lake Perugia. Its cyclopean walls are said to be 3,000 years old. Certainly very ancient, it ranked among Etruria's twelve cities.

Cortona fought Rome in every war down to 310 B.C. In that year Fabius Rullianus defeated the Etruscans and captured Perugia, after which Perugia and other cities made peace with Rome. Lombards later destroyed Cortona, but it was soon rebuilt. In the fourteenth century the Casali governed it, and it afterwards joined the great Duchy of Tuscany. Cortona's churches hold numerous art works, especially paintings of Luca Signorelli's and Fra Angelico's schools. The diocese counts 50 parishes, 60 churches and oratories, 85 secular and 36 regular priests, and 30,200 inhabitants.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cotenna:
Cotenna, a titular see of Asia Minor, hides behind a tangle of ancient names. Strabo's Katenneis of Pisidia, near Selge, left an inscription calling themselves Kotenneis, fixing the town's true name. Modern Godena, on the Alaghir stream in the Konia region, marks the site.

Listed as a suffragan of Side, the see counts six known bishops, from Hesychius in 381 to Macarius in 879. Debate follows whether the Kotenneis match the Etenneis of Polybius, a tribe perhaps split into northern and southern districts. Hierocles places the town in Pamphylia under the form Kotana.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cremona:
A diocesan entry covers Cremona, a Lombard city on the left bank of the Po, suffragan to Milan. Built by the Cenomanni Gauls, it became a Roman colony and frontier fortress, fell to Hannibal, and was pillaged by Vespasian before rising again. Captured by the Lombard king Agilulf about 600, it later won communal rights and became a citadel of Ghibelline loyalty to the emperors.

Its bishops once held temporal sovereignty, and the city passed through many lords, Pallavicini, Visconti, and Sforza, before joining the Duchy of Milan in 1328. Cremona venerates St. Sabinus as first missionary and bishop. In music history it is famed as birthplace of the violin makers Amati, Guarneri, Stradivari, and Malpighi. The diocese counted 350,000 people and 345 parishes.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-crypt-of-luci:
An archaeological entry presents the Crypt of Lucina, the oldest section of the Catacomb of St. Callistus at Rome. Following De Rossi's theory, it identifies St. Lucina, honoured on 30 June, as donor of the area and as Pomponia Graecina, wife of Aulus Plautius, conqueror of Britain.

Tacitus records that Pomponia was accused of a foreign superstition, tried before her husband and kinsfolk, and cleared, living forty years in mourning dress after Julia's murder. That superstition is now generally taken for Christianity. Inscriptions found in the crypt support the identification. De Rossi first offered it as a remote probability, but later finds raised it near certainty, making Pomponia one of Rome's earliest known Christians.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-curityba-do-p:
A diocesan entry describes Curityba do Parana, a suffragan see of Rio de Janeiro in Brazil. The city of Curityba, on the Iguazu River, was settled in 1654 and became capital of the state of Parana in 1831, on a fertile plain. It lies in a fertile plain 3,200 feet above sea level, with gold mines nearby.

Erected by Leo XIII in 1892, the diocese embraces Parana and Santa Catarina, an area of 114,087 square kilometres, with a Catholic population of 600,900. It counted 69 parishes, 68 secular and 21 regular priests, two men's orders and three women's, one seminary, two colleges, and one Catholic school with 350 pupils at the time of writing.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-daniello-conc:
A biographical entry presents Daniello Concina, a Dominican preacher, controversialist, and theologian born in Friuli in 1687 and dead at Venice in 1756. Schooled by Jesuits at Gorz, he joined the Dominicans in 1708, studied philosophy three years, then theology eight years at Venice under Andruisso and Zanchio. He taught philosophy and theology at Forli, then preached in Italy's chief cities, giving Lenten sermons seven times in Rome's principal churches.

His writing centred on morals. A first book refuted the claim that Saint Dominic borrowed his poverty ideal from Saint Francis, sparking sharp dispute. A second controversy over the Lenten fast ended when Benedict XIV's encyclical of 1741 favoured his view. His History of Probabilism and Rigorism then carried his moral theology further, and his works remain a landmark of eighteenth-century rigorism.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-diamantina:
Diamantina is a diocese in the north of Minas Gerais in Brazil. It took shape under the Brazilian Empire and won confirmation from the Holy See in 1854. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry traces its roots to the older Diocese of Mariana. Its land covered twenty townships split into more than one hundred parishes across half the state.

The entry counts about two hundred churches and one hundred priests. It names schools run by the Lazarists in Diamantina itself, among them a seminary and a college for girls. It also follows missionaries at work among the Botocudo people along the Mucury River. Two periodicals carried Catholic news across the region, closing the portrait.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-dioceses-of-v:
Valva and Sulmona are two Italian dioceses joined together under one bishop. Valva grew around a medieval castle near Corfinium, the ancient capital of the Peligni people, a Samnite tribe. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry recalls that Corfinium served as capital of the Italici in the Social War, taking the name Italia, found on coins of the time. The church of Saint Pelino still recalls the Peligni people.

Sulmona, the old Sulmo, lies in a rich plain watered by the Gizzio beneath the Maiella and Morrone mountains. Together the sees counted some two hundred secular and forty-eight regular priests, with houses of monks and nuns and schools for boys and girls. A grotto shrine of Saint Michael near Valva adds a note of pilgrimage.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-domenico-font:
Domenico Fontana was a Roman architect of the late Renaissance, born at Melide on Lake Lugano in 1543. He reached Rome before Michelangelo's death and studied the masters ancient and modern. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry tells how he won the trust of Cardinal Montalto, later Pope Sixtus the Fifth. In 1584 the cardinal charged him with the Chapel of the Manger in Saint Mary Major, a domed building over a Greek cross.

Well balanced despite rich ornament, the chapel wears a dome in the early style of Montepulciano. For the same patron Fontana built the Palazzo Montalto with skillful massing. His brother Giovanni, born in 1546, matters less, though his great fountains stand at Frascati and Rome. Domenico died at Naples in 1607.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-dominic-gravi:
Dominic Gravina was a Dominican theologian born in Sicily about 1573 who died at the Minerva in Rome in 1643. He joined the order at Naples and studied in its schools, then taught theology at Naples, at the Minerva, and elsewhere. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry names him Italy's most celebrated theologian of his day. A general chapter made him master of sacred theology in 1608.

In the pulpit he won equal fame, preaching Lenten courses and before Pope Paul the Fifth. He also served tirelessly as prior, provincial, procurator general, and vicar-general. His writings fill seven volumes of theological and polemical works, plus a mystical touchstone for telling true revelations from false. The entry lists them in full.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-duccio-di-buo:
Duccio di Buoninsegna was a painter and founder of the Sienese school, born about 1255 or 1260 and dead on 3 August 1319. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry sets him in Siena at its peak, fresh from beating Florence at Montaperti in 1260. The building of the cathedral began, with Nicholas of Pisa's great pulpit started in 1266, and Duccio learned his art amid that flourishing city.

He owed nothing to the Gothic manner nor to the naturalism of Nicholas, holding wholly to Byzantine tradition. Called the Last of the Greeks, his genius gave exquisite voice to the refined feeling of the Byzantine masters. The entry cites Italian histories and French studies of a painter who shaped Siena's sacred art.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-egidio-colonn:
Egidio Colonna, better known as Giles of Rome, was a scholastic philosopher and theologian born at Rome about 1247 and dead at Avignon in 1316. He joined the Augustinian Hermits at Rome, studied at Paris under Thomas Aquinas, and became the first Augustinian to teach in the University of Paris. His learning won him the title Doctor Fundatissimus, the most deeply grounded teacher.

In 1281 he sided with the bishops against the mendicant orders at the Council of Paris, and a contemporary called him the most renowned theologian in the city. King Philip III gave him charge of his son, the future Philip IV, and Egidio told the young king that justice was a ruler's first virtue. After a forced retraction in 1285, his order in 1287 ordered all its members to accept and defend his teaching. He became superior-general in 1292 and Archbishop of Bourges in 1295.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-elias-of-cort:
Elias of Cortona was Minister General of the Friars Minor, born near Assisi about 1180 and dead at Cortona in 1253. He called himself Brother Elias, Sinner, and the town name came later; his family name was Bonusbaro, his father came from near Bologna, and his mother was Assisian. Before joining Francis he worked at his father's mattress trade and taught Assisi children to read the Psalter. He was never a priest.

One of Francis's earliest companions, he led missionaries to Palestine in 1217 and became first provincial of Syria in 1219. Back in Italy, he served as vicar-general from 1221 until Francis died in 1226, and later as Minister General. The entry weighs a able, controversial organiser whose building and rule shaped the young order, and whose later years drew sharp criticism from stricter friars.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-felice-fontan:
Felice Fontana was an Italian naturalist and physiologist of the Enlightenment. Born in 1730, he taught philosophy at Pisa before his summons to Florence. The Grand Duke made him court physician and organiser of the Florentine museum. His wax anatomical models won wide fame across Europe.

Fontana studied the eye, poisons, gases, and sheep disease with patient care. He found the staggers came from hydatids in the brain. Joseph II hired him to make wax models for the Academy of Surgeons in Vienna. He died from a street fall in 1805 and lies in Santa Croce near Galileo.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-fonte-avellan:
Fonte-Avellana was a strict order of hermits in the Apennine mountains of Italy, named for the spring among pine trees where its first hermitage stood. Ludolph, born about 956 to a German family settled at Gubbio, left home in 977 with a companion named Julian to live as a hermit. Disciples gathered, and by 989 they were numerous enough to receive a rule from St. Romuald.

Life under that rule was hard: separate cells, prayer, study, and manual work, with bread and water most days and no meat at all. St. Peter Damian, prior from about 1043 until his death in 1072, softened some extremes while keeping the stern spirit. The order later declined, and Pope Pius V suppressed it in 1569, moving its members to Camaldoli and other houses.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francesco-lan:
Francesco Lana, born at Brescia on 10 December 1631 and dead there on 22 February 1687. He was a Jesuit mathematician and naturalist called the scientific founder of aeronautics, the science of flight. Trained in Brescia, he entered the Jesuit novitiate at Rome in 1647 and taught humanities at Terni. He then taught physical science and mathematics, chiefly at Ferrara, until delicate health sent him home to Brescia, where he worked as confessor while publishing his great work.

That work, Magisterium naturae et artis, aimed to treat the whole of natural science in nine volumes on strict geometrical principles and careful experiments. Only two volumes appeared in his lifetime, in 1684 and 1686, with a third after his death. Its most famous idea, a flying ship lifted by evacuated copper spheres, was never built, yet its principles form the basis of modern aeronautics. His importance has grown clearer with time.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francisco-ant:
Francisco Antonio de Lorenzana, born at Leon in Spain on 22 September 1722 and dead at Rome on 17 April 1804. He was a cardinal whose energy served Church, science, and society on two continents. Educated at the Jesuit college of Leon, he became a canon of Toledo and Bishop of Plasencia in 1765. The next year he became Archbishop of Mexico, where he advanced religious, scientific, and social interests, founded a foundling asylum at his own expense. He published the acts of Mexico's first three provincial councils.

In 1771 he held Mexico's fourth provincial synod, whose decrees were buried in Madrid's archives, and published a richly illustrated history of New Spain in 1770. Recalled to Spain in 1772 as Archbishop of Toledo, he built a great library there and collected the works of leading writers.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francisco-pen:
Francisco Pena, also spelled Pegna, was a canonist born at Villaroya de los Pinares near Saragossa about 1540 and dead at Rome in 1612. He studied law at Valencia, and Philip II appointed him auditor of the Rota, the papal court, for Spain, where he served fellow Spaniards and the Holy See with distinction. He sat on the commission that prepared the official edition of the Corpus juris canonici, the body of canon law, published in 1582. The anonymous notes on the Decretals are attributed to him.

He also worked on the canonizations of Didacus, Hyacinth, Raymond, Charles Borromeo, and Frances of Rome, publishing lives of several saints. His chief works comment on Eymerich's Directory of Inquisitors, on the office of the Inquisition, on heresy and its penalties, and on the temporal kingdom of Christ. Decisions of the Sacred Rota were published after his death.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gallia-christ:
Gallia Christiana is a documentary catalogue of every French diocese and abbey from the earliest times, with short histories of their holders. Jean Chenu's 1621 list missed nearly a third of the bishops, and Claude Robert's 1626 Gallia improved on it but still fell short. The French clergy then charged the Sainte-Marthe brothers with a definitive work.

The Sainte-Marthe sons issued it in 1656 in four folio volumes: archdioceses, dioceses, and abbeys in alphabetical order, rich in copied manuscripts. Faults showed at once, and a promised revision never came from the family. In 1710 the clergy paid the Maurist Denys de Sainte-Marthe to revise it, and his first volume appeared in 1715, opening a long Benedictine sequel.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gerard-of-cre:
Gerard of Cremona, a twelfth-century translator born at Cremona in 1114, opened Arabic science to Latin Christendom. Tiraboschi refuted Spanish claims for Carmona, showing manuscripts style him Cremonensis. Drawn by Ptolemy, Gerard went to Toledo, mastered Arabic, and rendered not only the Almagest but Avicenna's whole works into Latin. He died in 1187 and was buried at Saint Lucy's, Cremona, leaving his valuable library to the church.

Pipino's Chronicle credits Gerard with seventy-six translations across dialectic, geometry, philosophy, physics, and more. Whether he wrote original treatises is doubtful, since works ascribed to him likely belong to Gerard of Sabionetta. With Michael Scott and Toledo's college of translators under Bishop Raymond, Gerard's labor brought Arabian learning to Latin scholars and prepared the clash of ideas from which thirteenth-century Scholasticism sprang.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gerona:
Gerona, a diocese in Catalonia suffragan of Tarragona, guards a province between Pyrenees and sea. Bounded north by the Pyrenees, south and east by the Mediterranean, and west by Barcelona and Vich. Its pine, oak, and chestnut forests and springs frame manufacturing towns, coal mines, and the France-to-Barcelona railway. Its chief town stands at the Ter-Ona meeting.

Gerunda of the Ausetani claims Paul and James as preachers and Maximus, James's disciple, as first bishop, with the see erected in 247. A synod of June 18, 517, ruled on the Divine Office, infant baptism, and clerical celibacy. Twenty-five sieges and seven captures mark the city. Charlemagne's Moorish wars ended with expulsion in 1015. French sieges followed in 1653, 1684, and 1694, and the siege of May to December 1809 saw Alvarez hold against 35,000 French until disease and famine forced surrender. Its cathedral, once a mosque, boasts Christendom's widest nave vault at seventy-three feet.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giovanni-bona:
Giovanni Bona was a distinguished cardinal and author born at Mondovì in Piedmont in 1609, who died at Rome in 1674. Against his father's wish for a military career, he entered the Cistercians at Pignerola after Jesuit schooling. He labored fifteen years at Turin, served as prior at Asti and abbot at Mondovì, and in 1651 took charge of the whole congregation. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows a scholar who declined honors.

Alexander VII made him consultor to the Index and the Holy Office, and in 1669 created him cardinal. Yet his simple life never changed, and he gave his surplus income each year to needy priests. His Manuductio ad caelum, often likened to the Imitation of Christ, passed through fourteen Latin editions in four decades. His De Rebus Liturgicis of 1671 gathers seven years of work into an encyclopedia of the Mass.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giovanni-da-b:
Giovanni da Bologna, called Il Fiammingo, was a Flemish Renaissance sculptor born at Douai about 1524, who died at Florence in 1608. He studied at Rome and settled at Florence, adopted by the wealthy Bernardo Vecchietti, who treated him as his son. A Catholic Encyclopedia article presents a sculptor thoroughly Florentine in feeling, free and graceful without late-Renaissance exaggeration.

Florence keeps his two masterpieces, the Mercury in the Bargello and the Rape of the Sabines under the Loggia dei Lanzi. The Mercury, winged and borne on a head of Aeolus, comes nearer than any work of its age to swift motion. It catches flashing movement and airy lightness together. Other works include Hercules and Nessus, the bronze Cosimo I in the Piazza Signoria, and the bronze Neptune for the Bologna fountain.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giovanni-paol:
Giovanni Paolo Colonna was a church composer born at Bologna in 1637, who died there in 1695. After studies under Fillipucci at Bologna and Abbatini and Benevoli at Rome, he became organist at Sant' Apollinare in Rome. In 1659 he took the choir-master post at San Petronio in Bologna. A Catholic Encyclopedia article ranks him among the noted church composers of the seventeenth century.

He helped found the Accademia Filarmonica and opened a school of his own, whose pupils included Giovanni Maria Buononcini. His large output covers masses, psalms, motets, litanies, antiphons, requiems, and lamentations for one to eight voices, with organ or orchestra. They are seldom performed today, both because they lack the form and spirit of the great fifteenth- and sixteenth-century period and because they demand elaborate forces.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giovanni-pier:
Giovanni Pierluigi da Palestrina was a composer of liturgical music born at Palestrina in 1514 or 1515, by some accounts 1526, who died at Rome in 1594. His early life is almost unknown; tradition says a choirmaster at Santa Maria Maggiore heard the boy singing in the streets and trained him. A Catholic Encyclopedia article calls him the greatest composer of liturgical music of all time.

He began as organist and choirmaster at Palestrina in 1544. He moved to Rome in 1551 to train the choirboys at Saint Peter's. Julius III set aside the rules to make him a member of the papal chapel, and Paul IV later dismissed him with a small pension. His first book of masses, dedicated to Julius III in 1554, opened a flood of sacred music still held as the model of its kind.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giovanni-vinc:
Giovanni Vincenzo Gravina was an Italian jurist and man of letters born at Rogliano in Calabria in 1664, who died at Rome in 1718. At sixteen he went to Naples to study Latin, Greek, and law, then moved to Rome in 1689 to teach civil and canon law. A call to a law chair at Turin came just before the illness that killed him. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows a scholar whose pride made him many enemies.

In 1690 he co-founded the Academy of Arcadia at Rome under the name Opico Erimanto, then quarreled with its members and tried in vain to found an Anti-Arcadia. His Institutiones canonicae is a clear but very elementary handbook. His chief civil-law work, Originum juris civilis libri tres, was translated into French as Esprit des lois romaines. He also wrote on ancient fables, poetic reason, and tragedy, and patronized the poet Metastasius.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-girolamo-camp:
Girolamo Campagna was an able sculptor of Northern Italy, born at Verona in 1552, who died about 1623 or 1625. Jacopo Sansovino and Danese Cattaneo taught him, and he finished many works left by Cattaneo. A Catholic Encyclopedia article calls him able, but not strikingly individual.

At Padua he won the commission meant for Cattaneo in the church of Saint Anthony. He carved his masterpiece, a bas-relief of the saint raising a murdered man to life. He later made the bronze tabernacle for the chapel of the Blessed Sacrament there. Most of his life passed in Venice. His works there include the colossal Saint Sebastian at the Zecca, the figures on the Rialto Bridge, and the bronze Christ on a globe at San Giorgio Maggiore.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gortyna:
Gortyna is a titular see, and in the Greek Church a metropolitan see, of the island of Crete, at the foot of Mount Ida near the River Lethe. First called Larissa, then Cremnia, then Gortys, and finally Gortyna, it is mentioned by Homer as a fortified city. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows a see that rose with Rome and fell to the Arabs.

Before Roman rule it warred continually with Cnossus and Cydonia for supremacy, to the island's desolation. Under Rome it became the civil and ecclesiastical metropolis, prospering as never before, with Saint Titus, to whom Paul addressed an epistle, as its first bishop. In 825 the Arabs took the island and slew Archbishop Cyril for refusing to apostatize. They destroyed Gortyna so completely that it never rose again, and the metropolitan took the title of Crete.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-guarino-da-ve:
Verona's humanist Guarino, born in 1370 and dead at Ferrara in 1460, learned Latin under Giovanni da Ravenna.
