He then spent five years in Constantinople studying Greek in the household of Manuel Chrysoloras. He came home in 1408 with more than fifty Greek manuscripts and was welcomed with enthusiasm at Venice.

Teaching filled the rest of his life, in Florence, Venice, Verona, and Ferrara. There students flocked from Italy and England and Vittorino da Feltre numbered among his pupils. Engaged as tutor to Lionello d'Este in 1429 and professor of rhetoric at Ferrara from 1436, he translated Strabo and many of Plutarch's Lives. He commented on Roman satirists, recovered a manuscript of Pliny's letters, and left some 600 letters of his own.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-guiana:
Guiana once named the whole Atlantic coast of South America from the Orinoco to the Amazon, though the name now means the three colonies of British, Dutch, and French Guiana. The entry sketches a hot, humid lowland coast scourged by yellow fever, backed by high tablelands rising to Mount Roraima, with forests, jaguars, and deadly snakes.

From early explorers and Raleigh's hunt for El Dorado through the French, Dutch, and English struggle for the coast, the story turns to Catholic missions. Dominicans, Capuchins, and Jesuits worked at Cayenne, Indian settlements followed the Paraguay model, and the Jesuits were expelled in 1768. British Guiana's vicariate, its 1894 boundary dispute with Venezuela, and its mixed population of 307,000 close the survey.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-guibert-of-ra:
Parma-born Guibert, imperial chancellor for Italy from 1057, became the antipope Clement III and the long shadow over Gregory VII's reform papacy. After helping elect the antipope Honorius II in 1059 and losing his chancellorship, he rose again as Archbishop of Ravenna in 1072, then broke with Gregory over reform, simony, and clerical discipline.

At Brixen in June 1080 Henry IV's bishops deposed Gregory and elected Guibert, who was enthroned at the Lateran in March 1084 and crowned Henry emperor days later. Driven in and out of Rome through the reigns of Victor III, Urban II, and Paschal II, he kept a rival court alive until his death at Cività Castellana in 1100. He was recognized only inside Henry's dominions.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-havana:
Cuba's Diocese of Havana, San Cristóbal de la Habana, now covers Havana and Matanzas provinces, though its bishops long lived at the port for its defences and communications. The see passed from Baracoa in 1518 to Santiago in 1522. Rome split the vast Cuban diocese, then holding Louisiana and Florida too, by decree in 1787, with José de Tres-Palacios as first Bishop of Havana.

Tres-Palacios, a Salamanca doctor, fought Governor Las Casas's secularizing bent and crowned his rule by erecting New Orleans as its own see. His beloved successor Espada spent the see's revenues on schools, health, and the seminary. He backed the philosopher Félix Varela, drained marshes into the Campo de Marte, and preached vaccination, dying in 1832 to island-wide grief.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-helena:
Montana's Diocese of Helena, erected from the Vicariate of Montana on 7 March 1884, covers the state's western half across sixteen counties and 51,922 square miles. Montana Territory first fell under the Vicariate of Nebraska of 1851, then passed west of the Rockies to the Vicariate of Idaho in 1868, when nineteen priests served an estimated 15,000 Catholics.

Jesuits carried the Indian missions among the Flathead, Blackfeet. Cheyenne, while Sisters of Charity, Ursulines, and Sisters of Providence ran the schools. John Baptist Brondel, consecrated in 1879 and transferred to Helena in 1884, ruled until 1903, and John P. Carroll followed in 1904 over 50,000 Catholics, 45 priests, and 5,762 young people under Catholic care.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hermopolis-ma:
Hermopolis Magna was an ancient Egyptian city and titular see, now the village of Ashmunein on the left bank of the Nile. Its native name, Khmounoun, means the eight, for the moon-god Thoth, in ibis or baboon form, attended by four pairs of deities. The city mattered from the sixth through the eleventh dynasties, later becoming chief town of its nome, or district.

Tradition links the place to the Holy Family, St. Colluthus was martyred there under Maximian and Diocletian, and St. Athanasius lived there for a time. Eight bishops are recorded, and the see still serves Monophysite Copts; Leo XIII re-established it for Coptic Catholics in 1895, with the titular bishop living at Minieh. Ruins nearby include the animal burial ground of Thoth and the tombs of local rulers.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hirena: Hirena was a titular see of southern Tunis about which nothing is known of the city itself, whose own name might have been Hirina, Hiren, or Iren. Its bishops number three. Tertullian attended Carthage's conference in 311. Huneric exiled Saturus in 484 along with many fellow bishops. Theodore signed the letter of the Council of Byzacium in 641 to Constantine, son of Heraclius, against Monothelitism.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-history-of-ch:
This article opens the history of China with the debated question of Chinese origins. Foreign scholars have sought a common root in Armenia or Mesopotamia, compared Chinese and Aryan roots, and argued for an Egyptian origin. Others traced so-called Bak tribes migrating from Elam to the Hwang-ho around 2500 BC. The entry calls these clever theories lightly built and notes the only alternative is Chinese tradition with its legends.

Tradition begins with P'an-ku, the Chinese Adam, followed by celestial, terrestrial, and human kings across the early periods of Chinese history. Then come the Five Sovereigns. Fu-hi invented writing, and Shin-nung invented the plough. Wang-ti patronized fine arts and ships, and his wife taught silk raising and weaving. Shao-hao founded civil and military offices, and Chuen-hiu authored the calendar.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hosanna:
Hosanna is the cry of the crowds before and after Christ at his entry into Jerusalem. They sang welcome to the Son of David, blessing him who comes in the Lord's name, crying Hosanna in the highest. Thayer traced the word to a psalm of praise, but that view finds little support. The general opinion, following Jerome, traces it to two Hebrew words in Psalm 118, verse 25.

That psalm was recited daily by a priest during processions round the altar at the Feast of Tabernacles, when the people rejoiced before the Lord. On the seventh day it sounded at each of seven processions. When the priest reached verses 25 and 26, trumpets blew, the people waved palm, myrtle, and willow branches, and all shouted: O Lord, save us now. The Hebrew for save now, hoshi'a na, was repeated so often that it shortened into hosanna.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-indiana:
The nineteenth state to join the Union gets a full reference portrait here, from its borders to its church life. Indiana stretches 267 miles north to south, covers 35,885 square miles in ninety-two counties. It is bounded by Michigan and Lake Michigan, Ohio, the Ohio River, and Illinois and the Wabash. Indianapolis, at the state's center, serves as capital, with only three lake ports.

Flat or rolling land, broken ground along the Ohio, and fertile valleys frame the account of its resources, people, schools, and past. The entry then turns to religion, tracing Catholic growth and the dioceses that served the state. It closes with book sources. Those sources carry the history of its towns and settlements in fuller detail.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-indo-china:
Rule over the peoples of this peninsula was split four ways: British Burma, the Malay Peninsula shared with Siam, the Empire of Siam, and French Indo-China each held a part. French rule by itself covered Cochin China, the vassal kingdoms of Cambodia and Annam, the protectorates of Tong-king and Laos, and the leased port of Kwang-chau-wan. A final section on Christianity follows mission work through those lands.

The peninsula charted here stretches from mountain borders down to the seas. Assam, Yunnan, and Kwang-si hem it in on the north, the Gulf of Tong-king and the Sea of China lie to the east, and the Bay of Bengal lies to the west. Roughly 1,200 miles long and 1,000 miles across at its widest, it serves as both a political map and a record of Catholic missions in a land where faith and empire met.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jaffna:
Jaffna, in northern Ceylon, covers the island's northern and north-central provinces, and Christianity there dates back to St Francis Xavier's time. In 1548 Francis visited Manaar and came to Jaffna to persuade its king to stop persecuting Christians, and in 1580, under Portuguese protection, Jaffna's first Catholic church was built. The whole peninsula surrendered in 1591 to Andrea Furtado de Mendoza, and almost the entire population then abandoned idolatry and embraced Christianity.

The fort of Jaffna fell to the Dutch in 1658, when the peninsula held 50 priests, one Jesuit college, one Franciscan and one Dominican convent, and fourteen churches. The Dutch at once showed fierce hostility to Catholics: priests and monks were banished, and sheltering them became a capital offense, a thriving Catholic peninsula into Dutch persecution.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-scotus-e:
John Scotus Eriugena was an Irish teacher, theologian, philosopher, and poet at the court of Charles the Bald. His name means a native of Ireland, and though Wales and Scotland once claimed his birthplace, Ireland's claim is now universally admitted. About 847 he appeared in France, won the king's special favor, headed the palace school at Paris, and was commissioned to translate Pseudo-Dionysius into Latin.

That translation brought him prominence and drew him into controversies on predestination and the Eucharist. His Greek learning shows in his translations and poems, though claims of Hebrew and Oriental knowledge lack evidence, and he probably never traveled in Greece or Asia Minor. After leaving Ireland he spent his remaining days in France, at Paris and Laon most likely, a thinker whose bold synthesis of Greek theology and Latin philosophy has fascinated readers ever since.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-juan-bautista:
Juan Bautista de Lezana was a Spanish Carmelite theologian and canonist who lived from 1586 to 1659. Born at Madrid, he took the Carmelite habit in 1600, studied at Toledo, Salamanca, and Alcalá, and stayed in Rome after the general chapter of 1625 as professor of theology. He later served as assistant general and procurator general of his order.

Lezana taught metaphysics at the Sapienza for sixteen years and advised the Congregations of the Index and of Rites. His Summa of regular questions, his sacred theology, and his four-volume Annals of the Carmelite Order still carry weight, though his history is judged below his law and dogma. He refused a bishopric as more perfect for his soul.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-juan-de-la-en:
Juan de la Encina was the Spanish poet called the father of the secular drama. Born at Encina near Salamanca in 1468, he studied at Salamanca University and joined the household of the Duke of Alba at twenty-five. He took orders in Rome, where Leo X made him master of the chapel for his musical skill.

Encina's Cancionero, reprinted five times in the sixteenth century, holds songs, lyrics, and eleven representaciones, short eclogue plays with singing and once a dance. Acted as early as 1492, these crude, plotless pieces are the oldest surviving monuments of Spanish secular drama. He also wrote an Arte de Poesia Castellana about 1497 and died at Salamanca in 1534.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-juan-de-medin:
Juan de Medina was a leading Spanish theologian of the sixteenth century. Born at Medina de Pomar in 1490, he entered Alcalá's College of St. Ildefonsus in 1516, took doctorates in philosophy and theology, and became canon and master of theology. From about 1526 for twenty years he held the first chair of theology with great distinction.

Pupils praised Medina's gift for making the hardest questions plain, so that even the slowest grasped them. His works treat moral theology and ethics, though some opinions clashed with the Council of Trent, notably on absolution by an excommunicated priest. His brother published his theological books at Alcalá from 1544, and he was buried at St. Ildefonsus.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-juan-de-mena:
Juan de Mena was a Spanish court poet of King Juan II of Castile. Born at Cordova in 1411, he served as the king's secretary for Latin letters and then as royal historiographer. His verse shows little originality but bears the clear stamp of the Renaissance, with Dante and Lucan as his models.

Mena's masterpiece, the Laberinto, pictures the poet lost in a forest until Providence guides him through three wheels of fate, past, present, and future, pointing out famous persons. His Coronación crowns his friend Santillana on Parnassus, and his Seven Deadly Sins teaches in verse. His prose Iliad is a dry summary of Troy, and he died at Torrelaguna in 1456.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-juan-ignacio-:
Juan Ignacio Molina was a Chilean Jesuit who became the leading historian of his homeland. Born near Talca in 1740, he joined the Society of Jesus at fifteen, excelled in languages and natural science, and was sent to Italy in 1767. Ordained at Imola, he lived as a tutor at Bologna and wrote his works in Italian.

Molina's histories of Chile, geographic, natural, and civil, appeared at Bologna from 1776 to 1787 and were translated into German, French, Spanish, and English. Chile named a town for him in thanks. Botanists also honored him: Schrank named the grass genus Molinia for him in 1789. He died in Italy in 1829.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-juan-mariana:
Juan Mariana was a Spanish Jesuit historian whose book on tyrants made him infamous. Born at Talavera about 1536, he joined the order in 1554, taught theology at Rome, Sicily, and Paris, and spent his later years writing at Toledo. He died there in 1624.

Mariana's History of Spain, first in Latin in 1592 and then in his own Spanish in 1601, stayed in print into the nineteenth century. His De rege et regis institutione of 1599, a mirror for princes, argued that a tyrant may be killed, a view later blamed for regicide plots. The entry calls him one of the most maligned Jesuits, since the book aimed to form a virtuous king.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-konrad-wimpin:
Konrad Wimpina (about 1465-1531) was a German theologian of the Thomist school, born at Buchen to a family named Koch from Wimpfen. He studied at Leipzig from 1479, rose through baccalaureate, mastership, rector, and dean, and took his theology doctorate in 1503.

In 1505, Brandenburg's Elector Joachim I called him to organize the new university at Frankfort-on-the-Oder as its first rector, with canonries at Brandenburg and Havelberg. Wimpina became one of Luther's earliest opponents: he defended the legend of St. Anne's three marriages in 1518 and wrote the theses Johann Tetzel debated at Frankfort in January 1518. In 1530 he attended the Diet of Augsburg as the elector's theologian.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-la-plata-arge:
La Plata is an Argentine diocese whose city, capital of Buenos Aires Province, stands on the Rio de la Plata thirty-five miles south-east of Buenos Aires. Founded by stone-laying on 19 November 1882 after Buenos Aires passed to the federal government, it grew fast, stalled in 1890, and counted 80,000 people by 1907, mostly foreigners.

Its National University, developed in 1905, held four faculties, a 41,000-volume library, the Museo de la Plata with anthropological and fossil collections, and an observatory from 1882. San Ponciano church served as pro-cathedral until the great Gothic cathedral replaced it in 1901. Leo XIII founded the see on 15 February 1897, suffragan to Buenos Aires, under the Immaculate Conception.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-la-serena:
La Serena is a Chilean diocese, suffragan of Santiago, erected 1 July 1840 over Atacama and Coquimbo provinces. Its bounds were fixed on 26 March 1844, and its first bishop, Jose Agustin de la Sierra, was installed on 5 June 1844.

The territory runs past 60,000 square miles with about 250,000 Catholics, served by 64 secular and 35 regular priests, 30 parishes, and 145 churches and chapels. The town of La Serena, near 20,000 people, holds 20 churches, including an imposing cathedral built from 1844 to 1860. A seminary teaches 160 students, and Sisters of Mercy, of the Good Shepherd, and of Piepus run an orphan asylum, a lazaretto, and a foundling home.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-la-verna:
La Verna is a lone Tuscan mountain, hallowed by St. Francis of Assisi, rising some 4,000 feet over the Casentino valley. Its name is said to come from vernare, to freeze. Count Orlando of Chiusi gave it to Francis on 8 May 1213 as a retreat fit for contemplation.

Francis withdrew there in August 1224 for a forty-day fast before Michaelmas. While praying on the mountainside he received the stigmata, on or about 14 September. A church rose in 1260 before St. Bonaventure, and the Chapel of the Stigmata followed near the miracle's spot. Friars still process twice daily from the great church to that chapel. On the Feast of the Stigmata, crowds of priests and people climb the mountain, sometimes 2,000 to 3,000 pilgrims at a time.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lanciano-and-:
Lanciano and Ortona form a united Italian archdiocese in Chieti province, Abruzzi, between the Pescara and Trigno rivers, under Mount Maiella's view. Lanciano, ancient Anxia of the Frentani, holds the cathedral of St. Mary of the Bridge, built on bridgework over a precipice, and St. Mary Major with its Norman portal.

Subject to Chieti until 1515, Lanciano became an archdiocese without suffragans under Pius IV in 1562. Ortona, ancient and Adriatic, with a small Dalmatian trading port, was a see even under Gregory the Great, lapsed after the tenth century, and was restored by Pius V in 1570. Pius VII joined the sees in 1818, leaving 20 parishes with 61,000 faithful.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-leptis-magna:
Leptis Magna was a titular see of Tripolitana, founded by Sidonians in fine, fertile country. It was the chief of the three towns of the Tripoli Confederation.  It later centred a Greek city, Neapolis, mostly buried under sand. Pliny apart, Ptolemy, Strabo, and Scyllax identify them.

Leptis sided with Rome against Jugurtha.  Trajan made it a colony, Colonia Ulpia Trajana, named on many coins. It was the birthplace of Septimius Severus, who adorned it. Sacked in the fourth century by Libya's Aurusiani, it never fully recovered. Justinian retook it from Vandal hands in the sixth century, rebuilt it, and built five churches. Sergius's 543 massacre of Berber chiefs there nearly lost Rome Africa. Arabs took it in the seventh century and let sand invade it. Now a ruin called Lebda, sixty-two miles from Tripoli to the east, it shows a vast circus 380 yards by 66 yards. Five bishops are recorded.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lesina:
Lesina, Pharia or Hvar, is a diocese in Dalmatia covering three islands: Hvar, the ancient Pharia settled by Greeks in 385 B.C.; Brac, once Brattia or Brachia, also Greek-settled; and Lissa, once Issa. Lesina town, where St. Doimus, a disciple of St. Peter, is said to have first preached, holds the residence. The diocese was founded about 1145 by Lucius II, and Martinus Manzavini, elected in 1147, was its first bishop; Jordanus Zaninovic, O.P., consecrated 19 April 1903 by Leo XIII, is its fifty-first and present bishop.

The diocese counts 6 deaneries, 28 parishes, and 62,290 faithful. The cathedral, built in 1637 with a Lombard facade, holds a Palma painting. In 1899 Pius X, then Patriarch of Venice, gave the head of St. Stephen to Fulgentius Carey, Bishop of Lesina. Two of its bishops became cardinals: Giovanni Battista Pallavicini in 1524 and Zaccarias Delphina in 1553. Under Pietro Cedulini (1581-1634) two synods were held.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-liutprand-of-:
Liutprand of Cremona was a tenth-century Lombard bishop and historian, born early in the century and alive past 970. A fine voice won him favour at the Pavia court, where he was schooled, made a cleric, and rose to deacon of the cathedral.

Berenger II made him chancellor and sent him to Constantinople in 949, where he learned Greek and studied Byzantine court life. After a quarrel he joined Otto I of Germany, who made him Bishop of Cremona in 961. Liutprand then wrote his sharp, partisan history of the age, backed Otto against Pope John XII, and served as envoy to Rome and Byzantium.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-louisiana:
Louisiana is the story of the vast Mississippi valley region named for Louis XIV, from its first European sightings to its place in the American Union. De Soto reached the great river in 1541, and Joliet and Marquette rediscovered it in 1673.

La Salle floated down in 1682, claimed the whole watershed for France on 9 April, and named it Louisiane for his king. French and Spanish rule, failed colonies, and English rivalry fill the colonial pages, while later sections trace statehood, the Civil War, and the Church's growth. The entry's romance lies in explorers, priests, and settlers staking a continent on a river.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-luis-de-molin:
Luis de Molina was a Jesuit theologian famed for grace and free will, born at Cuenca in 1535 and dead at Madrid in 1600. He joined the Society at Alcala at eighteen, studied at Coimbra, and taught philosophy there, then theology at Evora for twenty years on Aquinas's Summa.

Retiring to Cuenca in 1590 to write, he was called to a new moral philosophy chair at Madrid in 1592, dying within six months of taking it. His Concordia, thirty years in the making, sought to join free will with grace, divine foreknowledge, and predestination. On the very day he died, Rome's commission reported against the book to Clement VIII, opening the great grace controversy that bears his name.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-manna:
Manna was the food sent by miracle to the Israelites through forty desert years. Exodus 16 and Numbers 11 tell its story. It first fell in the desert of Sin, six weeks after the flight from Egypt. It answered the people's complaints over lack of food.

Scholars have sought a natural match for it. Many point to juice from a tamarisk, Tamarix gallica, pricked by an insect, Coccus manniparus. Others point to a lichen, Lecanora esculenta, found in western Asia and North Africa. Neither match settles the question. Christ then uses manna as a type of the Eucharist, the true bread from heaven and bread of life, life-giving in a far higher sense than the desert food.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mariana:
Mariana was an archdiocese in Minas Geraes, Brazil's great mining state, bounded by its suffragans Diamantina, Pouso Alegre, Goyaz, and Uberaba. The city of Mariana, once Ribeirao do Carmo, founded in 1711, lies seven miles east of Ouro Preto, the old state capital. Benedict XIV erected the bishopric in December 1745, with Frei Manoel da Cruz as first bishop.

For over a century Mariana was the church centre of Minas Geraes. Parishes were cut off for Diamantina in 1854 and Pouso Alegre in 1900, and in May 1906 Mariana became an archdiocese, once suffragan to Rio de Janeiro. It spans 110,000 square miles, nearly half the state, with over two million Catholics and only about two thousand Protestants. It holds 311 parishes and 611 churches or chapels, served by 545 secular and 104 regular priests, with a Lazarist seminary. Its first archbishop, Silverio Gomes Pimenta, ninth ordinary and first Minas native to rule the see, succeeded in 1897.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-marina:
Marina, or de Marinis, was an ancient and noble Genoese family, famed on Chios, a Genoese dependency where it held rich estates. It gave the Church Pope Urban VII and adorned the Dominican Order with eminent theologians and religious. This entry follows four of its Dominicans.

Leonardo Marini, archbishop born on Chios in 1509 and dead at Rome in 1573, was famed as the most eloquent preacher of his day. Julius III made him titular Bishop of Laodicea and administrator of Mantua in 1550, and Pius IV raised him to Lanciano in 1562. Giovanni Battista, born at Rome in 1597 and dead there in 1669, became secretary of the Congregation of the Index in 1628 and bore abuse from censured authors. Domenico, born at Rome in 1599 and dead at Avignon in 1669, taught at Salamanca, Alcala, Toulouse, and Paris, rebuilt the Minerva convent as prior, and became Archbishop of Avignon in 1648.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-martyrs-in-ch:
Martyrs in China traces Christian martyrdom in China from the fourteenth century onward. The first martyrs appear to have been missionaries at Ili Baliq in Central Asia, Khan-Baliq or Peking, and Zaitun in Fu-kien, in the mid-fourteenth century. 

With missions revived under Matteo Ricci, dead at Peking in 1610, martyrs' blood soon fertilised the field again. A Fu-ngan libel brought a viceroy's inquiry into Fu-kien Catholics, and persecution raged under Kia K'ing from 1796 to 1820. Lazarists Louis-Gabriel-Taurin Dufresse and Jean-Gabriel Perboyre fell to mandarins, betrayed by renegades. After France's 1844 treaty won free Christian exercise, Franciscan vicar apostolic Giuseppe Rizzolati was expelled from Hu-pe. The long list runs through 1861, 1865, Korean massacres of 1839 and 1866, Yung-chang arrests of 1898, Chi-li Jesuits, Scheut Belgians, and beyond, with many more unrecorded sufferers.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-matteo-da-sie:
Matteo da Sienna, Matteo di Giovanni di Bartolo, was a painter born at Borgo San Sepolcro about 1435 and dead in 1495. His common name came from working chiefly at Siena. 

Matteo shared those traits and added dignity of female figures, gracious angels, and a rich, brilliant, harmonious colour scheme, making him critics' best fifteenth-century Sienese painter. His earliest authentic work, dated 1470, is a Virgin enthroned with angels for the Servites, now in Siena Academy. In 1487 he painted an Assumption for Borgo's Santa Maria de' Servi high altar, Apostles and saints watching, with the Virgin's history on the predella. He designed Siena Cathedral pavement subjects, the Sibyl of Samos, Deliverance of Bethulia, and Massacre of the Innocents, and painted Madonna della Neve in 1477. Lively action scenes, by contrast, grew confused and grimacing.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-messina:
Messina, in Sicily, lies like an amphitheatre along the Hills of Neptune, on a sea inlet at the Strait of Messina, which parts Sicily from the mainland. Its harbour, for size and fine position, ranks among Italy's most important after Genoa and Naples. Yet hopes for its trade after the Suez Canal opened were dashed. Between 1887 and 1894 its commerce fell from 940,000 tons to 350,000, though by 1908 it had grown again to 551,000 tons.

 The mountains yield calcic sulphate, alabaster, sulphates of argentiferous lead, antimony, iron, and copper. Messina is said to have been founded by pirates from Cumae, an ancient Greek colony, and named Zancle, sickle, for the port's half-moon shape. In 735 a colony of Messenians was brought there by Gorgos, son of King Aristomenes, the brave but unlucky defender against Sparta. Later, fugitives from Chalcis, Samos, and Euboea, fleeing Persian invasion, swelled the town.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-methymna:
Methymna, a titular see on Lesbos, was once the island's second city and enjoyed great prosperity. In the Peloponnesian War it played a major part, and in Christian times it likewise stood out in resistance to the Turks. Ancient poets praise its excellent wine: Virgil, Ovid, and Horace all name it. Methymna was the birthplace of the poet Arion and probably of the historian Myrsilus.

For its bishops, see Le Quien: one of them, Gabriel, in the seventeenth century united with Rome. In 640 the Ecthesis of pseudo-Epiphanius lists it as an autocephalous archdiocese, and about 1084, under Alexius I Comnenus, it became a metropolitan see. The Orthodox Church still grants it that rank, while Catholics now count it only as a titular archdiocese. Its present name is Molivo, and its district holds 37,000 people: 29,000 Orthodox Greeks, 9,000 Mussulmans, and 40 Catholics under Smyrna.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-metrophanes-o:
Metrophanes of Smyrna headed the bishops loyal to Ignatius through the Photian schism of 867. Baronius claims his mother took a bribe to accuse Patriarch Methodius I falsely of rape amid the Iconoclast troubles; if so, Constantinople was his birthplace. In 857, the year Ignatius lost his see, he was already Metropolitan of Smyrna, standing firm against Photius.

He wavered briefly when Photius vowed to leave Ignatius's rights alone, but, seeing that pledge worthless, he returned to his old stand for good. He headed the bishops that cast Photius out in 858, vowing they themselves would stand cast out if they ever gave him recognition. That bold pledge steered all that followed. The government chained, jailed, then exiled him, yet he came home after Photius's first fall in 867. At Constantinople IV, the eighth general council, in 869, he opened its sixth session with a speech and sat with the judges who condemned Photius.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-michael-of-ce:
Michael of Cesena, or Michele Fuschi, was a Friar Minor, Minister General of the Franciscans, and theologian, born at Cesena about 1270 and dead at Munich in 1342. Little is known of his youth. Joining the Franciscans, he studied at Paris, took his theology doctorate, taught at Bologna, and wrote commentaries on Scripture and Peter Lombard's Sentences.

At Naples in 1316 the general chapter elected him minister general. He went to Assisi, called a chapter to revise the order's Constitutions, and at Bologna issued Gravi qua premor, with other ordinances on poverty. These moved John XXII to publish Quorumdam exigit in 1317, explaining the decretals of Nicholas III and Clement V on the Franciscan Rule's chief chapter. The bull stirred great unrest, and Michael's party warmly opposed it, claiming strict poverty followed Christ and his Apostles.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-miguel-de-med:
Miguel de Medina, a theologian, was born at Belalcazar, Spain, in 1489 and died at Toledo in May 1578. He joined the Franciscans at Hornachuelos, in the Sierra Morena, in the convent of S. Maria de Angelis. Once professed, he moved to the college of SS. Peter and Paul at Alcala. Toledo gave him his doctorate, and in 1550 Alcala chose him by a unanimous vote for its chair of Holy Scripture.

In 1560 Philip II sent him off to the Council of Trent. On coming back he took charge of St. John's of the Kings at Toledo as its superior. Medina is best recalled for standing up for John Ferus, whose Commentaries came out at Rome in 1553 after a strict vetting, only to be censured by Dominicus a Soto at Salamanca. Medina's learned defence of Ferus kept the work in good standing and showed his command of Scripture and tradition.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-modena:
Modena, an archdiocese in central Italy between the Secchia and Panaro rivers, holds many fine buildings. Its Romanesque cathedral, begun in 1099 and consecrated by Lucius III in 1184, bears scenes from the Old and New Testaments sculptured in white marble on its interior facade. Its high altar holds a Purification by Guido Reni, and the choir's inlaid work by the Lendinara brothers, dated 1465, is very beautiful.

The belfry, called the Ghirlandina, guards the famed wooden pail seized from the Bolognese after Zappolino in 1325, which Tassoni made the theme of his heroic-comic epic. Modena's university, among Italy's oldest, and its archbishops, who guided the city through Este rule, complete a see rich in art, learning, and civic pride.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-modigliana:
Modigliana, a diocese in the province of Florence in Tuscany, stands on the banks of the Tramazzo and is the Castrum Mutilum of Livy. Ravenna's counts held it in the ninth century, and the Guidi ruled it after them until 1377, when Florence claimed its loyalty. In the sixteenth century the academy of the Incamminati thrived there.

Its bishopric goes back only to 1850, first under Faenza as suffragan. Julius II dedicated its cathedral, once a collegiate church, after its sixteenth-century rebuilding. Its first bishop was Mario Melini. The diocese is now suffragan of Florence, a small Tuscan see with an ancient civic past.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-montana:
Montana, the Treasure State and third largest in the Union, entered statehood on 8 November 1889. Its northern edge runs 549 miles along the forty-ninth parallel against Canada. The Rocky Mountains carve its western and southwestern borders. The eastern half spreads into plain and prairie.

Granite Peak, at 12,600 feet, is its highest summit. The Northern Pacific crosses the continental divide west of Helena at 5,573 feet. The entry then covers rivers, climate, minerals and farming. It traces the fur trade and gold rushes that drew settlers, the Indian wars, and the Catholic story. Missions among the tribes, the first bishops, parishes and schools grew alongside railways, mines and ranches.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-myrina:
Myrina was a titular see of Asia Minor, suffragan to Ephesus, counted by Herodotus among the eleven cities of Aeolia and said by Strabo to have been built by the Amazon Myrina. Artaxerxes gave it to the chieftain Gorgion, Pliny praised its oysters, and an inscription places it in the kingdom of Pergamus in the third century BC.

Earthquakes under Tiberius and again under Trajan levelled it, and each time it was rebuilt. It was the birthplace of Agathias, Byzantine poet and historian of the sixth century. Its bishops, known from Dorotheus in 431 to Cosmas in 787, served a diocese lasting into the fourteenth century. Its site lay at Kalabassary near the mouth of the Hodja-Tchai, where excavations in 1880 to 1882 uncovered some four thousand tombs.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-north-carolin:
North Carolina, one of the original thirteen American states, stretches 503 miles from the Atlantic to the Tennessee line. Bounded by Virginia, the ocean, South Carolina, Georgia, and Tennessee, it covered 52,250 square miles in 1910, held 2,206,287 people, and counted Raleigh its capital.

From tidewater marshes and longleaf pine through rolling hills to mountain peaks, the state yields pitch, tar, turpentine, tobacco, and cotton. The entry surveys its counties, cities like Wilmington and Charlotte, and its Catholic parishes, schools, and missions. Its population in 1910 reached 2,206,287, with ten congressional districts across ninety-eight counties.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-novena:
A novena, from the Latin word for nine, is nine days of private or public prayer in the Catholic Church to seek a special grace. Unlike the festive octave, the novena carries a tone of hopeful mourning and yearning, and Jerome links the number nine in Scripture with suffering and grief.

The entry sorts novenas of mourning, preparation, prayer, and indulgence, and traces the form from a Roman nine-day sacrifice after stones rained on the Alban Mount. Though no fixed place in the liturgy belongs to it, authority permits and even recommends the devotion.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nueva-pamplon:
Nueva Pamplona, a Colombian diocese erected in 1835, serves a city of 15,000 and a flock of 325,000 in Norte de Santander. Founded as a town in 1549 and suffragan to Bogotá, it counted almost all its people Catholic, with about a hundred dissenters, mostly foreigners.

Its first bishops died in exile in Venezuela, victims of liberal governments: Torres Estans in 1853 and Niño in 1864. Later bishops held synods, attended the Vatican Council, and endured exile, while Evaristo Blanco, transferred from Socorro in 1909, led the diocese into the new century. Its third bishop, Toscano, convoked the first diocesan synod and attended the Vatican Council.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-oppido-mamert:
Oppido Mamertina, a Calabrian diocese suffragan to Reggio, is famed for long resistance to Roger in the eleventh century. Its first named bishop, Stefano, dates to 1295, and in 1472 Athanasius Calceofilo united it to Gerace and abolished the Greek rite, though a few towns kept it.

Independent again in 1536 under Pietro Andrea Ripanti, Oppido gained a restored cathedral and palace under Montani and a seminary under Fili. Michele Caputo, transferred to Ariano in 1852 and later apostate, closes a troubled list, and the diocese counts 19 parishes and 28,000 people. Bisanzio Fili founded the seminary in 1696.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-orcagna:
Orcagna, the art-history name for Andrea di Cione of Florence, worked as architect, sculptor, mosaicist, painter, and poet in the fourteenth century. Son of a goldsmith and brother to painters Nardo, Jacopo, and Matteo, he joined the painters' guild in 1357 alongside Nardo.

His brother Nardo, not Andrea, painted the Strozzi chapel Last Judgment after Dante, despite old attributions, and Pisa's Triumph of Death likewise belongs elsewhere. Andrea himself planned Florence cathedral's enlargement with Talento and made mosaics for Orvieto's façade before his death in 1368. Vasari names Andrea Pisano as his sculpture master, a claim the entry doubts.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-palestrina:
Palestrina, ancient Praeneste, is a town in Rome province in central Italy, on the Via Labicana. Ancients credited its founding to Ulysses or another fabled figure. History first names it as Rome's ally against the Latins in 499 before Christ. From 373 to 370 it warred with Rome, lost land in 354 and 338, then stayed allied while scorning Roman citizenship until 90 before Christ.

Sulla sacked it in 82 for sheltering Marius, and under Tiberius it became a municipium and summer resort, mocked for its rough speech and manners. The modern town rises over the famed temple of Fortuna Primigenia. From the eleventh century it served as a Colonna fief and rebel refuge. It was wrecked in 1297 and 1436, rebuilt in 1447, sacked in 1527, and sold to the Barberini in 1630.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pamplona:
Pamplona is a Spanish diocese covering almost all of Navarre and part of Guipuzcoa, said to date from apostolic times. Tradition in Pamplona, Toledo, and Toulouse tells that Saint Saturninus, disciple of Saint Peter, sent the priest Honestus from Toulouse to preach in Navarre, then came himself. Honestus taught Saint Firminus, son of Senator Firmus, first Bishop of Pamplona, later martyred at Amiens.

No other bishop is noted until Liliolus signed at the Third Council of Toledo in 589. After the Saracen invasion no bishop is recorded until Opilanus in 829. The old cathedral lay in ruins, and bishops sheltered at San Salvador de Leyre. Inigo Arista retook Pamplona in 848 or 849, restored the monastery as a stronghold, and made it the episcopal court for a long age.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-parana:
Parana is an Argentine diocese, suffragan of Buenos Aires until recently, covering Entre Rios and Corrientes provinces and the Misiones territory. It belonged to Buenos Aires until 1854, when it became a separate pro-vicariate, and Pius IX raised it to a diocese by bull of 13 June 1859. Its area totals 69,870 square miles, its people 774,000, and Corrientes has lately been cut off as its own diocese.

Jose Gabriel Segura y Cuvas, born at Catamarca in 1802, took the see on 3 June 1860 as first bishop and died in 1862. Jose Maria Gelabert y Crespo followed in 1865 until 1897, then Rosendo de la Lastra y Gordillo until 1909. Abel Bazan y Bustos, born at La Rioja in 1867, took possession on 15 May 1910. Entre Rios holds sixteen parishes and ten chaplaincies, Corrientes twenty parishes, and Misiones one parish and three chaplaincies.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pedro-campana:
Pedro Campana was a Flemish painter known as Pierre de Champagne and Pieter de Kempeneer. Born at Brussels in 1503, he died in 1580, after most of his life in Spain. He is said to have studied under Raphael, doubtfully. He visited Italy, Venice, Rome, and Bologna, studying Raphael closely.

In 1530 he decorated the arch raised at Bologna for Charles V. Under Grimani's protection he went to Spain. He stayed at Seville between 1537 and 1552, founding a school with Louis de Vergas and sculptor Torrigiano. The school became an academy counting Morales among pupils. His masterpiece is the Descent from the Cross, painted in 1548 for Santa Cruz and moved to the cathedral when it was destroyed. Murillo admired its lifelike qualities and wished burial beneath it. Two more of his paintings hang there, with works at Carmona and Triana. He returned to Brussels in 1564. His pictures were painted on panel, faultless in draughtsmanship.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pedro-de-luna:
Pedro de Luna was an Aragonese churchman whose career ended as a rival pope. Born at Illueca in 1328, he studied law at Montpellier and later taught church law there. He rose to cardinal under Gregory XI. This Catholic Encyclopedia life then tracks his part in the Western Schism, the split that left rival claimants in Rome and Avignon.

Elected at Avignon in 1394 as Benedict XIII, he pledged again and again to resign for unity. Yet he refused to step down when councils and kings pressed him. His embassies crossed Spain and France, and his support slowly broke away. The Council of Constance removed him in 1417. He spent his last years at Peñíscola, keeping a small court until his death around 1422 or 1423.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-peter-blomeve:
Peter Blomevenna was a Dutch Carthusian prior and writer, born at Leyden in 1466. Greedy and cruel relatives made his youth poor and hard, yet he lived a notably pure and devoted life. Entering the Carthusians, he was elected prior of Cologne in 1506 and held the post for twenty-nine years until his death. As visitor of the Rhenish province he pressed strict observance on houses beyond his own.

Writing filled his remaining hours. His Enchiridion Sacerdotum of 1532 meditates on the Eucharist, and his De Bonitate Divina served preachers. In 1513 he put the Franciscan De Herp's golden guide to contemplation into Latin with notes, and he edited volumes of Denis the Carthusian. Against the rising Reformation he wrote the Candela Evangelica, a defence of purgatory, and tracts on church authority and devotion.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-piazza-armeri:
Piazza Armerina was a Sicilian diocese in Caltanissetta province, set on a high hill in fertile country. Its origin is obscure: William the Bad destroyed it in 1166 for rebellion, and William the Good rebuilt it with the church of the Assunta, now the cathedral, holding Paladino's fine Assumption. The priory church of St. Andrew also keeps fine paintings and frescoes.

The diocese, taken from Catania, was created in 1817 under its first prelate, Girolamo Aprile e Benzi, as suffragan to Syracuse. It counts 23 parishes with 184,500 inhabitants, seven houses of men and nineteen of women, a boys' school, seven girls' schools, and one Catholic weekly. This short Catholic Encyclopedia entry gathers town and diocese in a few lines.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pietro-alagon:
Pietro Alagona was a Sicilian Jesuit theologian best known for handbooks that put weighty moral theology within reach of ordinary confessors. He was born at Syracuse in 1549 and joined the order in 1564. He taught philosophy and theology and served as rector at Trapani. He published his first works under his mother's family name, Givarra.

His abridgement of Martin Aspilcueta's manual for confessors ran to at least twenty-three editions. His summary of the Summa ran to twenty-five, and he also condensed the whole of canon law, church law, into two volumes. A French version of his manual was condemned by the Parliament of Rouen in 1762, and he died at Rome in 1624.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-piscina: A piscina is a basin or drain in a Catholic church for water that has touched sacred things. The name comes from the Latin for fishpond. It covers a baptismal font, a cistern catching water from a baptism, or a small pit near the altar, some two or three feet deep, covered with a stone slab. Into it goes water from washing the priest's hands, from rinsing altar linens, and crumbs and cotton used after anointings, with ashes of sacred objects no longer fit for use.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-poona:
Poona is a diocese in India covering the Deccan plateau portion of the Bombay Presidency as far north as the Tapti River. It takes in Poona, Ahmednagar, Nasik, Sholapur, Bijapur, Satara, and Dharwar, with the states of Kolhapur, Miraj, and Sangli. Its Catholic population numbered 15,487, with twenty-two churches and twenty chapels.

Twenty-one Jesuit fathers of the German province and twelve secular priests serve the diocese, helped by the Nuns of Jesus and the Daughters of the Cross. Besides military stations and railway churches, three mission fields stand out: Ahmednagar from 1878 with 5,880 Christians, Gadag from 1868, and a new mission at Khandalla. The bishop's residence and cathedral are at Poona, and candidates for priesthood train at Kandy in Ceylon.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-porto-and-san:
The Porto and Santa Rufina diocese joins two suburbicarian sees. Porto stands now as a wretched village; once it served as Rome's chief harbour. Claudius built its port opposite Ostia; Trajan enlarged it. Julius Nepos forced Emperor Glycerius to abdicate near Porto in 474. In the Gothic War it served Goths and Byzantines as a base against Rome. Saracens sacked it repeatedly in the ninth and tenth centuries.

Leo IV fortified it in 849, but decay continued. Christianity came early: martyrs Herculanus, Hyacinthus, Martialis, Saturninus, Epictetus, Maprilis, and Felix are named. Gregorius was bishop in 314. Pammachius built a great hospice about 370. Later bishops include Donatus, builder of St Eutropius's basilica, and Felix, contemporary of Gregory the Great. Joannes was legate to the Sixth Council in 680. Gregorius went with Constantine to Constantinople in 710. The united see's bishops later ranked second among cardinals after Ostia, officiating Mondays in the Lateran.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-rajpootana:
Rajpootana, a Prefecture Apostolic in India attached to the Province of Agra, covers the native states of the Rajpootana Agency. This encyclopedia entry bounds it by Bahawalpur and the Punjab to the north, and by Alwar, Bharatpur and Dholpur to the east. Bhopal State and the River Nerbudda bound it to the south, and the Bombay Presidency to the west. Mount Abu and Abu Road station, however, belong to the Archdiocese of Bombay.

Catholics number about 3,846, of whom 656 are Europeans, 609 Eurasians and 2,581 natives. They have nine churches and eight chapels, served by 29 Capuchin Fathers of the Province of Paris, helped by ten lay brothers. Charities include a home at Thandla for 29 Bhil orphans, Saint Joseph's convent at Thandla for Bhil girls, a surgical home at Indore staffed by four nuns, and dispensaries in seven places. The Madras Catholic Directory and Fortunat's travel book supply the sources.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ratherius-of-:
Ratherius of Verona was born about 887 and died at Namur on 25 April 974. This encyclopedia entry follows a Liège noble, sent as a boy oblate to the Benedictine Abbey of Lobbes in Hainaut. There he studied diligently, gained much learning, and became a monk. From an early age he showed a restless nature, a hard temper, great ambition, and harsh zeal. Strict orthodoxy, wide learning and sober conduct could not save him from trouble in every post.

His whole life was wandering and unfruitful, and nowhere did he win lasting success. When Abbot Hilduin of Lobbes travelled to Italy in 926, then ruled by his cousin Hugo of Provence, he took Ratherius as his companion. After many difficulties Ratherius received preferment from the king, the entry notes, beginning a career of shifting posts. Hurter, Vogel and Hauck supply the entry's sources on a learned bishop who could never settle.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ravenna:
Ravenna, archdiocese and city, stands as capital of a province in Romagna, central Italy, on the left of the Montone and Ronco rivers. This long encyclopedia entry notes that the Corsini Canal, built by Clement the Twelfth in 1736, links the city and its wet dock with Porto Corsini on the Adriatic. Ravenna lies on an alluvial plain, partly marshy, and a pine grove beginning two miles from the city runs to Cervia, famous since antiquity.

That grove, once reaching north to Aquileia, suffered in the winter of 1879 to 1880 and in a fire of 1905. The plains are farmed intensively, and silk-making flourishes. In ancient and early medieval times Ravenna stood on the coast itself. Later lords include Lamberto, who abolished democratic government in 1297 to 1316. Guido Novello, lover of letters and arts, welcomed Dante with honours and summoned Giotto to paint the vault of San Giovanni Evangelista.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-regina:
The Diocese of Regina, created on 4 March 1910, covers the southern part of the Canadian province of Saskatchewan, up to the 30th township, about latitude 51 degrees 30 minutes north. This encyclopedia entry counts 58,771 Catholics: 19,563 of French descent, 16,318 Germans, about 13,000 Galicians of the Ruthenian Rite, 4,759 English-speaking, 2,312 Poles and 1,819 Hungarians. About 1,000 Catholic Indians stand among the rest. Fifty-nine priests attend them: 43 French, 15 German and one Scot.

The regular clergy includes the Oblates of Mary Immaculate, the country's pioneers, the Missionaries of La Salette and of Issoudun in France, the Redemptorists, and the Sons of Mary Immaculate. Nuns of five orders teach in schools or nurse the sick in hospitals. The diocese takes in Moose Jaw, Swift Current and Yorkton, headquarters of a large Galician colony. Mgr Oliver E. Matthieu, former rector of Laval University at Quebec, became its first bishop on 14 July 1911.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-remesiana:
Remesiana was a titular see in Dacia Mediterranea, suffragan of Sardica. It appears in the Antonine Itinerary, the Jerusalem Itinerary, the Peutinger Table, and the Ravenna Geographer, and Justinian rebuilt and fortified it while planting many fortresses nearby. In the sixth century this city of ancient Moesia was counted among the towns of Dacia Mediterranea, whose civil and religious capital, Sardica, stood under the Patriarchate of Rome.

Today the place is Bela Palanka, with eleven hundred inhabitants and a railway station between Nich and Pirot in Servia. Two of its bishops are known: Saint Nicetas, and Diogenianus, who attended the Robber Synod of Ephesus in 449. The entry traces the see through its ancient itineraries, its Justinian rebuilding, and its bishops.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-rhesaena:
Rhesaena was a titular see in Osrhoene, suffragan of Edessa, and an important town at Mesopotamia's northern edge near the sources of the Chaboras, now the Khabour. It stood on the road from Carrhae to Nicephorium, some eighty miles from Nisibis, forty from Dara, and nearby Gordian the Third fought the Persians in 243. Its coins show a Roman colony from the time of Septimius Severus.

The Notitia dignitatum places it under the governor, or Dux, of Osrhoene. Hierocles lists it in the same province under the name Theodosiopolis, taken from Theodosius the Great, whose favour it had won. Justinian fortified it, Tamerlane's troops nearly destroyed it in 1393, and today, as Râs-el-'Ain, it is the capital of a caza.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-rhithymna:
Rhithymna was a titular see of Crete, suffragan of Gortyna, named by Ptolemy, Pliny, and Stephen of Byzantium. Nothing is known of its ancient history, though some of its coins survive. It still exists as Rhethymnon, a small port on the island's north side, thirty-seven miles south-west of Candia. It has about ten thousand inhabitants, half Greeks and half Mussulmans, and some Catholics with a church and school.

The town exports oil and soap. Under Venetian rule in Crete it became a Latin see, which Corner identifies with Calamona. Eubel lists twenty-four of its bishops from 1287 to 1592, with three more names from 1611 to 1641. Its foundation date is unknown, it never appears in the medieval Greek lists of sees, and its bishop now bears the joined titles of Rhethymnon and Aulopotamos.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saint-marcell:
Marcellina, elder sister of Ambrose of Milan, was born most probably at Trier around 330 and died about 398. Before her father died she had already left worldly life behind in Rome and chosen a life of prayer and self-denial. Her entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia traces a quiet career spent beside one of the great bishops of the early Church.

On Christmas Day, probably in 353, Pope Liberius gave her the veil of a consecrated virgin, and Ambrose later kept her counsel on virginity in his own writing. After Ambrose became bishop of Milan in 374 he called her there, where she helped spread the disciplined religious life among the city's young women. She outlived her brother and was buried beneath the altar of his basilica, with her feast kept on 17 July.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saint-philome:
Philomena, a young maiden whose tomb was opened in the Catacomb of Priscilla on 25 May 1802, became one of the nineteenth century's most popular saints almost overnight. Because the grave held a glass vessel, then wrongly thought a sure mark of martyrdom, the remains were taken for a virgin martyr, and slabs bearing the name Filumena fixed her identity. Her entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia tells how a name became a cult.

Translated to Mugnano near Naples in 1805, her relics drew pilgrims, and Leo XII gave the church the inscribed tiles in 1827. Alleged revelations then supplied a life story and a martyrdom that no ancient source supports. The entry reports the devotion fairly while noting that De Rossi's research overturned the vessel test, leaving the saint's history resting on very thin ground.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saint-thomas-:
Saint Thomas of Guiana names a Venezuelan diocese, suffragan of Caracas, erected by Pius VI on 19 December 1791. It covered the old state of Bermúdez, the districts of Nueva Esparta and Guayana, and the territories of Amazonas, Caura, Colón, Orinoco, and Yuruary across the south and east of the country. Its entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia lists bishops, parishes, and people.

Francisco de Ybarra served as first bishop, and after the wars of independence disrupted the see, Leo XII named a vicar apostolic and Gregory XVI restored the bishopric in 1841. By the early twentieth century the diocese counted over 400,000 Catholics, sixty parishes, thirty-six priests, and fifty churches and chapels. Spanish missionaries had earlier brought the Carib peoples of the east into the Church, and the entry records that hard frontier work.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-salve-regina:
Salve Regina, Hail Queen, opens the most celebrated of the four Breviary anthems to the Virgin Mary. It is sung from first Vespers of Trinity Sunday until None, mid-afternoon prayer, on the Saturday before Advent. Local variations exist: Châlons used it from the Purification until Holy Thursday. Its entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia traces text, use, and legend.

At Speyer the anthem was chanted solemnly every day in honour of Bernard, and two legends tie him to it. One says that on Christmas Eve 1146, entering the cathedral as legate while the anthem sounded, he knelt three times at the closing words, O clemens, O pia, O dulcis Virgo Maria. The commoner tale says he added that triple cry himself in a sudden flash of inspiration, and brass plates marked the spot.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-san-juan-arge:
San Juan de Cuyo, an Argentine diocese at the foot of the Andes between 28 and 41 degrees south, covers San Juan, Mendoza, and San Luis provinces with the Neuquén district. It spans 151,096 square miles and 540,000 people. Once part of Santiago de Chile until 1776, then of Córdoba, the region became a vicariate in 1826 and a diocese under Gregory XVI in 1834. Its entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia blends church and national history.

First bishop Justo de Santa María de Oro had represented San Juan at the Tucumán congress that proclaimed Argentine independence on 9 July 1816. There he firmly opposed a monarchy for the infant nation. He died in 1838, honoured by a handsome bronze statue in the provincial capital. The entry follows his successors and the diocese's parishes, showing a church woven into a new republic's birth.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-santa-cathari:
Santa Catharina, a Brazilian diocese suffragan of Porto Alegre, was created in 1906 and covers the whole state of Santa Catharina. In 1909 it counted 405,800 Catholics out of about 500,000 people. Its entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia opens with the first European landings on its coast.

Juan Díaz Solís and Vicente Yañez Pinzón may have explored the coast in 1515, landing in the Bay dos Perdidos. Sebastian Cabot landed in 1525 and Diego García in 1526 on the island of Santa Catharina, then called Patos, before sailing on to the River Plate. The state joined the Brazilian union in 1891, and the diocese lists fifteen vicariates, from Florianópolis, the bishop's seat, to Laguna and Tubarão.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-santa-fe-arge:
Santa Fe, an Argentine diocese suffragan of Buenos Aires, covers Santa Fe province with the governorships of El Chaco and Formosa. Split from Paraná on 15 February 1897, it spans about 145,100 square miles with 860,000 people, mostly Catholics. Its entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia gives a new diocese's first census.

Juan Agustín Boneo, born at Buenos Aires in 1845, had been made titular bishop of Arsinoe in 1893 as coadjutor to Archbishop Aneiros. He moved to the new see on 27 January 1898 as its first bishop. The diocese counted sixty-five parishes, forty-eight vice-parishes, four Indian mission centres, and 143 secular clergy. A conciliar seminary held forty-five students, and fifty-two Catholic colleges and schools served the region.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-santa-severin:
Santa Severina, a diocese in Catanzaro province in Calabria, perches on a rocky crag on the site of ancient Siberena. It grew into a key Byzantine fortress in the wars against the Saracens. Its entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia traces an archbishopric of the Greek rite turned Latin.

Probably an archbishopric by the tenth century, it once ruled Orea, Acerenza, Gallipoli, Alessano, and Castro as suffragans. The Greek rite vanished under the Normans, though it lingered in the cathedral through much of the thirteenth century. Giovanni is the earliest known bishop, and from Stefano in 1096 the list runs unbroken, through Ugo, once prior of the Holy Sepulchre, and Jacopo, who died in fame of holiness.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sarsina:
Sarsina, a diocese in Forlì province in Emilia, Italy, lives by farming, cattle, and sulphur and manganese works, with fossil carbon beds and sulphur springs nearby. Ruins of temples, baths, and walls, with urns, pillars, and bronzes, show an ancient importance, and Plautus was born here. Its entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia follows an Umbrian town through conquest and feuds.

Captured by Cornelius Scipio in 271, Sarsina became a Roman municipium. In the tenth century its bishops won temporal rule over city and district. From 1327 to 1400 Ordelaffi, popes, and bishops disputed it. Malatesta lords held it in turn, Cesare Borgia seized it in 1500, Venetians took it in 1503, and in 1518 it passed to the Pio di Meldola and later the Aldobrandini. Its cathedral stands as a notable monument.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-school-of-ion:
Iona, modern form of Adamnan's Ioua and Bede's Hii, is the Gaelic I or Y, becoming Hy with a euphonic h. This rugged, storm-beaten island, three miles long and one broad, lies a mile from Mull's Ross. It ranked next to Armagh as Gaelic Christianity's greatest centre: Patrick's city against Columba's monastic city, a primatial island and light of the north. Its entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia weighs exile against mission.

Columba, born in 521, landed with twelve monks at the southern tip, at a bay ever since called the Bay of the Island. The date was Whitsun Eve, 12 May 563. Whether he came in penance for his part in the battle of Cuildreimhne two years earlier cannot now be settled. The Irish Life says he came to preach to Alba's men, Britons, and Saxons. Either way preaching was his chief purpose, and the entry follows Iona's rise to primacy.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sehna: A small Chaldean see straddling Persia and Turkey, Sehna was erected in 1853 and placed under a patriarchal administrator of episcopal rank. This brief entry notes that it was administered in practice by the Archbishop of Kerkuk in the mid-1800s. It seemed likely to be joined to that see. Its chief town, also called Sinna, lay in Persia. The diocese counted only 700 Catholics, five priests, two primary schools, and two chapels.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-siena:
The archdiocese of Siena in Tuscany stands on three gently swelling hills, and this entry opens with its art, in which no other city kept so local and conservative a character. Gothic architecture produced its finest monuments here, both churches and civic buildings, and Sienese architects worked beyond their state, as at Orvieto cathedral. Sculpture took its first impulse from Nicolo and Giovanni Pisani, and painting counted Duccio, who surpassed his Florentine contemporary Cimabue in grace and accuracy of design.

History follows art. Siena repulsed Henry VI in 1194, joined the League of San Genesio, and at Montaperto in 1260, leading Tuscany's Ghibellines, humiliated Florence. Guelphs took sovereignty in 1277, and their merchant government of the Fifteen lasted seventy years. Plague in 1348 killed 30,000 in the city, tumults and constitutional changes filled the later 1300s, and Pandolfo Petrucci rose over fresh strife in 1480.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-simon-of-crem: A theological writer and celebrated preacher of the Augustinian order, Simon of Cremona flourished in the second half of the 1300s and died at Padua in 1390. His field was northern Italy, above all Venetian territory. Excerpts from his sermons appeared in 1484 as a Postil on the Gospels and Epistles of all Sundays. Several works survive in manuscript, including a commentary on the four books of Sentences and questions on the Portiuncula indulgence and on the blood of Christ.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-smyrna:
Smyrna, Latin archdiocese in Asia Minor, rises like an amphitheatre on its gulf and serves as capital of the vilayet of Aïdin. Founded over 1,000 years before Christ by colonists from Lesbos, it grew rich under Ionian rule. It was destroyed by Alyattes of Lydia about 580 before Christ, and rebuilt by Antigonus and Lysimachus on its present site. Ceded to Rome in 133 before Christ, it won fame for its school of rhetoric and its title of metropolis.

Christianity reached Smyrna early. By the year 93 a bishop-led community existed, praised by John in the Apocalypse, and Polycarp, its bishop, was martyred and honoured in an encyclical to Philomelium. The Latin see dates to Clement VI in 1346, and Pius VII erected the archdiocese in 1818. The archdiocese then counted 17,000 Latin Catholics, 8 parishes, 25 primary schools with 2,500 pupils, 2 hospitals, and 4 orphanages.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-solsona:
Solsona was a diocese in the Spanish province of Lerida, suffragan to Tarragona, and this entry traces its fortunes from foundation to suppression. Erected by Clement VIII in 1593 from the dioceses of Urgel and Vich, it was suppressed under the Concordat of 1851 after an eleven-year vacancy. And the planned union with Vich never took effect, leaving it under an apostolic administrator.

Bounded by Urgel, Lerida, Tarragona, and Vich, the diocese held 152 parishes, 330 priests and clerics, 259 churches, and about 120,000 people. The entry also lists its religious houses, from Cistercians and Benedictines to Carmelites and Dominicans, giving a snapshot of Catholic life in a Catalan diocese at the start of the twentieth century.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-south-carolin:
South Carolina, one of the thirteen original colonies of the United States, is surveyed here in land, people, and church life at the time of the 1910 census. The state covered 30,570 square miles across 35 counties. It rose from eastern tidewater marshland to mountains in the west. Columbia was the capital, and the Pedee and Santee rivers ran to the Atlantic.

Population climbed from about 503,000 in 1820 to 1,515,400 in 1910. The entry tracks that growth county by county. It notes Beaufort County's place among the densest Black populations in the nation. Its later sections turn to the Catholic Church in the state, giving readers a full portrait of a southern state on the eve of the First World War.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-alexander-:
St. Alexander, called the charcoal burner, was bishop of Comana in Pontus, and this entry delights in the oddity of his election. Whether he was the see's first bishop is debated. And the Bollandists weighed the several towns named Comana before settling on Pontus near Neo-Caesarea. But the saint's nickname is clear: out of humility he had taken up charcoal burning to escape worldly honours.

Called a philosopher, though the term may mean only his preference for heavenly over earthly things, he was discovered through the very contempt he drew. When Gregory Thaumaturgus came to help choose a bishop and rejected every candidate, someone mockingly proposed Alexander the charcoal burner. And Gregory, seeing his virtue, chose him, a story the entry tells with evident pleasure.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-baithen-of:
St. Baithen of Iona was an Irish monk specially chosen by St. Columba for the band of missionaries who sailed for Britain in 563. This entry follows a boy born in 536, son of Brenaron, and an ardent disciple of Columba. He was appointed abbot of Tiree Island, a monastery founded by St. Comgall of Bangor. Adamnan, recording Columba's death, tells us the dying apostle's last words as he copied the fifty-third psalm.

Columba said he must stop there, and let Baithen write what follows. Baithen had long been seen as the most likely successor of Columba. On the great apostle's death in 596, the monks unanimously confirmed their founder's choice. Baithen stood high in esteem as a wise counsellor, and many Irish saints, including Fintan Munnu of Taghmon, sought his advice. Adamnan, Columba's biographer, tells many incidents from Baithen's life.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-balbina:
St. Balbina is remembered at Rome in three different spots connected with early Christian antiquities. This entry follows the tangled evidence for her. In the purely legendary account of the martyrdom of St. Alexander, mention is made of a tribune Quirinus. He died a martyr, and his burial was in the Praetextatus catacomb on the Via Appia. His grave drew great veneration and appears in the old pilgrim guides to the Roman catacombs.

Tradition said his daughter Balbina, baptized by St. Alexander and unmarried all her life, was buried after death near her father in the same catacomb. Her feast is celebrated on 31 March. Usuardus speaks of her in his martyrology, and his account rests on the record of Alexander's martyrdom. Another Balbina gave her name to a different catacomb, and the entry sorts the two apart.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-bernardine:
St. Bernardine of Siena was a Friar Minor, missionary, and reformer, called the Apostle of Italy. This entry follows a boy of the noble Albizeschi family, born at Massa, where his father was then governor, on 8 September 1380. He died at Aquila in the Abruzzi on 20 May 1444. Orphaned at six, Bernardine was raised with great care by his pious aunts, and his youth was blameless and engaging.

In 1397, after studying civil and canon law, he joined the Confraternity of Our Lady at the great hospital of Santa Maria della Scala. Three years later, when pestilence revisited Siena, he left his life of seclusion and prayer to minister to the plague-stricken. With ten companions, he took entire charge of that hospital for four months. Despite his youth he proved fully equal to that task, but the heroic, unremitting labour shattered his health, and he never fully recovered.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-bibiana:
St. Bibiana, or Vibiana, was a Roman female martyr whose earliest mention in an authentic historical authority occurs in the Liber Pontificalis. This entry follows that single solid witness. In the biography of Pope Simplicius, who reigned from 468 to 483. It states that this pope consecrated a basilica for the holy martyr Bibiana, holding her body, near the palatium Licinianum. That basilica still stands.

So in the fifth century, St. Bibiana's bodily remains rested within the city walls. No further historical particulars about the martyr or her death's circumstances survive. Why she was buried in the city itself is also unknown. A legend about her sprang up in later times. It connects her with the Acts of Sts. John and Paul, but has no historical claim to belief, and the entry tells that legend as legend.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-blandina:
St. Blandina was a virgin and martyr of the band of martyrs of Lyons, who suffered a glorious martyrdom in the reign of Marcus Aurelius in 177. This entry follows the moving report the Church of Lyons sent to the churches of Asia Minor, preserved by Eusebius. Heathen populace fanaticism in Lyons had been stirred against the Christians, so that venturing to show themselves publicly brought harassment and ill-treatment.

During the imperial legate's absence, the chiliarch, a military commander, and the duumvir, a civil magistrate, imprisoned a number of Christians who confessed their faith. On the legate's return, those imprisoned believers faced trial. Among those Christians was Blandina, a slave, arrested along with her master, also a Christian. Her companions greatly feared she would fail under torture, and the entry follows her steadfastness.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-catherine-:
St. Catherine of Bologna was a Poor Clare and mystical writer, born at Bologna on 8 September 1413. She died there on 9 March 1463. This entry follows a girl sent by her father, at ten years old, to the court of Niccolo d'Este, Marquis of Ferrara, as companion to Princess Margarita. There Catherine studied literature and the fine arts. A manuscript illuminated by her, once belonging to Pius IX, is now reckoned among Oxford's treasures.

After Margarita's marriage to Roberto Malatesta, prince of Rimini, Catherine returned home. She determined to join a little company of devout maidens living in community under the Third Order of St. Augustine in neighbouring Ferrara. Later the community, yielding to Catherine's entreaties, took up the Rule of St. Clare. In 1432 the provincial of the Friars Minor clothed them with the Second Order's habit.

St. Catherine of Siena was a Dominican tertiary, born at Siena on 25 March 1347. She died at Rome on 29 April 1380. This entry follows the second-youngest of a very large family. Her father, Giacomo di Benincasa, was a dyer, and her mother Lapa was a local poet's daughter. They were part of the lower middle-class faction of tradesmen and petty notaries called the Party of the Twelve. Between one revolution and another, that party ruled the Republic of Siena from 1355 to 1368.

From earliest childhood Catherine saw visions and practised extreme austerities. At seven she consecrated her virginity to Christ. In her sixteenth year she took the Dominican tertiary habit, renewing the desert anchorites' life in a little room of her father's house. After three years of celestial visitations and familiar talk with Christ, she underwent the mystical experience known as the spiritual espousals, probably during carnival season.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-crispina:
St. Crispina was a martyr of Africa who suffered during the Diocletian persecution, born at Thagara in the Province of Africa. She died by beheading at Thebeste in Numidia on 5 December 304. This entry follows a woman of a distinguished family, a wealthy matron with children. When the persecution came, she was brought before the proconsul Anulinus, and ordered to sacrifice to the gods, she declared she honoured only one God.

The judge had her head shaved and exposed her to public mockery, yet she stayed steadfast in the Faith, unmoved even by her children's tears. Condemned to death, she thanked God and joyfully offered her head for execution. The Acts of her martyrdom, written soon after the event, are a valuable historical document on the persecution period.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-dymphna:
Dymphna, virgin and martyr, is honoured at Gheel in Belgium, where her story has shaped care for the troubled mind for centuries. Her earliest life, written in the mid-thirteenth century by Pierre, a canon of Cambrai, rests openly on oral tradition. It tells of an Irish king's daughter, secretly baptized, who fled her father's incestuous suit with the priest Gerebernus to Gheel. The Catholic Encyclopedia article of 1913 follows the tale to her murder there.

From time immemorial she has been invoked as patroness against insanity. Gheel grew a singular custom: after brief observation, sufferers lodged with local families, shared farm work, and were watched without knowing it. As many as fifteen hundred at a time found shelter there. The entry joins a martyr's legend to a living tradition of gentle, household care.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-emerentian:
Emerentiana, a third-century Roman martyr, is remembered for praying at a friend's grave and dying there. Foster-sister of Agnes in legend, she was still a catechumen, not yet baptized, when she visited Agnes's tomb some days after the burial. Pagans attacked her at prayer and killed her with stones. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 places her burial in the great cemetery on the Via Nomentana, near Agnes's own.

Old pilgrim itineraries list her grave beside Agnes's, and a church rose over it. Armellini believed he had found her original burial chamber. Her feast falls on 23 January, though the Hieronymian Martyrology names her under 16 September. Art shows her with stones in her lap. The entry is short, but it anchors a cult in cemetery, church, and martyrology alike.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-eulalia-of:
Eulalia of Barcelona, martyr of 12 February 304, is defended in this entry as a saint distinct from her namesake of Mérida. Patron of Barcelona's cathedral and city, and of sailors, her Acts were copied in the early twelfth century by Renallus Grammaticus. Their chief source is a seventh-century Latin hymn by Quiricus, bishop of Barcelona. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 stresses that hymn's path through the Visigothic church and Mozarabic liturgy.

Doubters have called the Barcelona Eulalia a doublet of Mérida's, but the entry rejects hasty scepticism. Quiricus and Oroncius of Mérida both attended Toledo's tenth council in 656, and Oroncius had founded a nunnery by Mérida's basilica in 651. Two saints, two cities, one shared hymn tradition: the entry argues the record supports both.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-florentina:
Florentina, virgin of sixth-century Spain, anchors a rare family in which four siblings all reached the altars. Younger than Leander, later archbishop of Seville, and older than Isidore, his successor, she was sister also to Fulgentius, bishop of Ecija. Through Leander, once a monk, she embraced the ascetic life and gathered virgins into a community. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 dates her death to about 612.

Later sources place the community at S. Maria de Valle near Ecija, though the entry treats the site as less certain than the life. Born toward the middle of the sixth century, she consecrated her virginity to God while her brothers led the Visigothic church. The entry offers a household of sanctity: three bishop brothers and a sister who built a women's community beside them.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-fructuosus:
Fructuosus of Tarragona, bishop and martyr of 259, died in fire with his two deacons, praying with outstretched hands. Seized with Augurius and Eulogius on the night of 16 January, he was tried five days later by the judge Aemilianus. Confessing himself Christian and bishop, he heard all three sentenced to burn alive. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 dates their death to 21 January 259.

They met the ordeal courageously, and art still shows them in that final posture of prayer. Augustine mentions them in a sermon, and the Spanish poet Prudentius celebrated them in a hymn of his Peristephanon. The entry is among the slice's shortest, yet it preserves a complete martyrdom: arrest, trial, confession, sentence, and a death remembered by poets and preachers alike.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-godelina:
Godelina, murdered bride of Ghistelles, chose the cloister, was forced into marriage, and died for resisting it. Born about 1049 at Hondeforte near Boulogne, youngest child of Hemfrid of Wierre-Effroy and Ogina, she practised piety from childhood with a solidity rare for her years. The poor flocked to her, and her generosity often clashed with her father's steward and even her pious father. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 dates her death at Ghistelles to 6 July 1070.

By eighteen her beauty and virtues were famed through Artois and Flanders, and suitors crowded. Left to decide, she held to renouncing the world for the cloister. Bertolf of Ghistelles, undeterred, invoked Count Eustache II of Boulogne, whose pleading won the day. After the wedding the couple set out for Ghistelles, where the entry's tragedy unfolds: a bride who would not yield her vow.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-helena:
Helena, mother of Constantine the Great, rose from humble birth to become the empire's most generous pilgrim. Born about the middle of the third century, possibly at Drepanum on the Nicomedian Gulf, she was called by Ambrose a stabularia, an inn-keeper, yet became lawful wife of Constantius Chlorus. Her only son Constantine was born at Naissus in 274. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 dates her death to about 330.

English medieval chroniclers made her a British prince's daughter, a claim the entry calls wholly unfounded, born from misreading a panegyric. In 292 Constantius set her aside for political marriage, but her son's rise restored her honour. At Jerusalem she built churches of the Nativity and Ascension and adorned the sacred grotto, and her sojourn started Rufinus's legend of the True Cross's discovery. Eusebius praises a charity that aided whole communities.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-juliana:
Juliana, martyr of the Diocletian persecution, is attested earliest by a single manuscript's martyrology line. Both Latin and Greek churches list a holy martyr Juliana. The oldest historical notice stands in the Hieronymian Martyrology for 16 February, giving her birthplace as Cumae in Campania. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 stresses that the notice survives only in the Codex Epternacensis, the martyrology's chief manuscript.

That notice is certainly authentic, the entry argues, because Gregory the Great's letter testifies to Juliana's special veneration near Naples.
