A pious matron, Januaria, built a church on one estate and sought relics, objects touched to graves, of Severinus and Juliana for its consecration. Gregory wrote to Fortunatus, bishop of Naples, telling him to grant Januaria's wish. Bede used Acts of Juliana whose later fortunes the entry follows with scholarly caution.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-lidwina:
Lidwina of Schiedam, mystic of the sickbed, broke a rib skating in 1395 and never rose again. Born at Schiedam on 18 April 1380 to Peter, of noble family, and Petronella, a poor country girl of Kethel, she was drawn early to Mary. Both parents were poor, and she prayed much before Schiedam's miraculous image of Our Lady. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 dates her death to 14 April 1433.

Skating with friends in the winter of 1395, she fell violently on ice through a companion's fault and broke a right rib. That fall began her martyrdom. No medical skill cured her, gangrene spread from the wound over her whole body, and for years she lay in ever-growing pain. Some suspected evil spirit influence, but her pastor Andries tested her with an unconsecrated host, which she distinguished at once. God rewarded her with prayer and visions, and miracles crowded her bedside.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-margaret-o:
Margaret of Cortona, Franciscan penitent, fled home at seventeen, lived nine years unmarried, and turned after her lover's murder. Born at Laviano in Tuscany in 1247, she lost her mother at seven. Two years later her father married again, with little sympathy between daughter and stepmother. Craving affection, she met a young cavalier at seventeen, some say a son of Guglielmo di Pecora, and fled with him one night. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 dates her death at Cortona to 22 February 1297.

For nine years she lived with him near Montepulciano and bore a son. She often begged him to marry her, always promised, never wed. In her confessions she says she yielded unwillingly. Later writers who painted her as abandoned, the entry argues, misread her legend. Her lover's murder on a journey, announced by his hound leading her to his body, ended her old life. Blaming herself, she returned his jewels.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-martina:
Martina, a Roman virgin martyred in the 220s, is remembered in this short Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Daughter of an ex-consul and orphaned young, she openly professed her Christian faith during the reign of Alexander Severus. Arrested and ordered to return to idol worship, she refused, endured torture, and was finally beheaded.

Her surviving passion narratives date from a much later period, and the entry warns that their colourful additions carry no historical weight. Her relics were found in 1634 in a crypt near the Mamertine prison, and Urban VIII had her church repaired and hymns composed for her office, kept on 30 January. It suits readers tracing how a thin early record grew into a lasting Roman cult.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-peter-of-v:
Peter of Verona, a Dominican inquisitor martyred in 1252, preached against the Manichaean heresy across Italy. Born at Verona in 1206 to Manichaean parents, he was sent to a Catholic school and then to Bologna, where he met Dominic and joined the Friars Preachers. Gregory IX made him general inquisitor for his severity of life, doctrine, and preaching.

He evangelised nearly the whole of Italy, preaching at Rome, Florence, Bologna, Genoa, and Como, drawing crowds and many conversions. He denounced Catholics who professed faith in words but denied it in deeds. Manichaeans tried persecution, calumny, and threats to silence him. Returning from Como to Milan, he was struck down with an axe by the assassin Carino on 6 April 1252.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-sabina:
Sabina, a Roman martyr of about 126, is honoured in one of Rome's most beautiful early basilicas. Widow of Valentinus and daughter of Herod Metallarius, she was converted, according to Acts of no historic value, by her slave Serapia. Serapia died first for her faith. Sabina followed her in martyrdom before the year ended.

Her relics reached the Aventine in 430, and a basilica there now bears her name, a landmark in the history of art. The church was first dedicated to both saints. Her feast is kept on 29 August. The entry is candid that its narrative rests on worthless Acts, and it points readers instead to the church, its mosaics, and its place in Roman topography.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sts-cyprian-a:
Cyprian and Justina of Antioch, martyred at Nicomedia in 304, are known through a legend the entry treats as allegory rather than history. Cyprian begins as a pagan magician dealing with demons, hired to ruin the Christian virgin Justina, yet her sign of the cross defeats three demonic attacks and frees him from Satan's grip.

Converted, Cyprian rises through deacon and priest to bishop, while Justina heads a convent, until Diocletian's persecution seizes both and beheads them on a riverbank. Gregory Nazianzen and Prudentius already knew the tale in the fourth century, though both confused this Cyprian with Cyprian of Carthage. Calderón later turned the story into his drama El mágico prodigioso.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sts-rufina:
Rufina is a name shared by several martyrs, and this entry takes them day by day. On 10 July come Rufina and Secunda, Romans said to have suffered in 287. They were buried at the ninth milestone of the Via Cornelia, where Damasus built a church and a town later became a suburbicarian see.

On 19 July come Justa and Rufina, martyrs of Seville, both certainly historical figures of the Spanish Church. On 31 August stand Theodotus, Rufina, and Ammia, said to be the parents of the famed martyr Mamas of Caesarea. On 24 or 25 August, Rufina and Eutyche of Capua are recorded, and nothing further is known of either.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sts-tiburtius:
Tiburtius and Susanna, Roman martyrs kept on 11 August, come to us through the legend of Sebastian. Tiburtius, only son of the prefect Chromatius, was baptized after his father's conversion, with Sebastian as godfather. Hidden during the Diocletian persecution, he was betrayed, tried by the prefect Fabianus, and walked barefoot over red-hot coals unharmed, guarded only by the sign of the cross.

Judges called the feat magic, and he was beheaded in 286 at the third milestone of the Via Lavicana, at the two laurel trees. Susanna, daughter of Gabinius, was beheaded about 295 in her father's house. Both houses became the church of St Susanna. The Acts are questioned, but the martyrdoms and the day rest on the oldest martyrologies.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sts-trasilla-:
Trasilla and Emiliana were aunts of Gregory the Great, virgins of the sixth century kept on 24 December and 5 January. Gregory himself tells their story. His father, the senator Gordian, had three sisters who vowed themselves to God. They lived in virginity, fasting, and prayer in their Rome home on the Clivus Scauri.

The third sister, Gordiana, drifted back to the world, but Trasilla and Emiliana held fast. Their ancestor Felix III appeared to Trasilla and called her to glory, and she died on Christmas Eve seeing Jesus beckon. Days later she appeared to Emiliana and invited her to keep Epiphany in heaven. Tradition places their relics, with their mother Silvia, in the Oratory of St Andrew.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-tarazona:
Tarazona is a Spanish diocese covering Saragossa, Soria, Navarre, and Logroño provinces. Its city of 8,650 people stands on a commanding height above a fair plain watered by the Queiles. Ancient Turiaso ranked among the Celtiberians' chief towns. Its diocese holds many ancient cities, from Bilbilis and Alhama to Borja, Cascante, Corella, and Munébrega. Its arms bear the motto Tubal-Cain built me and Hercules rebuilt me.

Christianity's origins here are obscure, though disciples of James may have visited early from nearby Saragossa. The first reliable bishop appears only in the fifth century. Idatius names Leo, living in 449 and killed in a rising. The lists name St Prudentius, dated 390 in the local breviary but perhaps as late as the ninth century. Gaudiosus, bishop in 530, fought Arianism and died at Escoron.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-tarragona:
Tarragona is an archdiocese of Spain, bounded by Barcelona, Lérida, Tortosa, and the Mediterranean. It covers the civil provinces of Tarragona and Lérida. Its capital city holds 24,335 people. Its suffragans are Barcelona, Lérida, Gerona, Urgel, Vich, Tortosa, and Solsona. The city is among Spain's most ancient, probably Iberian, as coins and Cyclopean walls show. Romans made it the centre of their government in Spain.

It was capital first of Hither Spain, then of Tarraconensis. Vandals, Suevi, and Alani overran it in the fifth century. Euric took it in 475 and demolished it. Visigoths revived it, but Arabs destroyed it again in 719. Its church claims the coming of James and Paul. Paul's visit is possible if he reached Spain from Rome, as Jerome affirms. Written bishops begin in the third century with the martyr Fructuosus and his deacons Augurius and Eulogius.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-taxa-innocent:
The Taxa Innocentiana is a decree of Innocent XI, dated 1 October 1678. It sets the fees bishops' offices may demand or accept for acts and papers. Bishops and officials may accept nothing, even freely offered, for ordinations, letters of leave, gifts of benefices, or marriage dispensations. For dispensations, however, alms for pious uses may be demanded. The chancellor may exact a moderate charge, fixed by Innocent, for rushing papers through.

That charge excludes permissions to say Mass, administer sacraments, or preach. The decree says nothing on disputed cases, such as copies of trial papers. Some held it applied to Italy only, but it showed the Church's mind and applied in substance everywhere. In 1896 the Council's Sacred Congregation changed it. It allowed fair fees for benefices and sacraments, while the sacraments themselves must stay free and the poor must not be taxed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thacia-montan:
Thacia Montana was a titular see in Africa Proconsularis. An inscription among ruins called Henshir Bedji, near Bordj Messaoudi, marks Thacia, which gave Wadi Tasaa its name. It lay on the highway between Carthage and Theveste, midway between Musti and Drusiliana. Ptolemy, the Peutinger Table, and the Ravenna geographer mention it. Byzantines fortified it, and there in late 545 the general John was defeated and slain.

At Eufida, six and a quarter miles west of Botria, another inscription proves a second municipium called Thaca, Byzantine-fortified. Toulotte assigns to the first place Cresconius at Cabarsussi in 393 and Victor in 646, and to the second Rufinus at Carthage in 525 and Probus in 646. The last two bore the title bishops of Tacia Montana. Whether they belonged to Thaca, or a nearby place bore the epithet, remains open. Rome's list names only Thacia Monana, identified with Bordj Messaoudi.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-church-in:
Christianity in China, from ancient rumour to modern missions, is the vast story told here. Arnobius in the third century already named the Seres among peoples reached by the new power from the Lord and his Apostles. Some ascribe China's first evangelisation to Thomas, apostle of India, or to Bartholomew. Proof fails for those early claims, though Persian Christians suffered under Sapor from 345.

Nestorius's condemnation at Ephesus in 431 scattered his disciples across Asia, and the Si-ngan-fu inscription puts them in China by the seventh century. Some say Archæus of Seleucia founded a Chinese metropolitan see in 411, others date metropolitans from Saliba Zacha. Franciscans, Jesuits, persecutions, and modern vicariates carry a long tale of faith planted, uprooted, and replanted.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-universit:
Europe's oldest university city, Bologna, shakes off a legend in this entry. Thirteenth-century tradition credited Theodosius II in 433 with its foundation, a tale now generally rejected. Frederick Barbarossa's Habita of 1158 at best implied a school's existence, and Clement III's bull of 1189, speaking of masters and scholars, mentions no university organisation.

Schools of the Liberal Arts, flourishing early in the eleventh century, truly birthed the university. Dictamen, the art of composition for briefs and legal documents, joined grammar and rhetoric to law. Lombard cities' political, commercial, and intellectual growth demanded legal teaching, and as Ravenna faded through papal conflict, Bologna succeeded it as law's home.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-tortona:
Tortona is a diocese in Piedmont, Italy, set on the northern Apennine spurs above the Scrivia, in a plain rich in grain, wine, hemp, rice and silk. Its sixteenth-century cathedral rose after Charles V destroyed the old hilltop cathedral to build a fort. Inside it stands an ancient sarcophagus carved with Phaeton and Castor and Pollux, and other churches include Santa Maria Canale and San Giacomo.

Founded as a Roman colony in 147 BC on the Via Posthumia between Piacenza and Genoa, Dertona became an important military station. Ruled by its bishop from the ninth century, it became a commune in 1090 and a faithful Guelph ally, destroyed by Barbarossa in 1155 and by the Pavians in 1163. From 1347 it shared Milan's fate until Sardinia took it in 1735.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-tyana:
Tyana was an ancient city of Cappadocia in Asia Minor, near the Taurus mountains and the Cilician Gates. Its plain took the name Tyanitis, and its first name is said to come from Thoas, its supposed Thracian founder. In the first century it gave birth to Apollonius, the famed wonder-worker. Under the emperor Caracalla it gained the rank of a Roman colony. Later it sided with Queen Zenobia of Palmyra and fell to Aurelian in 272, who spared it from pillage.

The entry follows the city into Christian times, when it became the metropolis of a second Cappadocia under Valens in 371. That promotion sparked a sharp quarrel between Anthimus, its bishop, and St Basil of Caesarea. Each claimed ground the other held. Later bishops of the see close the account, tracing a town that moved from pagan fame to a prize in an episcopal dispute.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-university-of:
The University of Barcelona grew from ecclesiastical schools founded in the eleventh century. To these were added, step by step, chairs held by Dominicans in their convent and chairs set up in the Academia by the kings of Aragon. In 1430 the town council moved to found a Studium Generale, hoping to stop young men migrating to Lérida and to foreign universities at Paris, Toulouse, and Bologna.

The university as such dates from 1450, when Alfonso V of Aragon granted its charter, confirmed by the bull Constitutus in Speculo of Pope Nicholas V. The pope gave the new university all the privileges of Toulouse and authorized chairs in theology, canon and civil law, arts, and medicine. The entry follows its later fortunes, its colleges, and its scholars, giving a compact history of Catalonia's chief seat of learning.

Siena's advanced school, teaching grammar and medicine, is noticed as early as 1241. In 1246 Emperor Frederick II forced Sienese students at Bologna to leave that hostile city. That must have enlarged Siena's school, then boasting famed professors of law such as Pepo, of grammar such as Tebaldus, and of medicine such as Petrus Yspanus. In 1252 Innocent IV granted the university of masters and doctors at Siena, with their scholars and beadles, exemption from certain city taxes.

He named the bishop as their conservator. In 1275 and 1285 the commune of Siena, acting on its own authority without regard to pope or emperor, took further steps for the school. The entry follows its privileges, its student body, and its growth into a full university, showing how a Tuscan commune built higher learning beside the great school of Bologna.

Vienna's university, next to Prague the oldest in the former Holy Roman Empire, was founded on 12 March 1365 by Rudolph IV, Duke of Austria. Urban V confirmed its charter on 18 July of that year, though the papal authorization left out a faculty of theology. The school was planned too grandly and endowed too thinly to prosper, and the duke died at Milan on 27 July. Around 1380 his successor Albert III called teachers from Paris and won permission from Urban VI in 1384 for a theological faculty.

After statutes for the university in 1385 and for its faculties of theology, law, medicine, and philosophy in 1389, the school took shape on the Paris model. The entry follows its growth, its nations, and its scholars through the Hussite troubles, the Turkish sieges, and the reforms of later centuries. It gives a full history of the Habsburg capital's great school.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-uruguayana:
Uruguayana is a Brazilian diocese, suffragan of Porto Alegre, formed when the See of São Pedro do Rio Grande rose to archiepiscopal rank on 15 August 1910. Three new dioceses were cut from its territory, and fifteen parishes fell to Uruguayana, covering the western part of Rio Grande do Sul. It is bounded in the south by the Uruguayan provinces of Artigas and Rivera and in the west by the River Uruguay.

The fertile territory lives by stock breeding and the dried beef trade. The town of Uruguayana, with 14,000 inhabitants, stands on the River Uruguay 360 miles west of Porto Alegre, linked to it by rail. It faces the Argentine town of Restauración across the water. It trades widely by river and rail with Montevideo and Buenos Aires. The entry sketches a young frontier diocese of ranching country.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-uthina:
Uthina was a titular see of Africa Proconsularis, suffragan of Carthage, named by Ptolemy, Pliny, and the Peutinger Tables. Pliny and an inscription call it a colony. Its site seems to be the ruins called Henshir Oudna, near a railway station between Tunis and Kef in Tunisia. The ruins stretch nearly three miles around a hilly plateau above the left bank of the Milian wadis.

Within them stand a fortress, cisterns, an aqueduct, a triumphal arch, a theatre, an amphitheatre, a basilica with a round crypt, and a bridge, with many fine mosaics. Uthina already had a bishop in Tertullian's day, whom Tertullian sharply criticized. Five more bishops are known, beginning with Felix at Carthage in 256. The entry gives a brief record of a Roman town's church.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-valona:
Valona was a titular see, suffragan of Dyrrachium in Epirus Nova, whose ancient name was Aulon. Ptolemy first mentions it, and later geographies such as Peutinger's Table and the Synecdemus of Hierocles name it too. Known bishops include Nazarius in 458 and Soter in 553. At that time the diocese belonged to the Patriarchate of Rome.

In 733 it passed, with all eastern Illyricum, to the Patriarchate of Constantinople, yet it appears in none of that church's lists of sees. The bishopric had probably been suppressed, for even under Bulgarian rule Aulon is absent from the lists of the Patriarchate of Achrida. Under Latin domination a Latin bishopric arose, and the entry traces its later bishops and fate.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-verona:
Verona is a diocese in Venetia, northern Italy. Its city straddling both branches of the Adige and serving as a centre of farm industry and a fortress under Venice, Austria, and the Kingdom of Italy. Its twelfth-century Romanesque cathedral holds an ambo by Sanmicheli, pictures by Liberale da Verona and Titian, and a capitular library rich in manuscripts.

Nearby stand the Scaliger tombs, Gothic shrines enclosing the sarcophagi of Verona's lords. History dominates the second half: the Scaliger family, Can Grande and his successors, their beautifying of the city with palaces, aqueducts. Bridges, and their custom of fratricide, as Can Grande II was killed by his brother Cansignorio, who in turn killed another brother. The entry moves from churches and monuments to the violent politics that shaped the city.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-vienna:
Vienna is the capital of Austria-Hungary, the emperor's residence, and the seat of a Latin archbishopric, lying at the Alps' northeastern end mainly on the Danube's right bank. Celts settled the site five centuries before Christ, Romans under Tiberius built a permanent camp for the thirteenth legion, and Pliny called the place Vianiomina.

Inscriptions use Vindobona, later a naval port and station of the tenth legion, where Marcus Aurelius died campaigning against the Marcomanni. Christianity had reached Vienna by the martyrdom of St Florian about 303, and the entry follows the city through Eastern Roman, German, and Habsburg hands to its modern archdiocese. Its churches take pride of place, above all St Stephen's Cathedral, dedicated as a small Romanesque church in 1147. Rebuilt in Gothic style after the fire of 1293, with a south tower 449 feet high, the most important Gothic building in Austrian lands.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-vilna:
Vilna, capital of Lithuania at the junction of the Vileika and Vilja rivers, numbered 165,000 people in 1910. Its historical origins lie in 1323, when Grand Prince Gediminas made it his capital, wrote to John XXII, and treated with the Brethren of the Sword. German crusaders partly devastated it in 1383, but Jagiello's baptism and marriage to Hedwig of Poland that year, uniting Poland and Lithuania, began its religious and political prosperity.

In 1577 it gained a flourishing academy, famed especially under the Jesuits, and suffered war, fire, and pestilence in the late seventeenth and early eighteenth centuries. United with Russia in 1794, it ceased to be the grand duchy's capital, and the insurrections of 1831 and 1863 brought cruel reprisals, before industrial growth from 1870. Its diocese, founded through Jagiello, holds splendid churches, above all a cathedral dedicated to the Trinity, St Stanislaus, and St Wladislaus.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-visit-ad-limi:
Visit ad limina, to the thresholds of the Apostles, is the obligation on certain members of the hierarchy to visit Rome at stated times. Honour the tombs of Sts Peter and Paul, present themselves before the pope, and report on their dioceses.

No trace of a fixed obligation appears in the earliest age, though bishops from remote times referred causes to Rome and visited personally when need arose. First vestiges lie in twice-yearly provincial councils of Italian bishops of the Roman province. In customs such as Leo I's insistence that Sicily send three bishops yearly to Rome, later relaxed by Gregory I from three years to five. Later sections trace how the obligation was systematized for bishops worldwide.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-vittoria-colo:
Vittoria Colonna was an Italian poet born at Marino in 1490 and dying at Rome in 1547. Daughter of Fabrizio Colonna, lord of Roman fiefs and grand constable of Naples. Agnese da Montefeltro, daughter of Urbino's first duke, she married in 1509 Ferrante Francesco d'Avalos, Marquis of Pescara, a chief general of Emperor Charles V.

Pescara's career peaked at Pavia in February 1525, after which he joined Morone's conspiracy to free Italy and was tempted by Naples's crown. Vittoria dissuaded him, declaring, as her cousin Cardinal Pompeo Colonna records, that she would rather die wife of a most brave marquis and upright general than live consort of a dishonoured king. Widowed that November, she devoted herself to religion and literature, living in conventual simplicity at Rome, Viterbo. Elsewhere, centre of the age's noblest intellectual and spiritual life, and bound to Michelangelo by a remarkable spiritual friendship.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-winona:
Winona is the Minnesota diocese set up in 1889 as suffragan of Saint Paul, spanning twenty counties of southern Minnesota across 12,282 square miles. Early voyagers and missionaries crossed its ground long before it existed. Groseilliers and Radisson visited Prairie Sioux in 1660, Hennepin explored the Upper Mississippi in 1680, and Perrot with Jesuit Marest set up a Wabasha trading post in 1683. A century and a half passed before Bishop Loras reached Mendota in 1839.

Father Galtier, sent to Mendota in 1840, became Minnesota's first parish priest and said Mass at Wabasha in Rocque's home. Ravoux found Winona a prairie without inhabitants in April 1843. Cretin, Saint Paul's first bishop in 1851, organized Winona's parish in 1856 under Thomas Murray. Michael Prendergast became first resident pastor in July 1858, serving Catholics across six counties besides Winona itself.
catriona:
Robert Louis Stevenson continued David Balfour's story in Catriona, the sequel to Kidnapped, named for the Highland girl David meets and loves. Part one, The Lord Advocate, puts David in Edinburgh trying to clear James Stewart and himself after the Appin murder. Prestongrange, the Advocate, receives him with smooth, dangerous politeness.

Alan Breck returns, the heather catches fire, and David is kidnapped to the Bass Rock to keep him from the trial. Catriona Drummond, daughter of the outlawed James More, crosses his path in Edinburgh and Holland. Stevenson mixes legal intrigue with a shy love story, and David's honor is tested as hard by manners as by swords.
china:
Demetrius Charles Boulger's China is a short history of the Chinese empire, carried from the early ages through its great dynasties to recent events. A supplementary chapter by Mayo W. Hazeltine brings the story up to date, and Boulger dedicates the work to Sir Halliday Macartney, praising his defence of China's right to dignified treatment by European governments.

Contents move from the first national dynasty and a long period of disunion through the Sungs and Kins, the Mongol conquest under Kublai, the Ming dynasty, its decline, and the Manchu conquest. Later chapters treat the Manchu rulers and China's dealings with foreign powers. The book suits readers who want a compact, older-style narrative history of China before turning to modern scholarship.
clementina:
Clementina, by A. E. W. Mason, dedicated to Andrew Lang, is a Jacobite romance in twenty-five chapters and an epilogue. Its hero is Charles Wogan. In September 1719 his horse goes lame on the road from Florence to Bologna, and fortune, he is sure, will still serve him.

The contents chart a rescue. Wogan makes a proposal, finds hiding places better than a window curtain, and is mistaken for a more notable man. The Prince of Baden visits Clementina, and a night of the 27th in Innsbruck brings the escape. Flight to Italy follows, with an attack at Peri and complications at Bologna. Maria Vittoria reappears before the last chapter closes the design.
doe-osti-2572518-incorporating-the-lates:
Report LA-UR-25-26492, issued July 9, 2025, is a fiscal year 2026 project proposal from a Los Alamos team led by Megan Booher. The subject is INCC6, the International Neutron Coincidence Counting software the IAEA uses for nondestructive assay of nuclear material. Advanced analysis tricks now sit scattered in one-off tools built for single instruments. The proposal asks $275,000 to fold them into the shared platform.

Three features headline the plan: position-corrected efficiency, a local coincidence veto, and distributed source term analysis. The same team added self-diagnostic features to INCC6 with fiscal 2025 support. An updated release would go to safeguards users such as the IAEA, Japan's JAEA, and JNFL. The promised payoff is lower measurement uncertainty, which saves inspector time in the field. Team members Joe Longo, Robert Weinmann-Smith, Marc Ruch, and Virginia Lucas fill out the roster.
doe-osti-2575017-eureica-efficient-ultra:
Final scientific and technical report DE-OE0000920, from MIT under Anuradha Annaswamy and submitted June 30, 2025, reports the EUREICA project. Partners included Princeton, West Virginia University, two national laboratories, and industry teams. The grid is now a cyber-physical system studded with distributed resources, renewables, storage, and flexible loads. Those assets help efficiency, but they also open doors to cyberattack.

EUREICA's answer is coordination with proof of trust. A local electricity market tracks which nearby devices can inject power or cut demand, and rates how trustworthy each one is. With that situational awareness, experiments showed attacks could be blunted using local resources alone, without stressing the bulk grid. A large workstream hardened the learning layer itself: the Princeton team mapped durable backdoor attacks on federated learning, named Neurotoxin, and built a defense called SparseFed.
doe-osti-2585489-quantifying-the-economi:
Laura Price, Cathy Ottinger Farnum, and Elena Kalinina of Sandia National Laboratories wrote report SAND2025-10269, printed in August 2025, on the cost of handling irradiated high-assay low-enriched uranium fuel. Advanced reactors plan to use this HALEU fuel, and once it is irradiated it must be stored, shipped, and disposed of like other spent fuel. The study puts dollar figures on each of those steps.

The authors compare several fuel types against a light water reactor baseline: accident tolerant fuel, TRISO fuel, and metallic fuel from sodium fast reactors. Separate chapters build up storage costs, transport fleet and operating costs, and disposal costs. Disposal cases include a repository much like Yucca Mountain and a bedded salt concept with about 100 panels spread over 30 square kilometers. Results are given in both 2012 and 2024 dollars.
doe-osti-3006777-shallow-cumulus-entrain:
Final grant report for DE-SC0020083, dated December 8, 2025, comes from Daniel Kirshbaum at McGill University with co-investigator Tim Merlis of Princeton. The grant ran August 2019 to August 2025 under DOE's Atmospheric System Research program. It studied cumulus entrainment, the process by which a shallow cumulus cloud ingests surrounding air through its sides, diluting the cloud. Four objectives structured the work.

The team set out to build records of bulk entrainment rate at two ARM observatories. Large-eddy simulations then interpreted the patterns physically. Two further objectives quantified how subcloud circulations change entrainment, and what flow-dependent entrainment variations do to climate. The report synthesizes six years of work that joins ARM field data with large-eddy simulations. A long reference list closes the report.
doe-osti-3007679-rebound-reverse-enginee:
Pacific Northwest National Laboratory report REBOUND, led by co-principal investigators Stephen Young and Mavis Boamah-Agyemang with a nine-member team, tackles rare earth element recovery. The method pushes two liquids side by side through a Y-shaped channel, so elements diffuse across the boundary and precipitate out under non-equilibrium conditions.

Experiments used a dysprosium-bearing feedstock solution flowing at 4 millilitres per hour against 25 millimolar sodium oxalate as the precipitating agent. Computer fluid dynamics models explored how inlet size, flow rate, field strength, and outlet layout change the yield from different feedstocks. The aim is a cleaner separation route for elements that magnets and electronics depend on.
doe-osti-3009109-exploring-anomalous-ele:
How electrons vanish from nanosecond pulsed discharges is traced by Purdue's Alexey Shashurin, working with Princeton partners, in a final report for DOE award DE-SC0023209, dated December 18, 2025. Such sparks, about ten nanoseconds long, serve plasma-assisted combustion, flow control, and biomedicine.

Laser interferometry measured peak electron density of ten to the seventeenth to ten to the eighteenth per cubic centimetre, arriving 15 to 20 ns after the pulse. Shorter electrode gaps gave higher peaks, matching their higher energy density. Vibration readings started near 4,000 to 6,000 kelvin about 50 ns in and decayed over roughly 500 ns as the plasma cooled and recombined.
doe-osti-3009720-gulf-coast-basin-core-c:
Final report for the Gulf Coast CORE-CM Initiative, cooperative agreement DE-FE0032053, led by Bridget Scanlon of the University of Texas Bureau of Economic Geology with partners including the U.S. Geological Survey and the Universities of Kentucky, Wyoming, North Dakota, and Alabama. The initiative ran from October 2021 to April 2025, hunting critical minerals in the region's carbon ores and coal measures.

Beach placer sands along old shorelines concentrate heavy minerals rich in titanium, rare earths, thorium, and uranium. In south Texas localities, magnetite and ilmenite make up 50 to 87 percent of the heavy fraction, with zircon carrying much of the rare earth content. The basin-wide assessment maps where such feedstocks could supply domestic critical mineral production.
doe-osti-3015896-colorado-residential-re:
John Kisacikoglu and Brent Rice were the National Laboratory of the Rockies technical contacts for this January 2026 cooperative research final report, NLR/TP-5400-95337, and Beth Chacon is also named on the record. Working with Xcel Energy in Colorado, the project studied home electric vehicle charging, home backup power, and ways to manage charging so it costs households less.

Tasks included checking how home charging loads affect the small transformers that serve streets, and hunting for risk factors across varied grid locations and layouts. The team aimed to deliver design tools and typical vehicle load curves, plus updated construction standards for transformers, secondary lines, and services. Later tasks compare five control approaches for managed charging across future scenarios. The filing gives utilities a playbook for fair, affordable residential charging.
doe-osti-3018001-lignin-first-catalytic-:
Gregg Beckham of the National Laboratory of the Rockies was technical contact, with James R Bielenberg also named on the record, for this February 2026 cooperative research final report, NLR/TP-2A00-99086. It is Project 3 under agreement CRD-18-00765. The approach is called lignin first: instead of burning or wasting the lignin in plant material, pull it out first as a valuable product.

The context is an ExxonMobil program with Clariant and Genomatica. In today's pioneer cellulosic fuel plants, all the biomass is processed together through hydrolysis, which creates operating trouble because biomass varies widely in composition and handling. The proposed route starts with fractionation, using solvolysis and reductive catalysis. It yields a lignin oil of well-defined monomers, dimers, and oligomers, plus a delignified cellulose and hemicellulose pulp for fuels. Splitting the stream first gives each half a cleaner path to value.
doe-osti-3019241-tcf-base-commercializat:
Suma Sathyanarayana, Alec Schulberg, and Becca Sweet of the National Laboratory of the Rockies closed the MATCH Prize in NLR/TP-6A50-98443, February 2026. MATCH stands for Making Advanced Technology Commercialization Harmonized. The prize ran under the Technology Commercialization Fund's base program. Its aim was to harmonize how laboratories help their technologies reach market. The competition moved in phases. Early phases judged teams on resources, partnerships, and funding plans. Phase 3 turned to action, including a 90-second video.

Winning teams from Phase 2 worked closely with mentors and made significant commercialization progress. The final report records the prize design and what the teams produced. For the Office of Technology Commercialization, harmonization means a researcher at any laboratory meets the same support playbook. Prize competitions surface that playbook faster than committees do. This report is the program's own record of the experiment.
doe-osti-3020102-feasibility-and-compati:
Argonne National Laboratory report ANL-25/33, by Nazib Siddique, Farhad Masum, Tai-Yuan Huang, and co-authors, weighs seven alternative fuels for United States freight railroads. Rail moves about 40 percent of long-distance freight ton-miles each year, and demand is expected to grow. The study checks each fuel for engine compatibility, cost, lifecycle emissions, and supply chain readiness.

Renewable diesel made from sewage sludge by hydrothermal liquefaction came out cost competitive, at $3.48 per diesel-gallon equivalent before incentives, with deep lifecycle emission cuts. Ordinary diesel averaged about $2.76 per gallon in 2024. The cost of avoiding emissions ranged from $48 per metric ton of carbon dioxide for sludge-based renewable diesel to $87 for pure biodiesel. The report gives railroads and fuel producers a side-by-side basis for choosing low-carbon fuels.
doe-osti-3023854-identification-of-hydro:
Marina Miletic and Brian D Ehrhart of Sandia National Laboratories catalogue the hazards inside a hydrogen rail maintenance facility, in report SAND2026-17116, printed March 2026. Hydrogen trains are new, and their upkeep brings fuel-system work indoors, where leaks behave differently than outdoors. The core of the study is a hazard and operability analysis of maintenance tasks and equipment.

Some of the sharpest scenarios involve quiet degradation. Water, corrosive cleaning agents, or de-icing salts can seize thermal pressure relief devices over time, raising the chance of a high-pressure release during defueling, and instrument errors can compromise that process too. Lower-rated risks are chronic integrity failures: slow leaks from gaskets, seals, and valves, which carry less flow and are more easily handled by the building's active ventilation.
doe-osti-3363708-preparing-large-area-of:
Jie Li and Owen Wostoupal of Argonne National Laboratory, with Baoquan Huang of Ge Solartech, report on thermochromic films for smart windows (ANL/AMD-C2022-22148). The films use vanadium dioxide nanoparticles, which change how much solar heat they pass as temperature shifts, trimming both electricity and heating gas bills.

Making large area films required keeping the particles dispersed. Coating them with a PFDA surface treatment beat dopamine and SDS coatings, and solar modulation could be tuned through particle loading, from 5 to 15 weight percent, and film thickness. Modulation peaked at a thickness of 14 micrometers, beyond which particles began to aggregate. The underlying flow synthesis work appeared in an ACS journal in 2026.
doe-osti-3412025-agc-4-irradiated-materi:
Idaho report INL/RPT-26-93675, dated August 2026, analyzes irradiated graphite from the AGC-4 test train. David T. Rohrbaugh and Austin Matthews wrote the analysis. AGC-4 is the fourth of six planned irradiation trains for nuclear graphite grades.

The capsule ran in the Advanced Test Reactor at Idaho. Specimen temperatures ranged from 773 to 931 degrees Celsius, with an average of 845. Density change showed no real split between hotter and cooler groups. Stressed and unstressed samples from five graphite grades were tracked by dose. Reactor designers need such data to predict graphite life in new cores.
doe-osti-3484940-national-carbon-capture:
Southern Company Services closes agreement DE-FE0022596 with a final report on the National Carbon Capture Center, covering June 6, 2014 to March 30, 2026. The center in Wilsonville, Alabama tests carbon capture gear from developers worldwide. It bridges lab ideas and large demonstrations.

Since its creation in 2009, the center has hosted many technology teams. One long campaign tested MTR polymer membranes on coal flue gas, ending in August 2015. New sensor evaluations run beside current capture campaigns. Developers get real flue gas trials that lab benches cannot offer, speeding the path to market. Test campaigns at the center run capture systems at scales beyond bench rigs.
doe-osti-3683877-particle-physics-on-the: A short final report for award DE-SC0025946 covers Particle Physics on the Plains 2025, a theory conference at the University of Kansas. Ian Michael Lewis was lead principal investigator. The meeting ran on November 15 and 16, 2025, the eighth in a series begun in 2017. It exists to give Plains-region students and postdocs a nearby, low-cost conference. Seventy-five people registered, and thirty-five talks filled seven sessions. Thirty-three talks came from students or postdocs, and a parallel session ran for the first time.
dutt-mahabharata-shanti-anushasana:
Dutt joined the Shanti and Anushasana Parvas in one English volume in 1908. The Mahabharata's two great books of teaching stand together here. Bhishma on his arrow-bed speaks the epic's whole moral system.

Kings learn how to rule, judge, tax, and wage just war. Plain folk learn duty, charity, and the path to release from rebirth. Question and answer carry the vast counsel at a calm pace. Few single volumes hold so much of ancient India's wisdom teaching. The pairing lets readers take Bhishma's full course without a break in study. Together the books form a true manual of the righteous life.
dutt-markandeya-purana:
Dutt's 1896 English Markandeya Puranam honors the deathless sage Markandeya. The sage, blessed with long life, recounts worlds made and unmade. Inside stands the Devi Mahatmya, the great hymn to the Goddess.

That hymn tells how the Goddess fights demons no god can beat. Her fierce and tender forms anchor India's worship of the Mother. Kings, birds, and sages frame tales of fate, duty, and release. Dutt opens the core text of Goddess worship to English readers. Its blend of battle myth and deep devotion still moves readers today in India. The Goddess as savior of the gods stands at its blazing center.
dutt-vishnu-purana:
Dutt put the Vishnu Puranam into English in 1896, a first full version. The great Vaishnava scripture honors Vishnu as the highest god. Its tales shaped how millions have pictured the divine for ages.

The making of the world opens the book in grand cosmic strokes. Vishnu's descents as Rama and Krishna fill its beloved middle tales. Kings' lines, floods, and the duties of the faithful fill the rest. Clear, faithful prose carries the old Sanskrit into plain English here. The most trusted purana on Vishnu's worship stands open to new readers now. Its cosmic frame gives the beloved tales their full weight.
elizabethan-sonnet-cycles-delia-diana:
Martha Foote Crow edits two Elizabethan sonnet cycles in an 1896 volume from Kegan Paul, Trench, Trübner of London. Samuel Daniel's Delia comes first, with a critical life of the poet. Henry Constable's Diana follows. Crow notes that Daniel's series has often been taken as the prototype of Shakespeare's sonnets.

The same stock of conceits runs through both books. Verse makes beauty immortal, time steals it, and the lover woos a cold mistress by night thoughts. Crow traces the common storehouse back through Sidney, Lodge, and Watson to Petrarch and the Italian makers. Daniel, she shows, left Oxford without a degree, his genius prone to smoother studies than logic, and turned his Italian to early profit. Students of the sonnet vogue get two full cycles with a scholar's map of who borrowed what.
erotica-romana:
Johann Wolfgang von Goethe sings his Roman love affair in the Erotica Romana, elegies in English verse presented here without a named translator. The first elegy plants his garden and sets good Priapus at his side, warning hypocrites away from nature's pure fruit. The second asks Rome's stones and palaces to speak, and calls the city a whole world that without love would cease to be Rome.

The numbered elegies follow the affair through windows, churches, and ruins. Fame and Cupid quarrel in the twenty-second, an old story the poet retails. Quirites are begged, near the close, to let him keep the first and last of earthly pleasures. Goethe wrote the cycle out of his Italian journey, in classical couplets after the Roman love poets.
farina:
George Meredith's Farina is an early tale in prose and verse set in medieval Cologne. Rich Gottlieb Groschen, the Kaiser's money-lender, rules the city's trade from his fig-tree's shade. His daughter Margarita is the White Rose of Germany. Young men of the White Rose Club break heads daily in her honour.

Farina, the hero, loves Margarita and must win her against wealth and rivalry. The tale moves through Rhine towns, vine-hills, and old German legend. A magic draught and the bandit world of the Rhine deepen the romance. Meredith wrote it young, and its style is lush, arch, and playful. Readers meet a Germany of emperors, burghers, and minstrels, more fairy tale than history. The book shows the novelist learning his trade on romantic ground.
farmers-of-forty-centuries-or-permanent-:
F. H. King's Farmers of Forty Centuries, published in 1911 with a preface by L. H. Bailey, reports permanent agriculture in China, Korea, and Japan. King, a soil physicist, travelled to see how the East had farmed the same fields for four thousand years. Bailey's preface states the lesson: farming stands or falls on keeping the soil fertile. The oriental peoples solved it.

Chapters survey canal digging, surface fitting of fields, and the fuel problem. The utilization of waste in Shantung shows every scrap returned to the soil. Rice culture, silk culture, and the tea industry receive full treatment. King measured densities Western farmers found incredible: crowds of people fed from tiny, manured plots. His book founded a Western tradition of organic and sustainable farming. It still reads as fieldwork, not theory, from a scientist who went to learn.
frus-1901China:
This appendix prints William Rockhill's report on his China mission. Roosevelt transmitted it to Congress in December 1901. Rockhill served as commissioner during the post-Boxer settlement. The papers print the powers' negotiations with China. An Anglo-German agreement of October 1900 anchors the file. It states their mutual policy toward China. Telegraphic correspondence fills the second half.

The mid-volume letters turn to court ceremony. Envoys debate where the Emperor should receive them. A palace hall, Chien-ching Kung, is proposed for audiences. Colleagues weigh the change through formal notes. Such ritual questions carried real weight in Peking. Access to the throne measured foreign standing. The volume joins high diplomacy to protocol. It is the settlement's working record.
frus-1942China:
The 1942 China volume is a wartime alliance file. General relations and military aid open it. China's armies need supply through a closed coast. Politics at home take the next file. Chungking and the Communists circle each other warily. Foreign courts are surrendered in long talks. A five-hundred-million-dollar credit is then bargained. The finance pact signs in March at Washington. Spending the credit raises fights over rates and inflation. Lend-Lease signs its pact in June. Aid under it fills a shorter run.

Supply routes are sought over Iran and Tibet. Strategic goods flow back the other way. A mid-volume talk guards the court treaty's signing. A late change of preamble might delay it, Washington warns. Texts are swapped and confirmed that day. The volume is partnership being priced.
frus-1943China:
Devoted wholly to China, this 1943 volume of Foreign Relations of the United States prints the wartime record of ties between Washington and Chungking. It follows China's weak military position and American efforts to give aid. It also tracks politics inside China and the strained ties between the Kuomintang and the Communists.

The papers cover Lend-Lease aid, loans, and the fight against inflation. They trace supply routes through Tibet, Iran, and India, plus the new treaty that ended extraterritorial rights. Cables, memoranda, and notes show both governments at work. Readers get a close view of an ally under severe strain.
gjellerup-minna:
Gjellerup wrote Minna in Danish, a novel of love tested by high ideals in modern Denmark. Young hearts meet, and fine principles soon strain their bond. The author, later famed for tales of the spirit's quest in the East, here stays close to home.

Daily life, pride, and tender feeling pull the lovers in opposed ways. Gjellerup blends thought and feeling, asking what love owes to truth. The prose is quiet rather than showy, and the pain feels earned. Readers who know only his Indian novel will find a gentler, nearer Gjellerup here, writing of his own land and people.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-PsychicPhenomen:
Time magazine made psychic phenomena its cover story on March 4, 1974. The title is 'Boom Times on the Psychic Frontier.' The story covers psychic healers and spoon-bending. It also covers the new scientific interest in the paranormal, as laboratories began testing claimants.

The early 1970s gave the paranormal a mass market: bestsellers, television spots, and campus lectures. Time's cover treated the boom as news, part fad and part research story. Spoon-bending parties and university labs sit side by side in its account. The cover story preserves the moment's balance of mockery and curiosity, and the sales figures of wonder in a skeptical age.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_china_Re:
American spy flights and naval patrols near China have caused crises more than once. William Burr edited this briefing book, posted in October 2020, on those encounters and what they did to United States-China relations.

Over the years, aerial and naval incidents have threatened to destabilize ties between the two powers. Each side claims rights in international airspace and waters that the other contests. The declassified records let readers see how close calls were handled at the time, and why a single collision or interception can carry such large diplomatic weight.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_colombia:
Thirteen Chiquita officials were accused of crimes against humanity in a Colombian case over company payments to armed groups. Michael Evans edited this briefing book, number 654, published in December 2018. It profiles those thirteen men one by one.

Documents obtained under freedom of information law reveal what each executive did in the payment scheme. The profiles connect names and job titles to specific decisions, instead of blaming a faceless company. For readers following the case at The Hague and in Colombia, the set gives the cast of accused officials in a single, checkable place.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_cuba_US-: US-Cuba: Secrets of the 'Havana Syndrome' - the National Security Archive briefing-book page capture. The archivists capture, complete. A single capture. Dated material. From the archive's collection, for researchers of the records and readers.
helena:
Mrs Humphry Ward published this novel in 1919, just after the Great War. Lord Buntingford, a tired peer, faces new social fights at home. Young Helena, bright and bold, enters his circle and stirs it. Talk of class, work, and duty runs through the country-house scenes.

Dances, debates, and quiet talks carry the plot along. Helena draws both praise and blame for her free style. Ward uses the pair to test old rank against new ideas. The result is a social novel about a changing England, seen through one house and its guests.
juana:
Juana, also called The Maranas, is a story by Honoré de Balzac, translated by Katharine Prescott Wormeley. Balzac dedicates it to Madame la Comtesse Merlin. The opening chapter is named Exposition. It begins with the taking of Tarragona by Marshal Suchet's army in Spain.

Discipline failed for a short spell after the victory, and the sack looked much like pillage. Suchet restored order, appointed a commandant, and set French administration running. Yet Spaniards kept their own ways in private, giving the city a mongrel aspect. One Italian regiment, full of troublesome sons of good families, stands out in Balzac's account. From this occupation world, his tale of Juana and the Marana family grows.
life-s-progress-through-the-passions-or-:
Eliza Haywood's novel follows Natura through life's passions. T. Gardner printed it in London, opposite St. Clement's Church. An advertisement dated April 2, 1748, announces the edition. The author is identified only as the writer of The Fortunate Foundlings.

That earlier book's demand had quickly exhausted its print run. A new edition of it was already in the press. Natura's adventures promise love, error, and experience in sequence. The novel shows Haywood's gift for amatory fiction at work. Gardner's printing office stood at Cowley's Head in the Strand. Original spellings survive in the modern proofreaders' edition.
manuel-pereira-or-the-sovereign-rule-of-:
Manuel Pereira tells of a sailor jailed under South Carolina law. F. C. Adams wrote the book in Charleston, and it appeared in 1853. Its subtitle promises views of Southern laws, life, and hospitality. The tale opens with an unlucky ship and a steward's bravery.

Storms drive the ship to Charleston, where the police take charge. Chapters move through the sheriff's office and the old jail. Manuel Pereira is committed, and the law's intricacy is laid bare. A mayor's verdict and a captain's protests move the case along. Adams wrote to expose how Carolina treated foreign sailors. His book is both a story and a legal protest.
memoir-of-the-proposed-territory-of-ariz:
Sylvester Mowry wrote a Memoir of the Proposed Territory of Arizona in 1857. Henry Polkinhorn printed it in Washington that year. Mowry signs himself as a U.S. Army man and delegate elect.

The land he treats is the Gadsden Purchase, south of the Gila River. It runs six hundred miles long and some fifty miles wide. He puts its size at some thirty thousand square miles. He argues for a port on the Gulf and for the rich silver lands near the line. Three great rivers, he claims, would sit inside the new bounds. Sales talk and survey facts blend in the delegate's case.
myths-and-legends-of-china:
E. T. C. Werner, a retired British consul at Foochow, wrote this survey. Harrap issued it in London, Bombay, and Sydney. Werner had served on China's own history bureau in Peking. The book is dated from Peking in February 1922.

Early chapters weigh Chinese society and how its myths work. P'an Ku and the creation myth come first among the tales. Gods, stars, thunder, waters, and fire each get a chapter. The Goddess of Mercy and the Eight Immortals follow. Fox legends and a godlike monkey close the set. Werner writes as a scholar who lived in China, not a tourist.
nasa-tm-19660013086-static-longitudinal-:
Odell A Morris and Gerald V Foster tested an advanced airplane shape in Langley's supersonic pressure tunnel at Mach 2.20. The shape was a V/STOL design, meant to take off and land vertically or in short distances. Two wing ideas were tried on it. One wing swept its outer panels back seventy-five degrees. The other was a skewed wing, turned at angles up to ninety degrees.

Pitching moment changed in a straight line with lift for both layouts, at modest settings. Raising the skew angle changed that behavior step by step. Such bold wings promised one aircraft for both slow lift and fast flight. Tunnel data at high speed was the first check on whether the promise could hold.
nasa-tm-19670005581-orbital-investigatio:
H. J. Buchanan and F. M. Bugg, of the Aero-Astrodynamics Laboratory at NASA's Marshall Space Flight Center, wrote this memorandum on December 1, 1966. It investigates how liquid propellant moves inside a large rocket booster. Loose liquid sloshing in a tank can disturb a vehicle's flight, so its motion matters.

The authors present experimental data on liquid hydrogen in the wide tank of an S-IVB stage. The data cover the boost phase, the moment of stage cutoff, and time in orbit. During boost, they report, the height of the sloshing liquid fell as the flight went on. Such records help designers predict and calm slosh.
nasa-tm-19680017989-vacuum-hot-pressing-:
Donald R. Rummler of Langley Research Center studied vacuum hot pressing of magnesium aluminate in this paper, presented in October 1966. Magnesium aluminate, also called spinel, is a ceramic oxide powder. Hot pressing squeezes the powder at high heat until it becomes a dense solid.

Rummler tested whether a proposed rate equation could describe the pressing process. He tracked densification across a wide range of temperatures and pressures. Below the top range, the material behaved much like other oxide systems. Above it, neither standard creep nor plastic flow models fit the observed behavior. The rate equation, treating porosity as its own variable, described the results well overall.
nasa-tm-19680027027-radar-scatterometer-:
Radar Scatterometer Data Validation is the final report of the Flight Research Projects Branch at the Manned Spacecraft Center in Houston. Dated March 29, 1968, and numbered MSC-CA-R-68-1, it checks data from a radar scatterometer. That instrument measures how strongly the ground or sea reflects radar signals at slanting angles, a clue to surface type and wind.

Chapters move from theory to the validation test procedure, then to results and discussion. Tables give rolloff functions for missions over land and over water, plus antenna pattern factors. Appendices supply reference data for many terrain types and samples of scatterometer data. Figures trace how radar return changes with wind speed over the sea.
nasa-tm-19690012889-tos-evaluation-cente:
Robert R. Golden of Goddard Space Flight Center, with Duane A. Kaeding and David E. Briggs of RCA Service Company, report TOS Evaluation Center test results for ESSA 4. Their paper, X-481-69-37, is dated January 1969. ESSA 4 was a working weather satellite, and the center tested how its command, control, and working systems had degraded in service.

The tests fall into three groups, each run under stated purpose, procedure, and results headings. Group one covers spacecraft receiver degradation after operations. It also covers pictures taken while the spacecraft sat in darkness. A third test probes how vulnerable the command system is to false or stray signals. Later groups extend the checking across further subsystems of the satellite.
nasa-tm-19700025402-csm-rendezvous-proce:
Command and service module rendezvous procedures for the G mission fill this Houston final report, number MSC-CF-P-69-11. The G mission was Apollo 11, the first landing flight. If the lunar module could not complete its own rendezvous, the command module would have to fly down and fetch the crew.

The report lays out rules, detailed step-by-step procedures for the normal mission, and a summary of command module attitudes. A long later section describes fifteen abort and rescue cases, one by one. Each case carries a one-page onboard rescue checklist, a relative motion plot, and a pad page. The cases run from partial descent burns to missed powered descent starts.
nasa-tm-19710007848-prejud-a-computer-co:
Thor T. Semler of the Lewis Research Center wrote this report on a computer code named PREJUD. The code gives a first analysis of data from two-dimensional pulse height analyzers. Such instruments count radiation events by their energy and kind.

PREJUD sorts gamma ray counts apart from neutron counts on its own. It then puts the results into a form that spectrum codes can accept. Semler details the strategy used for that separation. He also describes the smoothing methods and the curve fitting the code applies. Clean sorting at this first stage decides how much the later analysis can be trusted.
notable-women-of-modern-china:
Margaret E. Burton published Notable Women of Modern China with Fleming H. Revell in 1912. Burton had written The Education of Women in China before it. A picture shows Dr Hü King Eng at her graduation from medical college. The book costs a dollar and a quarter in the publisher's list.

That list calls the lives striking biographies, and Burton able to treat them with interest and discernment. If such women are types for a great company to follow, it says, a nation's future is assured. Her earlier book was called thrilling and revealing by the Christian Advocate. Chinese women in medicine and study stand at the centre here.
plotinus-enneads-mackenna:
Plotinus, the founder of Neoplatonism, wrote the treatises of the Enneads in the third century AD; his pupil Porphyry arranged them after his death. Stephen MacKenna's English translation, made between 1917 and 1930, is praised as a work of art in itself. The text here follows that version in five volumes.

Plotinus teaches that all things flow from the One, a source beyond being and thought. Soul descends into body and can climb back by beauty, thought, and contemplation. The 54 treatises treat the soul, the stars, providence, beauty, and the mystic union with the One. His system shaped Christian, Jewish, and Muslim theology for a thousand years.
podcast-joerogan-R9x8betNlNA:
Nature and ancient ruins humble the host in this reflective Joe Rogan Experience segment. Rogan talks about how wild places and the remains of old civilizations cut people down to size. Awe, he argues, is the proper response to deep time and raw nature.

The talk moves from forests and oceans to the stones of peoples long vanished. Rogan and his guest weigh how short a human life is against mountains and empires of dust. They ask what such humility does to a person's pride and plans. Humble and awestruck listeners get the host pondering deep time in a quieter register.
podcast-tuckercarlson-3XgusCSBtNA:
Tucker Carlson hosts debate night from Bedminster, Donald Trump's New Jersey club. Guests and friends gather to watch the candidates clash on screen. The host gives his crowd a ringside role.

Reactions come live as lines land and gaffes pile up. Carlson scores the night for viewers who trust his read. The setting adds wealth, loyalty, and spectacle to the show. The episode works as both watch party and instant analysis. It captures how a campaign night feels inside the winner's circle, among people sure of the outcome they want.
podcast-tuckercarlson-JaKuo6w9TnA:
Official stories about 9/11, the Kennedy assassination, and Gaza come under attack in this Tucker Carlson episode. Carlson argues that lies about these events serve the same goal: pushing America toward wider war, even nuclear war. The survey is dark by design, linking decades of deception.

Carlson moves case by case through the claims he says do not hold up. He asks who gains when the public accepts a false story and stops asking questions. The episode ends on his warning about escalation with Iran and Russia. Questioning viewers get the host's full charge against the war machine.
podcast-tuckercarlson-rFgLe03bVnA:
Tucker Carlson reports on how Christians are treated in the Holy Land by an Israel backed by US funds. The episode title calls the truth of it shocking. Carlson builds the report from tales on the ground.

Carlson shares cases of blocked worship, seized land, and fear among old Christian towns. He argues US cash props up the state that lets it stand. He asks why US churches stay so quiet. Listeners get a report that cuts against the grain of most US press. The library keeps the episode as a record of his stated case.
pollyanna:
Eleanor H. Porter created the most famous optimist in American fiction in Pollyanna, the story of an orphan sent to live with her stern Aunt Polly in a Vermont town. The contents lay out the machinery: Miss Polly, old Tom and Nancy, the coming of Pollyanna, the little attic room, and then the chapter simply called the Game. The game is the glad game, taught by her minister father: find something to be glad about in everything, even a pair of crutches.

Pollyanna plays it on the whole town, on the bedridden Mrs. Snow, the recluse John Pendleton, and the orphan Jimmy Bean, until an accident stops her own legs and the town must play it back to her. Porter's novel, dedicated to her cousin Belle, named an attitude for the language itself. Sentimental, engineered, and utterly effective, the book still defines the word it invented.
ramona:
Ramona, by Helen Hunt Jackson, opens at sheep-shearing time in Southern California. The scene is the ranch of the Señora Moreno. The shearing is late because her eldest son Felipe has been ill. Since his father's death Felipe has stood at the head of the house, and nothing, the Señora holds, can be done without him.

In truth, the narrator says, it is the Señora, Gonzaga Moreno, who decides everything from the sheep-pastures to the artichoke-patch, though only she knows it. Quiet and reserved, with rosary in hand, she veils an imperious, passionate nature. That nature had been tossed by the Bay of Biscay, the Gulf of Mexico, and the Pacific.
religions-of-ancient-china:
Herbert A. Giles, professor of Chinese at Cambridge, wrote this short survey for the series Religions: Ancient and Modern. Constable of London first published it in 1906. A preparer's note lists its companion volumes, on subjects from Judaism and Shinto to ancient Egypt and Islam.

Chapter one, The Ancient Faith, opens with a striking claim about Chinese thought. The problem of the universe, Giles says, never offered the slightest difficulty to Chinese philosophers. His survey then sets out their theory of how the world is ordered. Giles had also written Historic China and a history of Chinese literature, and he writes here for general readers.
strange-true-stories-of-louisiana:
George W. Cable, author of The Grandissimes and Bonaventure, published Strange True Stories of Louisiana in 1890, with illustrations. A first chapter explains how he got the tales, which he presents as true accounts drawn from old papers and memories of the state.

The contents open with The Young Aunt with White Hair. They then follow Francoise and Suzanne on an expedition down Bayou Plaquemine. Storms, robbers, and a ball follow. Partings in a place called Little Paris close their tale. Alix de Morainville gets her own section, and a life of Salome Muller, called the white slave, follows. Creole Louisiana, with its mix of French grace and hard history, fills the book.
the-awakening-of-china:
W. A. P. Martin, once president of the Chinese Imperial University, wrote a survey of China in two large parts. Martin is also named for A Cycle of Cathay and The Siege in Peking. Part one, called the empire in outline, tours China Proper province by province.

Chapters move from Kwangtung and Fukien through the river provinces to the north-west and outlying lands such as Manchuria, Mongolia, Turkestan, and Tibet. Part two gives history in outline, from early origins and a mythical period through the Three Dynasties and the house of Chou. Sages, warring states, and later dynasties carry the account toward the eighteenth century.
the-chinese-classics-prolegomena: James Legge's prolegomena to The Chinese Classics is named here as the second item in a series of his works, but only the Project Gutenberg header is present. That header carries the standard copyright warnings and notes on keeping the file for later readers.Its contents rest on the strength of the title page alone.
the-civilization-of-china:
Herbert A. Giles, Professor of Chinese at Cambridge and once a British consul at Ningpo, wrote this outline of Chinese civilization. His preface, dated Cambridge, May 12, 1911, sets a modest aim. The book sketches that civilization from the earliest times down to a present period of rapid and startling transition.

Giles wrote first for readers who know little or nothing of China, hoping to draw them toward a wider, more ordered survey. Chapter I, The Feudal Age, starts with a plain question: what does the term China mean? In its widest sense it covers Mongolia, Manchuria, Eastern Turkestan, Tibet, and the Eighteen Provinces. That whole spans some five million square miles, more than twice the size of the United States. For manners, customs, and thought, though, he narrows the field to the Chinese heartland.
the-commonwealth-of-oceana:
James Harrington's Oceana sets out his design for an ideal commonwealth, and a long introduction here gives his life first. Harrington, eldest son of Sir Sapcotes Harrington of Exton in Rutlandshire, was born in January 1611, in the reign of James I. He came five years before Shakespeare's death and was two or three years younger than John Milton.

His great-grandfather, Sir James Harrington, married Lucy, daughter of Sir William Sidney, and lived with her to their golden wedding day. Through eighteen children he counted himself, before his death, patriarch of a vast kindred. That family produced dukes, marquises, earls, viscounts, and barons by the dozen, sixteen of them Knights of the Garter. The introduction stresses the point: Oceana's designer stood close to England's chief nobility. As a child Harrington was studious and unusually sedate.
the-fight-for-the-republic-in-china: Only the old Project Gutenberg header is present here, before the book itself begins. It names The Fight for the Republic in China by B. L. Putnam Weale, and gives the book's release data. No title page, contents list, or chapter text is included in this portion, so nothing about the author's account of China can be judged from the front pages alone.
the-first-discovery-of-australia-and-new:
George Collingridge wrote this account of the first finding of Australia and New Guinea, first printed in 1906. He draws on the tales of Portuguese and Spanish voyages between 1492 and 1606 and on their old charts.

The contents run from the hunt for the Spice Islands to maps by Ribero, Desceliers, and Desliens that show a great south land. Chapters take up Villalobos, Mendana's finds in the Solomons, Queiroz, and Torres. Pictures of Prince Henry, Magellan, and old ships fill the front. Collingridge argues that Iberian sailors charted these coasts long before the Dutch or English came.
the-gentleman-from-indiana:
Booth Tarkington wrote The Gentleman from Indiana as a novel of a young editor in a flat-land Indiana town. John Harkless stands at the center from the first chapter.

Tarkington opens on the level fields of Indiana, bleak with mud and snow in winter and hot and dusty in summer, where small frame stations stand far apart. Into such a town comes Harkless to run a paper and stay. Chapters bring a strange lady, a court-house bell, a rescue, and a treachery by a man named Fisbee. Tarkington draws small-town pride, rough politics, and a young man's fight to be both firm and kind.
the-girl-from-montana: Grace Livingston Hill wrote The Girl from Montana. Grosset and Dunlap printed it in New York, dated 1922. Only front matter is present here. It gives the title page and a long list of other books by Hill. That list names April Gold and The Beloved Stranger. It names The Honor Girl, Kerry, Marigold, and Crimson Roses. It also names The Mystery of Mary and A Girl to Come Home To. No chapter text is present. Nothing about the plot of this novel can be told from what is here.
the-naval-war-of-1812-or-the-history-of-:
Theodore Roosevelt's The Naval War of 1812 is present here only in front matter from a later edition, so Roosevelt's history itself does not appear. The full title adds an account of the Battle of New Orleans. An introduction by Edward K. Eckert is announced on the title page, though its text is not among the pages shown.

What the pages do show is a list of illustrations. Captain Isaac Hull and three views of the Constitution fighting the Guerriere open it. The Wasp against the Frolic, Captains Decatur, Bainbridge, and Lawrence, the Chesapeake against the Shannon, the Battle of Lake Erie, and the Essex follow. A contents list promises only illustrations and an index by name.
the-pioneers-or-the-sources-of-the-susqu:
J. Fenimore Cooper's The Pioneers, or The Sources of the Susquehanna, is introduced as a descriptive tale. Cooper warns that he mixed literal fact with a general picture of the country. Scenes and characters familiar from his own youth tempted him toward what he had known. He might otherwise have imagined more freely. The county, he notes, can only be Otsego, and the lake only the source of the Susquehanna.

His short history of the district follows Otsego from its days inside Albany County, through Montgomery, to county status shortly after the peace of 1783. The lake sits among low spurs of the Alleghanies, on some of the highest land in New York. Settlers' manners, the face of the country, and its climate are all described from the author's own recollections. He offers those memories as his apology for their detail.
the-problem-of-china: Bertrand Russell's The Problem of China was first published in 1922; the copy described is a 1966 second impression. Its epigraph retells Chuang Tze's parable of Chaos, whose well-meaning friends bored him seven orifices and killed him. Chapter I, Questions, begins with a receptive European newly arrived in China facing puzzling questions. Only the title pages, epigraph, and the chapter's first lines are present in the pages at hand, so Russell's argument is not yet under way.
the-tragedy-of-st-helena:
Sir Walter Runciman's Tragedy of St. Helena, published by T. Fisher Unwin in 1911, opens with a sailors' song: 'Oh! Boney was ill-treated.' Runciman, a seaman himself, once held anti-Napoleonic ideas, yet the chant impressed him. Years later, on a bookstall before a long voyage, he bought Scott's Life of Napoleon meaning to have his opinion confirmed. Careful reading convinced him instead that Boney was ill-treated, and that Scott had collected evidence to exonerate the English government.

That reversal launched Runciman's own study of Napoleon's exile. He writes as a sailor judging landsmen's treatment of a prisoner, with sympathy from forecastle songs. Readers interested in the St. Helena controversy get an unusual witness: a merchant seaman turned baronet arguing that England shamed itself over its captive emperor.
the-two-gentlemen-of-verona: Shakespeare's Two Gentlemen of Verona is named by this record, but the pages present again carry Michael S. Hart's general editor's note on old printing errors, the same note found before several other plays in this set. It explains cliches of type, exchanged u and v, and scholars' reverence for the old spellings. The note closes by presenting 'the first Part of Henry the Sixt,' which is not this play at all, a plain mismatch. No Valentine, Proteus, or line of the comedy appears in what is shown.
their-mariposa-legend-a-romance-of-santa:
Charlotte Herr opens Their Mariposa Legend, a romance of Santa Catalina, in a mythic island spring. She dedicates the book to little Bruce Parker, who loved stories. Centuries ago, rain brought spring to Punagwandah, fairest of the Channel Islands. Lilac bloomed on steep hillsides above a radiant sea. Larks sang while lilies filled shadowed canyon niches with light. Princess Wildenai watched the dawn from her cavern bower.

Wildenai was the sweetest blossom of that spring, Herr writes. She was loveliest among the Mariposa maidens and of royal blood. Chief Torquam, sleeping below on the beach, knew more of her birth than he told. Legend, romance, and California island scenery blend here. Herr also wrote The Wise Mamma Goose for children.
tomlinsoniana:
Edward Bulwer-Lytton presents the posthumous writings of Augustus Tomlinson, celebrated professor of moral philosophy at an unnamed university. The writings comprise maxims on creating, illustrated by ten characters, and a second part of critical, sentimental, and moral essays called Brachylogia. An introduction recounts the editor's German travels.

At Tomlinson's university he learned the professor died in early 1822 after a lingering illness, still discussing ethical philosophy on his deathbed. universite-de-paris-faculte-de-theologie: Paris printers issued this censure by the Faculty of Theology of the University of Paris in 1784. The printer Alexandre Jombert the younger sold it on the rue Dauphine, with royal approval. The pages present here are the Latin and French title pages only, in rough old type.
